title: City of Cambridge Outlines Property Owners' Responsibilities
author: Lily Tierney
content:
City of Cambridge outlines property owners' responsibilities

 September 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 424
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Cambridge officials have created a document outlining the responsibilities of residents to help clarify what property owners must take care of versus what falls to the city, a merchant or a utility company.Officials decided to create this document because of increasing code enforcement issues within the past year that caused city staff to spend more of their time handing out citations and going to look at properties.
At a meeting in June, City Manager Glenn Steckman said Cambridge was stepping up its code enforcement as trash cans are increasingly left on the sidewalk, grass is going uncut and cars are parked in the wrong direction.
"There seems to be a lack of lawnmowers in our community because the grass and grass height has been an ongoing issue in the town, and we're having to send violation notices out," Steckman said.
Per the document released this month, property owners are responsible for the following:
Maintaining the weatherhead, the cap where the service line meets the building.Maintaining wiring from the weatherhead to the meter, and from the meter into the building.Maintaining and marking privately owned underground lines such as pet fences, sprinklers and outbuildings.Maintaining all piping from the outlet side of the gas meter through the building.Performing annual checks of gas line connections.Maintaining clean access points for plumbers.Maintaining the sewer service line from property line to building.Maintaining all plumbing within the building.Preventing unauthorized stormwater connections like sump pumps and downspouts.Maintaining sidewalks, driveways, aprons, sod, and ensuring they are safe for public use.Removing snow from sidewalks within 36 hours after snowfall.Trimming trees and shrubs so they don't obstruct sidewalks. Must have seven-foot clearance on sidewalks or 12-foot clearance on streets.Immediately removing animal excrement from sidewalks, streets, parks or other public places unless physically unable.Maintaining the water service line from the curb stop to the building.Maintaining plumbing inside meter pits and within the building.Installing and maintaining a Pressure Reducing Valve (PRV) if required.Keeping the water pit visible and maintaining plumbing inside it.Keeping weeds, grass, and vegetation under 6 inches.Keeping property free of litter, refuse, and unsightly growth.
The city is responsible for the following:
Maintaining, repairing, operating public sewer mains under streets and public areas.Repairing and maintaining curbs, gutters, streets.Maintaining water mains.Maintaining service line up to curb stop.If a water meter is in an outdoor pit the city owns and maintains the meter and the pit.
The utility companies are responsible for the following:
Maintaining meters and transformers on property that are part of the utility system.Servicing lines from pole to weatherhead.Maintaining all equipment and piping up to and including the gas meter.

title: Dorchester Council Talks Juvenile Crime, Other Priorities with State Legislators
author: Konner Metz
content:
Dorchester council talks juvenile crime, other priorities with state legislators

 September 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Dorchester 
 
 643
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Dorchester County Council members provided a number of requests to local legislators on Tuesday in advance of the 2026 General Assembly, including an ask to tighten up on juvenile crime.During an annual meeting outlining the county's goals for statewide legislation this winter, Eastern Shore delegates and senators weighed in on the logistics of potential bills the county would like to see offered.
Del. Sheree Sample-Hughes (D-Dorchester, Wicomico) acknowledged the request for more stringent laws on juvenile crime. She noted that she and others are looking to see what comes out of the state's juvenile reform commission, which was created last year.
"I hear you loud and clear and know that there's something needs to be done," Sample-Hughes said. "But I think we're in the trenches of trying to figure out what is in this task force."
Youth crime in Cambridge has raised concerns in recent weeks, especially from Dorchester County Sheriff Jimmy Phillips. On the second day of school at Cambridge-South Dorchester High School, two students were arrested after assaulting the school safety monitor.
Sample-Hughes noted that last winter, a failed piece of legislation would have increased the age minimum from 14 to 16 for a juvenile to be tried as an adult. County Council Vice President Mike Detmer said it should go the other way, if anything.
That legislation even being proposed last year is a sign that "the well's gonna be poisoned" for any commission or task force recommendations, Detmer said.
"This is not hypothetical. This is reality that unfolds weekly in our town," Detmer said. "And it's a hazard to people around and it's a hazard to them."
Council Member Ricky Travers said state youth justice laws are "setting up a whole group of juveniles for failure."
Meanwhile, Council President Lenny Pfeffer said the county's warden has raised concern about separation requirements between juvenile and adult inmates.
"Our facility, being limited on staff, and size and logistics, sometimes finds it difficult to house a juvenile," Pfeffer said. "We have to sometimes bring in additional personnel above the normal shift size."
Pfeffer said it's a "one size fits all" conundrum, where the rural and small Dorchester County can't as easily comply with state regulations.
For his part, Detmer said he's "increasingly concerned about the legislature's encroachment on local control," noting he doesn't think the Eastern Shore legislators are responsible.
"We need to have something where there can be more nuance with blanket laws," Detmer said.
WORKERS' COMP
Pfeffer said the county is bound by state law to pay out equal workers' compensations to all fire service volunteers, whether they perform on-duty or administrative roles. He asked if there's a way for state law to be adjusted so those working in purely administrative roles, and with less risk of workplace injury, could be classified differently.
Del. Christopher T. Adams (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) addressed the council's request. He warned that a workers' comp bill won't be easy. He added that it's important the county doesn't get caught reducing workers' comp for someone who may switch between field service and office work.
"Don't get mixed up in these scenarios where you have an audit and/or you have a person that does clerical work on Monday through Wednesday, but then ends up on a fire call Thursday or Friday and then gets hurt," Adams said.
Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) asked council members to take a look at workers' compensation laws that other counties are bound by to see if there's something that could work.
Other potential legislation discussed by the County Council and state legislators on Tuesday included:
Outlawing the use of shoulders to pass vehicles in left-turn lanes. Dorchester County Sheriff's Office Sgt. Robbie Larimer said there's been accident concerns.Reducing or removing the requirements for the county to advertise leases in newspapers. Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) said he's tried to see through a bill on the matter multiple times, though it's never passed.

title: Dorchester County Council to Submit Five Legislative Initiatives
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Dorchester County Council to submit five legislative initiatives

 June 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 379
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Dorchester County Council Members are planning to submit five recommendations for the Maryland Association of County's 2026 legislative initiatives.MACo will select four initiatives based on feedback and suggestions from Maryland's county jurisdictions and Baltimore City to prioritize during the state's General Assembly beginning in January.
MACo's 2025 initiatives focused on local revenue structures, infrastructural funding, the Blueprint for Maryland's Future and clean energy. Dorchester County's recommendations for 2026 do not differ too much.
The Dorchester County Council's five recommendations are:
To consider a pause or suspension of the Blueprint for Maryland's Future education plan to allow counties to catch up financially.To rethink or review existing rules or policies that override local control over energy regulations.To improve infrastructure related to transportation and water drainage in Dorchester County.To introduce an initiative regarding safety concerns of solar battery storage and concerns regarding the sufficiency of the decommissioning bond that covers the cost of removing solar infrastructure once it's no longer in use.To continue to reform juvenile justice. This recommendation came after a 15-year-old resident shot and killed another resident in the 900 block of Cornelia Street on June 8.
County Council Vice President Mike Detmer said juvenile justice laws need serious reformation to make Dorchester County a safer place.
"Whether you're below 18 or over 18, you have to get some feedback for your actions," Detmer said. "Your terrible actions aren't in a vacuum; we all live here."
The purpose of MACo's recommended initiatives is to address problems counties are facing with state legislators. County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said the organization collects concerns and information from counties to assist them in navigating the legislative process at the General Assembly.
Detmer said that these initiatives don't always align with Dorchester County due to the county's unique set of problems, and this misalignment has caused some tension with the state. "You know, things are complicated," he said. "I would say the tension really stems from the policies and laws that the state is enacting."
Elected officials from Maryland's 23 counties and Baltimore City can submit legislative proposal initiatives on behalf of the county as an elected body, generally at an open meeting or via a voting process, or not on behalf of the county, but as an individual.
Nominations can be submitted online through June 27 on the MACo website.

title: Cambridge steps up code enforcement
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Cambridge steps up code enforcement

 June 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: News

 CAMBRIDGE — City Manager Glenn Steckman said Cambridge is stepping up its code enforcement as trash cans are increasingly left on the sidewalk, grass is going uncut and cars are parked in the wrong direction."There seems to be a lack of lawnmowers in our community because the grass and grass height has been an ongoing issue in the town, and we're having to send violation notices out," Steckman said.
Code enforcement is a process used by local governments to enforce state and local laws, codes or ordinances regarding housing, building and health standards. The city's stepped-up code enforcement efforts became a topic of discussion at the Cambridge City County's meeting Monday after a resident raised concerns and confusion.
Cambridge resident Sharon Wilson was fined $200 due to a partially knocked down brick wall on her property. Wilson presented images of the fallen wall to the City Council, saying she feels zoning codes are being enforced unfairly.
Wilson said a city staff member stopped by her property asking her to clean up the bricks.
"They told me I had to clean it up, and he said, 'You cleaned it, but you didn't clean it up enough.' OK, so what is enough for you?" Wilson said.
She continued to address the council asking if this is something they do for all city residents.
"I said that's a lie. You're not fair," Wilson said. "Because if you're being fair you'd be going to the city limits checking all the properties."
Wilson said she "was shocked" when she drove around the city to look at the properties and saw many that were "more of hazard" than hers.
"We want to make sure she understands that she is not being picked on," Steckman said. "That this is not just her issue, this is a Cambridge issue."
He said that the city has received a growing number of code-related complaints, which is why the city is sending out more citations than in previous years.
Steckman said the city has sent out a notice to residents outlining the city's code standards and plans to send another one soon.

title: Civility on Easton Town Council

 Don Abbatielo has served on the Town Council representing Ward 2 for four years. During that time when the council presidency was open, his fellow council members voted him unanimously to be the interim president. He is intelligent, thoughtful, well versed in town issues, and, perhaps most important, listens respectfully to those who serve with him on the council and also to those bringing concerns to the council.He brings civility to a difficult job.
At the time, he did not run for president of the Town Council, as he was very busy with his family. Now he is ready to take on the extra work. His fellow council members are still supporting him for president. They are not supporting the present president of the council who is running again.
Don has been a high school teacher for 27 years in Dorchester schools and a volunteer firefighter for the Easton Volunteer Fire Department, where he rose in the ranks to become president of the fire department.
After knocking on a lot of doors and talking to groups, Don enumerated at a meet and greet what people care the most about and how he plans to deal with these concerns.

There are not enough doctors here to serve not only Talbot County but also surrounding counties whose residents come to our Memorial Hospital. He will ask University of Maryland Medical System and Anne Arundel Medical Center, what they are doing today to promote doctors to come to Easton.Finally, he also listed issues such as traffic; search for qualified candidates for Easton Police Department; and promotion of the new Easton Volunteer Fire Department training facility.Last but not least, civility on the Town Council, is high on his list.

title: Proposed Resolution Sets Off Tense Discussion at Cambridge Meeting
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Proposed resolution sets off tense discussion at Cambridge meeting

 April 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 470

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Tensions flared at the April 14 Cambridge City Council meeting over a proposed resolution directing the city manager to analyze the city's human resources capabilities and follow a specific process when hiring staff.The resolution was ultimately tabled.
Commissioner Frank Stout, who brought the resolution to the council, said he saw the resolution as a way to standardize the hiring process and ensure the city completes a broad search for job candidates, citing previous meeting discussions on the topic.
City Manager Glenn Steckman said he was not consulted about the resolution before it was sent to him. He said much of what is outlined in the resolution is already part of the city's process.
"I will tell you, I'm not real happy about this," he said. "It has bothered me through the weekend. And I appreciate the commissioners that hired me. They know about my experience."
Steckman was hired prior to the city's November election, after which several new faces were added to the council.
Bringing up part of the resolution that encourages the city manager to "expand recruitment efforts beyond internal applicants to include external candidates," Steckman said he's heard from city staff that they think the council wants to take opportunities away from them.
He said with most organizations, including the city, there is a five-day window where employees can apply to a job posting before the posting is made public. After the five days, management can make a decision about whether to expand the search externally, Steckman said.
"I'm not exactly sure why I need a resolution to tell me what I already know how to do," he said.
Stout said he sees the resolution as a way to "put words around" what the council had discussed in previous meetings.
"I don't want there to be anything misconstrued that I don't have full faith and confidence in city staff," he said.
Commissioner Brian Roche agreed with Stout's resolution, saying none of the language was "detrimental" and it just put into words what the council said it wanted to see.
Before calling on the commissioners to make a motion to table the resolution indefinitely, Mayor Lajan Cephas cut off discussion and spoke about the value of city employees.
As she spoke, Stout asked her to "please" not "steer" the discussion "in a different direction," and Cephas responded, "I didn't interrupt you when you were speaking, so can you please provide me the same respect?"
After talking about the importance of having opportunities for promotion in a workplace, Cephas said although she doesn't have a vote in council matters, she has a voice.
"I'm going to stand up for city employees every single time," she said.
Not long after Cephas' comments, the council opted in a 3-2 vote to table the resolution until after June 30, which will mark the end of the budget process. Stout and Roche voted against the motion.

title: Southern Dorchester Residents Share Thoughts on Town Incorporation
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Southern Dorchester residents share thoughts on town incorporation

 March 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 646
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WINGATE — Lifelong Dorchester County resident Dick Dawson thought the Lakes and Straits Volunteer Fire Company hall in Wingate on March 3 was busier than he's seen in 45 years, apart from luncheons and dinners."That tells you something," he said at the outset of a meeting at the fire hall to discuss efforts to incorporate a new town in the southern part of the county.
Dawson, his 17-year-old grandson Drew Dawson and Elijah's General Store owner David Beverley are working to incorporate Blackwater, a new town, in an effort to protect southern Dorchester County communities from disappearing due to sea level rise and state critical area regulations.
The communities included in the plan for Blackwater are Andrews, Robbins, Wesley, Lakesville, Crapo, Wingate, Toddville, Bishops Head and Crocheron. Each community would still exist within the new town. The planners believe incorporation would give the area a better chance of receiving funding from government agencies.
March 3, the planners shared their vision and heard from residents of the communities that Blackwater would encompass. Residents raised concerns about taxes, money management, residency requirements and the incorporation process. With multiple residents in the room opposed to the idea, tension ebbed and flowed throughout the meeting.
During a tense portion, with some residents visibly upset and yelling, Chuckie Hayward said he was tired of the "bickering." He said although he's against the idea to incorporate, he came to listen.
"I'm here because I want to hear everything out first before I really make a decision," he said.
Many residents shared concerns with having to pay taxes to the town. The Dawsons and Beverley have said the town would not impose new taxes.
Drew Dawson said 60% of residents would have to vote in favor of being taxed in order for the town to impose taxes. He said he doesn't see that happening.
County resident Matt Ritter said taxes often arise when communities experience growth.
"Once you allow building and allow all this excess to happen, growth comes down here and this becomes just like Cambridge," he said. "And then you've got all these city folk down here trying to change things up. And they always raise their hand to raise the taxes."
Former Cambridge Mayor Andrew Bradshaw, who shared his understanding of municipalities at the meeting, said the town would be able to secure federal and state funding that is only open to municipalities.
"If you all can get the kind of representation this would provide, it gives a force behind the effort that just doesn't exist right now," Bradshaw said.
In order for Blackwater to get incorporated, the planners need to gather signatures on a petition, then go to the county to submit the drafted town charter for review. If the county accepts the charter, the decision will go to the registered voters within the area that Blackwater would encompass.
Resident Scott Hughes spoke about the importance of forming the town the right way and having a "bulletproof" charter. He said he expects the push to create Blackwater will be a success.
"But let's make it happen so that nobody can take advantage of it," he said.
Lindsay Wheatley said she sees three options for the communities: Sell all the land to sika deer hunters who want to strip away houses and put up deer stands, stay and not do anything as roads and the area's heritage crumble, or fight.
"This might be our only opportunity ever," she said. "We're dwindling. Look around, right? I chose to come back here because I love it, and all of you love it too. I'm going to fight. I'm going to sign it. I'm going to do everything that I can do with integrity and honesty to protect this area for as long as I can."
Drew Dawson said he and the other planners will discuss the ideas raised during the meeting and decide how to amend the draft charter.
"I think there are some pretty good ideas," he said.

title: Six Months into the Job, Cambridge City Manager Says He's Ready to Tackle City's Challenges
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Six months into the job, Cambridge city manager says he'r ready to tackle city's challenges

 February 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 624
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Cambridge City Manager Glenn Steckman likes a challenge."I've dealt with cities on the verge of bankruptcy and cities going into bankruptcy," he said.
Although Cambridge is not on the verge of bankruptcy, the city does face challenges when it comes to housing, communication and certain delayed projects, Steckman said, mentioning the Cambridge Harbor project and the old city hall renovation project.
"That's sat vacant now for almost 18 years," he said about the old city hall, "and the cost of the project has doubled in those 18 years."
Nearly six months into the job, Steckman is working with his team to tackle these issues, which he knows can't be solved in a day.
"It's a process," he said. "No community gets into facing their challenge in a year, and it takes years to address a community challenge."
Ten years from now, Steckman would like to see better housing for residents, general improvements made that the city can afford to maintain and the Cambridge Harbor project at or near completion.
When it comes to housing, Steckman said improvements are already being made, but it's going to take time.
"But I also think there are a lot of people that I have interacted with that are committed to that," he said. "And I would like to see stronger collaboration with the area organizations so we're all rowing in the same direction."
Collaboration is important to Steckman, although he acknowledges it's not always easy.
"I think the challenge in any community is sometimes there are personalities and people who may have felt excluded, people that might have been hurt," he said. "How do we speak with them and look at their conditions and address them. But in any community, there are some very strong personalities, and Cambridge is no different."
Steckman said it's not realistic to ask for everyone to "sing by the same song sheet."
"But how do we work better together?" he asked.
Cambridge Mayor Lajan Cephas said Steckman has made an effort to work with the many different communities within Cambridge, from the Black community to the Hispanic community to the senior community to different neighborhoods.
"When you seek different perspectives, it always gives the best outcome," Cephas said. "Even myself as a Black woman. If I just go about my day every day from the perspective of a Black woman, I'm going to miss some things. So that's why it's always important to have a diverse staff, a diverse group of people that you can rely on to get information from."
Starting this Saturday, Feb. 15, Steckman will be at City Hall from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. one or two Saturdays per month to speak with any residents who aren't able to see him during the normal week day. Steckman has also made it easier for residents to come to City Hall by making it so they don't need to be buzzed in at the door. The city has also put in a railing and an automatic door opener for accessibility at City Hall.
"Because I try to maintain an open door policy," he said about the changes. "But I want to talk with people. ... I'm not a huge fan of just emails back and forth."
Born and raised in Baltimore, with experience serving on the Ocean City Council and a career spent managing cities as far away as Alaska, Steckman is no stranger to Maryland nor city management. In his free time, along with spending time with his wife and their two dogs, Steckman enjoys reading.
He said it's important to read about what's going on not only in his community, but in surrounding communities.
"We are not some little isolated community," he said. "And sometimes people in other communities have very good ideas that maybe we can export here or modify what they're doing."

title: Dorchester Burial Sites Preservation Board gets another chance
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Dorchester Burial Sites Preservation Board gets another chance

 January 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 717
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — A board designed to help preserve grave sites in Dorchester County has one year to prove it is able to accomplish its mission or it will face dissolution.After holding a public hearing about repealing a chapter of the county code regarding burial sites preservation, the Dorchester County Council agreed Jan. 21 to keep the chapter — which includes the Burial Sites Preservation Board established within it — for a test period.
"A one-year test from today to see what you can accomplish and see if it is a worthy board to have within this county," Council Member Ricky Travers said before making the motion.
Throughout the public hearing and following discussion, council members brought up concerns of past problems with the board's participation and its ability to work cohesively. Council President Lenny Pfeffer said that in the one-year test period, the board would need to prove it can fill its seats and provide a quorum at its meetings.
Travers said board members would need to work together, not against each other as has been the case in the past.
"As passionate as people might be about grave sites, ... we cannot have this controversy," Travers said. "So whomever comes on that board needs to be willing and ready to work side-by-side."
County Planning and Zoning Director Susan Webb said the Maryland Historical Trust is the state's enforcing entity regarding burial sites preservation.
"And we were basically duplicating the effort," she said. "While this may be a good board for a nonprofit, being under the county's umbrella, I don't think it's working out."
Dorothy Samonisky, the chair of the Burial Sites Preservation Board, said the Maryland Historical Trust only gives guidance and does not "act as an arm of the law" like the county can.
"So right now, this burial site preservation is the only thing that gives you as county members anything to stand on if there is an incident with a grave site."
Pfeffer clarified that the board is an advisory group to the council.
Samonisky said people have been buried in Dorchester County since 1669, and many of those burial sites are on private property. She said the policy in county code gives the county the authority to "act upon destruction of those cemeteries."
Ashley Samonisky, who also spoke during public comment, said the board can guide council actions and help with outreach and education. She said there needs to be something in the code that addresses what happens if a person "maliciously destroy(s) a property or (tries) to hide the fact that it was there," in order to build a beach house, for example.
"There needs to be fines," she said. "There needs to be penalties up to and including the cost of restoring it to the pre-demolition stage. These are just a few ideas that this body can help with."
Dorothy Samonisky acknowledged that there were "internal conflicts" between several board members at one point. She said she also was out due to two major surgeries in 2024.
"We had met up through '23 and had things on the agenda and topics to discuss," she said.
Council Vice President Mike Detmer, who ultimately voted in favor of the board having a one-year test period, said he thinks the board has value, but would function better if not affiliated with the county.
"It being a law and having to be constituted a certain way and done a certain way is holding an effort to preserve burial sites back," he said, later adding, "I think it could be more flexible and more dynamic as a stand-alone."
Detmer said as long as he is on the council, if someone comes to the council with "a salient point" about something in the county, it will get attention. That doesn't require a board, he said.
Before the council unanimously agreed to give the board a test period, Travers said the board had previously gone through an "extremely adversary" time that got to the point where some board members felt unsafe coming to the meetings. He said the county practically had to act as a referee.
"And that's not what we need on our boards," he said.
Pfeffer warned the this can't happen again.
"The last board that was assembled ... had brought things to this chamber," he said. "Had brought thoughts of slander. Had brought disagreements. I will not allow that to happen during these meetings."

title: Cambridge Mayor, Council Sworn in for Four-Year Terms
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge mayor, council sworn in for four-year terms

 January 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 502
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — As she spoke of goals to unite the city and stimulate economic development, Mayor Lajan Cephas made the Cambridge City Council meeting and swearing in ceremony a little more interactive for residents than the average City Council meeting.As part of her speech at the end of the meeting — which took place at the Elks Lodge on Pine Street on Monday — Cephas asked the audience to vote on a resolution to return Cambridge to the "innovative, industrial hub" of the Eastern Shore that it once was.
After voices of residents saying "aye" filled the room in response to the figurative resolution, Cephas responded, "the motion carries," signaling the city's next era of leadership.
"Where we are in this process is it's going to take all of us to create this 'one Cambridge,' united, abandoning differences," Cephas said. "And with this vision backed by faith, we will stimulate a living, economic workforce development, which will increase our tax base, providing the highest level of city services for residents and businesses while providing the most legacy outcomes for our youth, our elderly and also families."
Cephas and Cambridge commissioners Brett Summers, Shay Lewis-Sisco, Frank Stout, Sputty Cephas and Brian Roche were all sworn in that evening by Dorchester County Circuit Court Clerk Amy Craig. Claps and cheers from residents resounded through the Elks Lodge as each elected official was sworn into their four-year term.
Once sworn in, the new council unanimously elected Sputty Cephas, the Ward 4 commissioner, as commission president. This decision makes Cambridge's highest elected leadership — mayor and commission president — a pair of siblings.
After thanking his fellow commissioners for their vote of confidence, Sputty Cephas spoke about the importance of continuing to move forward as a city. He said that it will take "a collective effort" from all residents, including the youth and elderly, and called on those in the audience to look at their neighbors and say, "We need you."
"The only way this works, is if each and every one of you play your part," he said.
This was not the first rodeo for three of the five commissioners on stage that night. Sputty Cephas, Roche and Stout have all taken the oath of office before.
Roche, who represents Ward 5, and Cephas were re-elected to their positions in the city's October election. Stout, who represents Ward 3, served as the Ward 3 commissioner from 2008 through 2012.
Toward the end of the meeting, each commissioner spoke. Many of them thanked residents and reflected on their campaigns.
"I look forward to working on a lot of issues that I identified during the campaign," said Summers, who represents Ward 1. "And I look forward to working with my fellow commissioners and mayor on these issues."
Lewis-Sisco, who represents Ward 2, told residents that, in her new role, she will welcome their ideas, suggestions and expertise.
"Our city is not perfect," she said. "But what I do believe firmly is that when we come together and we unite as one, we can actually see our city progress."

title: Legislators Hear Cambridge's Priorities Before General Assembly Session Begins
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Legislators hear Cambridge's priorities before General Assembly session begins

 December 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 580
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Before the regularly scheduled Cambridge City Council meeting on Dec. 9, the council and city staff shared their priorities with state legislators, who are preparing to go back to Annapolis for the 447th session of the Maryland General Assembly.During the legislative delegation work session, Cambridge City Manager Glenn Steckman acknowledged getting state funding this year will be difficult and asked that the Lower Shore delegation notify the city if they come across anything during session that could benefit Cambridge.
Steckman said the city doesn't have a list of laws or law changes that it wants enacted by the General Assembly.
"We're not here to try to make laws and recommend the law changes, but to show you what the issues that the elected leadership here is dealing with and the appointed staff is dealing with," he said. "We're looking for your help and guidance on the legislative level."
The six priorities — which Steckman detailed during the meeting and said are in no particular order — are to:
Preserve and renovate Cambridge's historic City Hall on Gay Street.Continue to move the Cambridge Harbor project forward.Improve housing and revitalize the Pine Street neighborhood.Make enhancements and improvements to city youth services.Update and improve the city's water and sewer infrastructure.Provide local workforce development programs and opportunities.
Steckman said when it comes to workforce development, it can be difficult for residents without transportation who are seeking employment or training opportunities in other counties.
"Obviously, if we want to grow the industrial part of the economy or (the) commercial (part), we need more job training to prepare, not only our existing workforce, but our workforce coming up through the school system," he said.
After Steckman discussed the city's priorities, Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), Del. Sheree Sample-Hughes (D-Dorchester, Wicomico), Del. Chris Adams (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) all chimed in.
Hutchinson said he sees improving youth services as a very important priority, referencing a local teen who had been detained by the Department of Juvenile Services for stealing a car.
"This is a really serious issue," Hutchinson said. "If we have children who are saying, 'I'm bored and it's fine,' then we really need to work on that and correct that."
Sample-Hughes said that some of the bills on rentals and housing that didn't get passed during last year's session could come back to the General Assembly this year. She said it would be useful for the city to keep in touch as the legislators hear these bills brought back.
"I think your on the ground insight is very beneficial to what we have to do when it comes to the policy work and not only just the financial side of things," she said.
Adams told the council this year will be a "budget year." The state faces a predicted $2.7 billion budget deficit in fiscal year 2026.
"We know that this is going to be a tough year," Adams said. "So legislative requests that revolve around funding capital projects are going to be tough. There is always bond money, and we as a delegation will surely do our part ... in submitting those requests."
Mautz asked that the council stay in touch with the Lower Shore delegation throughout the upcoming legislative session. He said that when the governor's budget comes out, the city should make sure there aren't cuts that will negatively affect the city.
"If there's an actual cut that's going to affect something in the City of Cambridge, somebody needs to call (us)," he said.

title: Lajan Cephas Elected Cambridge's Next Mayor
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Lajan Cephas elected Cambridge's next mayor

 December 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 1027
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — After months of campaigning in a close election that stirred up controversies and got voters talking, Cambridge Commission President Lajan Cephas has been elected the city's mayor.Tuesday night, Cephas secured 53% of the vote, or 787 votes, in a run-off election against former Cambridge Mayor Andrew Bradshaw, who received 47% of the vote with 697 votes. There were 1,484 ballots counted in the election. Assistant City Manager Brandon Hesson told the Star Democrat Tuesday that there are 9,183 active, registered voters in Cambridge.
Cephas said she knew it would be a tight race.
"But I'm truly excited that the majority of the voters, that they've decided that they're happy with the direction the city is going and they want to see four more years of this," she said. "So it's my commitment to make sure these projects (get done) and to also make sure our neighborhoods are improved at the highest level."
A HEATED ELECTIONFrom past criminal charges to residency requirements to campaigning practices, the race gave voters a lot to talk about.
Bradshaw's bid for mayor came a little over two and a half years after he resigned from the position. He resigned after he was charged with 50 counts of distributing revenge porn on Reddit. He later pleaded guilty to five of those counts.
In August, Bradshaw told the Star Democrat he wanted to keep the focus of his 2024 campaign on where Cambridge is currently and where it is going, rather than on his past legal issues. He said he thought voters felt the same way.
During a Cambridge candidate forum conducted by the League of Women Voters in early October, Cephas questioned whether people would feel comfortable associating with a mayor known for an "embarrassing" national headline.
At the forum, Bradshaw said that in a city where many people have made mistakes, a large portion of the population shouldn't be disqualified from serving the city because of the "errors of their past." He said his convictions were withdrawn and removed by the state and his probation has been abated.
According to court documents, a judge ordered in November 2023 that the judgements of guilt for Bradshaw's five counts of distributing revenge porn be stricken and Bradshaw be granted probation before judgement.
Bradshaw wasn't the only candidate who has received criminal charges. In 2022, Cephas was charged with second-degree assault in connection with a domestic violence incident in her Cambridge home. The charges were dismissed in January 2023.
Along with past legal controversies, questions regarding candidate residency were also brought up as the two candidates vied for the open seat.
At a City Council meeting Sept. 9, one resident brought up the importance of verifying candidate applications. In response, Assistant City Manager Brandon Hesson said city staff has heard rumors regarding applicants and their residency, but no formal complaints had been filed. He encouraged residents to submit formal complaints so they could be looked into.
The issue was also mentioned during a peace order hearing in early October between family members of the mayoral candidates.
At the hearing, Lejan Cephas' brother Cambridge Commissioner Sputty Cephas, who was running for reelection at the time, was denied a final peace order against Bradshaw's wife, Natalee Bradshaw. Sputty Cephas said he filed the peace order after he noticed Natalee Bradshaw following him around the city one evening.
During the hearing, Natalee Bradshaw's attorney Philip Cronan brought up statements that have been made questioning whether Sputty and/or Lajan Cephas are following the city's residency requirements for candidates. In an interview, Andrew Bradshaw alleged Lajan Cephas has not been residing at the Cambridge address on her application. Lajan Cephas told the Star Democrat she has met every requirement to be a candidate in the city's election.
Cambridge residents also raised concerns regarding campaigning practices in the mayoral election. Last week at a Cambridge City Council meeting, residents brought up concerns with candidates door knocking in apartment complexes where elderly people and people with disabilities live. In a letter partially read at the meeting, resident GeriLeigh Farrow called out Cephas and her campaign for door knocking at Conifer Village at Cambridge, an apartment complex for seniors.
Cephas responded to the comments made at the meeting, noting that she had invites to two apartment buildings for meet and greets. She said canvassing is not illegal.
"And I just really find it a shame that we have other people who are trying to say that (canvassing is) being used to take advantage when we're trying to engage," she said during the meeting.
THE NEXT FOUR YEARSCephas said she is excited and "ready to work."
"What I'm most looking forward to are the residents," she said, adding that on the campaign trail, she was made aware of many concerns from residents.
Cephas said she is excited to follow up with those residents and help get their concerns addressed.
Bradshaw said he reached out to Cephas Tuesday night to congratulate her. He said he hopes Cephas will find a way to move the city forward.
"If that's not the case, then in four years, the voters will get the opportunity to make different choices," he said.
Bradshaw said he is "not giving any thought" to whether he will run in four years. He said he wants his supporters to know that although the campaign was a rough one, he tried to run it as clean as he could.
"And in spite of the loss, I feel a lot of pride that we tried to avoid going into the gutter," he said. "And that I think that though we didn't get the result that we expected or wanted to see, that we can have pride in trying to have been the best that we could as competitors, and as a candidate and as a movement or a campaign."
Cephas said this win means that the networks that have been built in the city can be made "even stronger." She brought up the idea of forming partnerships with the school system in an effort to support the city's youth.
"And economic development falls under that," she said. "So the better schools we have, the better opportunities that we'll have, not only for our youth, but also our young adults trying to get into the workforce."

title: CWDI Votes to Amend Articles of Incorporation
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
CWDI votes to amend Articles of Incorporation

 November 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 502
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. Board of Directors has voted in favor of amending the organization's Articles of Incorporation.With this vote, made during a closed session meeting on Nov. 20, the amendments will be sent for approval to Cambridge Mayor Stephen Rideout, who is CWDI's sole member.
CWDI Board President Angie Hengst said if Rideout approves the amendments, they will be sent to the Maryland Department of Assessments and Taxation.
"Once they have accepted and filed it, then it becomes our actual articles," she said.
During a Cambridge City Council work session on Nov. 4, City Attorney Patrick Thomas said that in September, a group — which included Thomas, Rideout, Cambridge City Manager Glenn Steckman, Dorchester County Manager Jerry Jones and Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) — met to discuss proposed revisions to the Articles of Incorporation.
At the council meeting, Thomas outlined proposed changes to the document and said that if the City Council, state and Dorchester County Council all favorably recommend the changes to the document, those changes could then be adopted by the CWDI board.
In an interview with the Star Democrat Thursday, Hengst said she was happy CWDI was able to work with the city, county and state.
"We're just happy that we were able to all work together and come up with something that everyone is happy with and can move forward," she said.
PROPOSED CHANGESIf approved by Rideout and filed by the state, the Articles of Incorporation amendments would address membership, board membership and the process of amending CWDI's Articles of Incorporation and bylaws.
Specifically, one amendment would expand the board of directors from seven to nine members. The two additional seats would be for the city and county managers, who would not be able to vote but would be entitled to attend all meetings, including closed session meetings.
Another amendment would increase the number of CWDI members from one to three. Members — which are different from board members — are comparable to shareholders of a company. Having three members would make it so that the city, county and state can be represented.
The city and county members would be made up of their respective councils. The state member would be made up of Dorchester County's state delegation and the state's secretary of housing and community development. This means that for the CWDI members to vote on a particular item, a majority of its commissioners, council members or state representatives would have to vote a certain way first.
The amendments also state that if the board of directors declines the removal of a director, then the appointing authority, such as the county or city, has the ability to remove them after 45 days of the request for removal.
Lastly, the amendments clarify that the CWDI Board of Directors has the authority to amend the Articles of Incorporation as long as it provides the amendments to CWDI members for approval first. It also clarifies that the board of directors can amend its bylaws as long as advance notice is provided to CWDI members.

title: Cambridge City Council Talks About Amending CWDI Articles of Incorporation
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge City Council talks about amending CWDI Articles of Incorporation

 November 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 634
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Cambridge — Changes to Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc.'s Articles of Incorporation could be coming down the pike.During a Cambridge City Council work session on Nov. 4, City Attorney Patrick Thomas outlined proposed changes to the document and detailed the steps necessary to make those changes. He said that if the City Council, state and Dorchester County Council all favorably recommend the changes to the document, those changes could then be adopted by the CWDI board.
In September, a group — which included Thomas, Cambridge's mayor and city manager, Dorchester County's manager and Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) — met to discuss proposed revisions to the Articles of Incorporation.
"So out of that came a working draft," Thomas said.
This is not the first time in the past year that there has been discussion surrounding CWDI's Articles of Incorporation. In April, Cambridge Mayor Stephen Rideout proposed amendments to the document that he felt would make the Cambridge Harbor project more likely to succeed.
Spearheaded by CWDI, the project is intended to develop land along the Choptank River.
Rideout's efforts to amendment the Articles of Incorporation were postponed in May when, in the midst of a lawsuit filed by the city against CWDI regarding a transfer agreement, the two parties entered into mediation. The lawsuit was settled in August.
PROPOSED CHANGESThe current proposed revisions to CWDI's Articles of Incorporation would address membership, board membership and the process of amending the Articles of Incorporation.
Specifically, if adopted, the amendments would clarify that the CWDI Board of Directors has the authority to amend the Articles of Incorporation as long as it provides the amendments to CWDI members (which are comparable to the shareholders of a company) for approval first. It also clarifies that the board of directors can amend its bylaws as long as advance notice is provided to CWDI members.
Another proposed revision expands the board of directors from seven to nine members. The two additional seats would be for the city and county managers. Thomas said the managers would serve in "an ex-officio, non-voting capacity," and would be entitled to attend all meetings, including closed session meetings.
The proposed amendments also include two new sections regarding the removal of directors. They state that if the board of directors declines the removal of a director, then the appointing authority, such as the county or city, has the ability to remove them. This authority can only be used if the board member hasn't been attending meetings, has acted unethically or unlawfully or has an unresolved conflict of interest.
Another revision would change the resident agent from the city's legal counsel to CWDI's legal counsel.
The last change would make it so that the number of CWDI members is increased from one to three. Currently, Rideout is CWDI's sole member. Having three members would make it so that the city, county and state can be represented. Thomas said that for the city or county member to vote on a particular item, a majority of its commissioners or council members would have to vote on the issue first.
"So any action taken by the city member would reflect the majority of the council," Thomas said.
During the council meeting, Hutchinson said that from the state's standpoint, for the state member to vote on a particular item, a majority of Dorchester County's state delegation should have to vote on the issue first. He said if a tie-breaker is needed, Maryland Secretary of Housing and Community Development Jake Day should take that role.
At the end of the meeting, CWDI board Secretary-Treasurer Frank Narr said CWDI's goal is to make sure the Articles of Incorporation continue to reflect "the original intent" of CWDI's formation.
"And I think this moves in that direction," he said. "So I appreciate everybody's willingness to work together on this, and I look forward to a true partnership going forward."

title: 4 of 6 Charter Amendments Pass in Dorchester County
author: Staff Report
content:
4 of 6 charter amendments pass in Dorchester County

 November 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Local News 
 
 514
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Voters in Dorchester County this general election were posed with six questions asking residents whether or not certain changes should be made to the county charter.Four of six proposed charter amendments were passed by Dorchester County voters, according to unofficial results from the Maryland Board of Elections.
As of Friday afternoon, Dorchester County election workers still had about 1,100 mail-in and provisional ballots left to canvas. This is not enough votes to alter the outcomes of these amendments, but exact vote totals may change in the coming days.
QUESTION AThe first question on the ballot for Dorchester County residents asked whether the county charter should be amended to say that the review of administrative structure be conducted within the first fiscal year of each Dorchester County Council term.
Currently, the charter says a review of administrative structure should take place at least every four years, but it does not state when in that four years it should take place.
Nearly 90% of Dorchester County voters chose to approve the amendment as of totals posted Friday.
QUESTION BThe second question on the ballot asked whether budget-related due dates should be pushed back 15 days in the county charter.
The first due date is for when the county must prepare the budget by. The ballot question asked if that due date should be changed to May 15 from May 1. The question also asked if the county council's budget adoption due date should be changed to June 15 from May 31.
About 76% of ballots counted by Friday voted to approve the change.
QUESTION CThe third question asked whether the county charter should be amended to remove the residency requirement for the county manager position.
Currently, the charter states the county manager does not have to reside in the county at the time they are appointed but must become a resident within six months. It states that the county manager needs to retain residency in the county for the duration of their time in that position.
About 61% of county voters chose to retain the requirements, according to totals posted Friday.
QUESTION DThe fourth question on the ballot asked whether the charter should be amended to clarify certain responsibilities of the county manager, including day-to-day operations, and establish procedures for certain vacancies.
Currently, the charter has procedures in place for council member and treasurer vacancies, as well as certain board and commission vacancies.
More than 87% of Dorchester County voters had chosen to approve the amendment as of Friday.
QUESTION EThe fifth question asked whether the county charter should be amended to remove the residency requirement for the finance director position.
Currently, the charter states the finance director must become a resident of the county within six months of appointment and stay a resident.
Just under 60% of county voters had chosen not to approve the change as of Friday.
QUESTION FThe final question on the ballot asked whether the charter should be amended to include language to ensure transparency of governmental functions as well as access to open meetings and public records.
Dorchester County voters overwhelmingly supported the amendment, which had received approval from almost 93% of the electorate as of Friday.

title: Cambridge Mayor Planning to Leave Before Term is Up, Looks Back on Term
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge mayor planning to leave before term is up, looks back on term

 October 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 765
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Cambridge — Cambridge Mayor Stephen Rideout is planning to step down as mayor a few weeks before his term ends.In an interview with the Star Democrat, Rideout said he and his wife are planning to move to a continuing care retirement community in Frederick. He is planning to resign sometime in early December as a result.
"Our children are in Alexandria or in North Carolina, and so we wanted to get closer to them," he said.
Rideout said although he hasn't made a formal announcement, he has advised multiple people of his plan to resign, including City Manager Glenn Steckman and City Council President Lajan Cephas.
Steckman said that when Rideout leaves, it will be up to the commissioners how they fill the open seat.
The last time the seat was made vacant — when former Cambridge Mayor Andrew Bradshaw resigned in January 2022 after being charged for distributing revenge porn on Reddit — Cephas took on the duties of mayor until Rideout took the helm.
Cephas and Bradshaw are currently vying to be mayor in the next term. The two candidates will go head to head in a runoff election on Dec. 3.
'PROGRESS IS BEING MADE'Looking back on his time as mayor, Rideout said his goals in office centered around crime and kids, two areas he felt the community most wanted addressed.
He talked about the importance of reducing criminal behavior and delinquency and finding ways to effectively divert children into programming.
Rideout said a challenge of the Eastern Shore and Cambridge is that there aren't enough strong nonprofits. He mentioned New Beginnings Youth and Family Services, the Cambridge Empowerment Center and MidShore Meals til Monday as nonprofits that have "really stepped up" and made significant progress over the last few years.
Rideout also talked about the Portia Johnson-Ennels Youth Internship Program, a summer program for Cambridge residents between the ages of 16 and 23 that are interested in local government.
"That's the kind of thing that I think we need to do," Rideout said.
Rideout thinks "progress is being made," in Cambridge but doesn't see that improvement as his or the City Council's accomplishment. He credits past city managers, city staff and staff leadership.
"We need to strengthen the existing programs so they can expand," he said. "And we need to find other people that have great ideas who want to bring another resource to the community for the kids."
One of the things Rideout is most proud of during his time in office are the recent changes in management and ownership at the Bradford House Apartments, which offers multifamily, subsidized housing for low-income individuals who are elderly or have special needs.
Over the past year and a half, residents have expressed concerns about the safety of the building, from bed bug infestations to call-for-aid systems not working to a lack of security.
Rideout said the city was able to get the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, Sen. Ben Cardin (D-Md.), Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) and the local state delegation involved, and city staff put in "so much work" to get the issues at Bradford House addressed.
"The changes now are happening," Rideout said. "And that to me is how government can work, should work."
Rideout said he decided to run for mayor after striking out on trying to find someone else for the job. He said he went to different people in Cambridge who he thought would make a good mayor and none of those people were interested in running to fill Bradshaw's seat.
"I felt it was important to have a calming voice during what I anticipated and expected would be a transition until this election," Rideout said. "Because I was only going to do it for the two years."
Cephas said Rideout "brought stability back to Cambridge" following Bradshaw's resignation. She said he also brought "steady decision making."
"He was extremely thoughtful of everyone on both sides," Cephas said. "It's something that I learned from him being the commission president while he was the mayor."
Rideout's main piece of advice to the next mayor of Cambridge is to listen.
"And listen again," he said.
He said the mayor should match their ideas to what the community wants and make sure the community knows they've been heard.
A decade from now, Rideout hopes Cambridge will be a place where students excel in schools, early childhood education programs are teaching kids how to read and write, and new businesses are moving in. He said focusing on the future generations is an important element of making progress in Cambridge.
"Because we aren't going to get businesses who come here who have employees who have children until our school system is improving," he said.

title: Cambridge City Council Members Talk CWDI After Lawsuit Settlement
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge City Council members talk CWDI after lawsuit settlement

 September 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 557
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Cambridge Harbor project was the overwhelming focus of a Cambridge City Council meeting on Aug. 26.Along with a presentation from a hotel developer interested in building on Cambridge Harbor and a decision to move forward with creating a tax increment financing policy — a financing method Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. has been looking into using for the Cambridge Harbor project — council members shared their thoughts on the project and the city's relationship with CWDI.
Tensions between the two have been bubbling to the surface for the past year.
In October, the city wrote a letter to CWDI expressing concerns with the Cambridge Harbor project. In March, then-City Manager Tom Carroll submitted his resignation and said he was resigning over concerns with the project.
On Aug. 21, the city and CWDI settled a lawsuit, which was filed by the city in May alleging CWDI was in violation of a transfer agreement it entered into with the city in June 2021.
After the settlement, both Mayor Stephen Rideout and CWDI Board President Angie Hengst expressed hopes for a stronger relationship between Cambridge and CWDI moving forward. Part of the settlement involves both parties entering into a memorandum of understanding to address issues between the city, county, state and CWDI that were not included in the lawsuit.
At the council meeting on Aug. 26, Commission President Lajan Cephas reminded everyone that CWDI's board is made up of volunteers. She said that the hotel presentation is an example of what CWDI can do.
"If we just give them just a little more faith, I know we can work together to make the project moved forward," she said.
Commissioner Brian Roche said he is excited to see the project move forward "despite the ups and downs."
"I think the progress — however uncomfortable it's been made — with the Yacht Maintenance expansion, the working waterfront, things that have been in our comprehensive plan, thank god we're moving that forward," he said.
Cephas asked about city spending on litigation with CWDI. She said the city has spent $34,000 and asked when it will stop. She said it looks like the project is moving in the right direction, and the money that has been going toward litigation should be saved.
"I'm hoping that maybe the next meeting, the next couple meetings, we can have a plan in place for how we can end that that process," she said.
Acting City Manager David Deutsch said the city would provide a report on the matter.
In July, CWDI Board Treasurer Frank Narr said CWDI was $200,000 over budget on legal expenses so far this year. He said the number was "strictly related to litigation."
Commissioner Jameson Harrington shared feelings on CWDI at the Aug. 26 meeting that contrasted Cephas and Roche's.
"I'll start off by saying not running for election again means I'm free to speak my mind, which also means I'm not going to sit here and falsely praise CWDI and give them thanks that they're not due," he said. "I've sat here, and over the past year, they have been unhelpful at best, antagonistic at worst."
Harrington said that it took a third party to get to this point in the relationship between the city and CWDI.
"And I'm not going to sit up here and pretend that didn't happen," he said. "So to sit here and praise them? No, that's not going to happen."

title: New Dorchester County Manager Says He Is Ready for the Role
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
New Dorchester County manager says he is ready for the role

 August 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 632
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Cambridge — The day that now-Dorchester County Manager Jerry Jones was sworn into office as Maryland State Police superintendent, then-Gov. Larry Hogan grabbed him and told him they needed to go to a press conference about COVID-19.It was March 2020, the month that the World Health Organization would declare COVID-19 a pandemic.
"We went through a lot of things nationally on the law enforcement level that was very challenging, COVID being one of them," Jones said. "But we had a bunch of other things going on. Some of the unrest that was going on in the country with law enforcement-related issues. So that was very challenging."
When he retired at the end of 2022, Jones needed a break. He had heard about the open Dorchester County manager position, but he wasn't ready for it.
"I knew this was going to be a lot of work, which I don't mind, but I just wasn't there then," he said.
Jones said that during his period of retirement, people would suggest the county manager job to him.
"It took a while to get there, but it just seemed like it made sense," he said about eventually applying for the job.
It was his love for the county he's spent his whole life in and seeing that county through his 2-year-old granddaughter Emma's eyes that made Jones realize this was the job for him.
"We forget I think, when we live here our whole lives, how beautiful this county is," Jones said.
Carrying Emma around, Jones noticed her amazement with the water and boats in the county.
"And I thought, maybe I can help ensure her future," he said. "That she has all this."
COMMUNICATION IS KEYSince taking on the role in May, improving communication has been a focus for Jones.
"I see opportunity here to create a more efficient, more professional government," he said.
Jones wants to ensure that when citizens calls the county, they get answers.
"I never want people wondering," he said. "If you've got a question, please ask. And if we don't have an answer, we'll get it for you. Because that's the kind of service people expect and deserve."
Communication with other agencies is also important to Jones. The county is working to develop its relationship with the City of Cambridge again, Jones said. Every few weeks, he meets with Cambridge Assistant City Manager Brandon Hesson.
Jones' experience at the state level benefits the county when it comes to communication with outside agencies. County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said Jones knows a lot of people at high levels of state government.
"So when he has a problem in our county relating to those agencies, he has been able to get on the phone and make some great connections with the people he already knew or the people that have taken over during the Moore-Miller administration," Pfeffer said.
Pfeffer said that Jones — who he called "a very good fit" for the county — jumped into the manager position "with both feet." Pfeffer talked about Jones' efforts in updating county policies so they "fit everybody fairly."
"He has a lot of experience on personnel policies and procedures and applying them to large organizations," Pfeffer said.
With some of the challenges the county is facing — from falling behind on submitting audits to staff turnover over the past few years to tight budgets — Jones recognizes the job he has taken on isn't an easy one. But he has hope.
"With a lot of the things that the county is working through right now," he said, "I think there's a lot of opportunity to be hopeful."
Jones hopes that along with being good stewards of what they have — so that his granddaughter can enjoy those things through her life — the county is "standing shoulder to shoulder" with its partners and helping them when they need it.
"Because we all win," he said.

 CAMBRIDGE — Dorchester County is taking back control of its water and sewage systems.At a County Council meeting on Aug. 20, the council voted in favor of a bill that establishes the Dorchester County Department of Water and Wastewater Services and abolishes the Dorchester County Sanitary District and commission.

Under the bill, the county council will take on powers and duties related to the new department.
For decades, a volunteer six-member Sanitary District Commission has governed the Dorchester County Sanitary District, which includes the county's water and sewage systems. The commission has been appointed by the County Council to six-year terms.
The county has worked for the past year to take control of the sanitary district, arguing the county has more resources to manage the services.
At a council meeting in April, two residents came to speak about issues relating to water and sewers, and County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said the sanitary district had grown too large for a voluntary board of members to handle.
Pfeffer asked for the residents' patience, saying that the county was in the process of taking back control of the water and sewage systems.
At the Aug. 20 meeting, the council voted unanimously to approve the bill that establishes the new department. Council member William Nichols was not present at the meeting and therefore did not vote.

title: CWDI, Cambridge City Council Come to Agreement in Lawsuit
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
CWDI, Cambridge City Council come to agreement in lawsuit

 August 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 611
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc., Yacht Maintenance Company and the Cambridge City Council have come to an agreement in a lawsuit filed by the city in May.According to Maryland court records, the case was closed on Wednesday. The suit was dismissed without prejudice, meaning that it could be refiled at a later date.
Cambridge Mayor Stephen Rideout said that the terms of the settlement include the ability for CWDI to transfer part of its property to Yacht Maintenance. Also a part of the settlement, the city and CWDI will enter into a memorandum of understanding to address issues between the city, county, state and CWDI that were not included in the lawsuit.
Rideout said the parties are currently working on developing the memorandum of understanding.
In May, the City Council filed a lawsuit against CWDI, the group spearheading the Cambridge Harbor project, and Yacht Maintenance, a boat service company. The lawsuit alleged CWDI was in violation of a transfer agreement it entered into with the city in June 2021.
The transfer agreement gave CWDI roughly 22 acres of land — including about 2.6 acres of land subject to a lease agreement between the city and Yacht Maintenance — for $5.
The city's lawsuit sought $75,000 in damages and requested temporary, preliminary and permanent injunctions stopping defendants from transferring any portion of the property in violation of the covenants of the 2021 transfer agreement.
In its lawsuit, the council argued that CWDI violated the agreement in March 2022 by transferring city-donated property to CWDI Holdings, a limited liability company also named in the suit.
Later that month, CWDI and CWDI Holdings filed a response to the lawsuit, alleging the city and CWDI agreed to CWDI creating CWDI Holdings to hold title to property named in the property transfer agreement.
With the settlement, the city and CWDI have entered into an agreement that allows CWDI to transfer property from the 2021 transfer agreement to Yacht Maintenance.
Rideout said the lawsuit was dismissed without prejudice for technical legal reasons.
"Something could come up in the future with regard to CWDI in the city or the county, and we didn't want to interfere or have this litigation be a roadblock to that litigation," he said.
'A FRESH START'
CWDI Board President Angie Hengst said CWDI's Board of Directors is feeling great about the settlement.
"This just allows us to move forward," she said. "Hopefully we've opened up lines of communication with all of our partners, and hopefully this is a fresh new start as we move forward and just advance the Cambridge Harbor project."
Hengst said they are "eager" to move forward with the property transfer to Yacht Maintenance, which she hopes will happen in the next few weeks.
At the most recent CWDI Board meeting on July 31, the board talked about concerns with finances and the need for CWDI to sell property so that it can use that money to pay for other things. On Friday, Hengst told the Star Democrat that being able to sell property to Yacht Maintenance will help the organization's financial situation.
"We need the proceeds from selling property to contribute to our operating budget," she said.
The settlement follows almost three months of mediation between the city and CWDI before a retired judge.
Rideout said the city is still in discussion with CWDI "on a number of issues." He said he thinks they will be able to reach agreements on these issues to "help the future development go more smoothly."
Hengst hopes CWDI will be able to make some significant progress on Cambridge Harbor now that a settlement has been reached in litigation between CWDI and the city. She said CWDI hopes to break ground on its promenade expansion project soon.
This report will be updated.

title: Leonard, CWDI 'Mutually Agree' to Terminate Leonard's Contract
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Leonard, CWDI 'mutually agree' to terminate Leonard's contract

 August 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 725
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Matt Leonard is no longer Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc.'s executive director.According to a Thursday news release from CWDI, the organization and Leonard have "mutually agreed" to terminate his contract, effective immediately.
In an interview with the Star Democrat, CWDI Board President Angie Hengst said that all board members and Leonard made this decision and signed an agreement on Thursday.
"It was just a mutual agreement, just deciding that moving forward it was best for both parties," she said.
Hengst said she could not elaborate on why it was best for both parties.
Leonard was hired as CWDI's executive director in January 2022. In the last year, Leonard and CWDI have been in the spotlight. The Cambridge Harbor project — a project to develop land along the Choptank River — has become a frequent topic of conversation in Cambridge.
In May, tensions between CWDI and the City of Cambridge came to a head when the city filed a lawsuit against CWDI alleging the organization had violated a transfer agreement it entered into with the city in June 2021. Later that month, the city and CWDI entered into mediation before a retired judge.
Hengst said the ongoing mediation had no part in the decision to terminate Leonard's contract.
"The board thanks Matt for his tireless efforts and commitment to the organization and its mission," Hengst said in the news release. "He has played a significant role in the success of the project to date. We enjoyed our time working together, and we wish him well in his future endeavors."
Some of the progress CWDI made during Leonard's time as executive director includes securing grant funding; creating Waterman Way, a new street on the Cambridge Harbor property that has yet to be paved; and moving the project to extend the promenade along the waterfront forward.
The news release says Leonard chose to retire to Cambridge five years ago after he fell in love with the city.
"I answered the call to help my chosen forever home by joining the CWDI team," Leonard said in the release. "All of the CWDI board members I worked with are talented professionals dedicated to CWDI's community-first mission. I'm proud of what we accomplished together. I wish them all the best going forward and look forward to enjoying the fruits of their efforts for a long time to come."
According to the news release, in the interim, CWDI's Board Secretary-Treasurer Frank Narr will serve as CWDI's "day-to-day contact," and the organization will "continue with its active projects" and continue working with its partners to advance the Cambridge Harbor project.
In an interview with the Star Democrat, Narr said he has been involved with the project for almost 31 years. He said he is passionate about what can and should be done at Cambridge Harbor and wants to do it right.
Hengst told the Star Democrat the CWDI Board of Directors hasn't started looking for a new executive director to fill Leonard's position and, at the moment, won't be.
"Unfortunately, based on our financials, which we presented at our board meeting, we do not have the funds to take a new executive director," she said.
At the most recent CWDI Board meeting on July 31, Narr brought up the need for CWDI to sell property so that it can use that money to pay for other things. Since the lawsuit was filed in May, CWDI has not sold a piece of property it has been planning to sell to Yacht Maintenance Company. That property is part of the land that the city transferred to CWDI in the 2021 transfer agreement.
Narr also told the board that CWDI is $200,000 over budget when it comes to legal expenses, which is due to litigation with the city.
Hengst said Narr will serve in the day-to-day role and the board will work through things as best it can without an executive director "for the time being." She said the board's financial situation will determine when it can begin the search for a new executive director.
Hengst said the organization's financial situation did not play a part in the decision to part ways with Leonard.
"We just really thank Matt for his time and efforts that he put into CWDI and the Cambridge Harbor project," she said. "He put in a lot of work, a lot of hours, and we couldn't have gotten to where we are today without him."
