title: Cambridge Harbor Closed Meeting Draws Objections - Meeting Includes Dorchester County Council and Cambridge City Council
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge Harbor closed meeting draws objections - Meeting includes Dorchester County Council and Cambridge City Council

 November 15, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 2 | Section: News 
 
 1176
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. held a closed meeting with stakeholders - including city officials, county officials and development consultants-at the Packing House on Monday.In an interview in late October, CWDI Executive Director Matt Leonard said the purpose of the meeting was "to review in detail, some of the more confidential matters we have going on with the development." The meeting comes about three weeks after a letter, signed by Cambridge City Manager Tom Carroll, expressed City Council's concerns with CWDI's Cambridge Harbor project. The letter said that the Cambridge council does not support CWDI's current plans for the project and that the meeting on Monday was "premature." Before the meeting went into closed session, Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said the County Council would be sitting in on the meeting for information purposes only and they would not deliberate.All members of the council were present at the meeting, as well as interim County Manager Jeff Powell.Cambridge City Council voted against going into closed session.Both Commissioner Laurel Atkiss and Commissioner Jameson Harrington voted against going into closed session.Commissioner Brian Roche voted in favor of it.Cambridge Mayor Stephen Rideout, who attended the meeting virtually for the first few minutes, said that one of the three commissioners in attendance would need to leave the meeting so that the council is not in violation of the Maryland Open Meetings Act. Harrington volunteered to leave the meeting.In addition to Atkiss and Roche, Carroll and Cambridge Assistant City Manager Brandon Hesson stayed for the meeting.In an interview, Pfeffer said that according to their county attorney's interpretation of the Maryland Open Meetings Act, there was no concern about violating the act because council members only attended for informational purposes and the meeting outside their "own council." Jim Brady, a reporter with WHCP in Cambridge, objected to the meeting being closed to the public. Jim Johnson, executive editor of the Star Democrat, also objected."This clearly does not fall under any of the exceptions of the closed meeting law and as such, we will be filing a complaint against this meeting," Johnson said.To justify the meeting being closed to the public, CWDI listed two exceptions from the Maryland Open Meetings Act: "to consider a matter that concerns the proposal for a business to locate, expand, or remain" and "to discuss a matter where public discussion would adversely impact the public body's proposal process." In a complaint sent to the state's Open Meetings Compliance Board, the Star Democrat and WHCP alleged nine potential violations of the Open Meetings Act, including that the agenda topics were not consistent with the exceptions CWDI used to justify the closed meeting.In a Nov. 9, Cambridge City Council administrative report, Carroll wrote that it was unclear to him how the meeting complied with Maryland's Open Meeting laws.In response to whether the meeting on Monday stayed on topic, Carroll said, "I didn't accept the topic," as Cambridge City Council didn't go into closed session.Pfeffer said that, to the best of his knowledge, the meeting stayed on topic. He said the County Council did not know exactly what the meeting would be about going into it.Pfeffer said the County Council attended the meeting with the purpose of obtaining all the available information about the project."It's a very dynamic project that has changed multiple times over many years, well before I even was an elected official," he said.Having more information on the project, Pfeffer said, gives the county a better idea of where the project is heading."We want to make sure that if (we're) ever ask to make any decisions regarding (the project), we are well-informed to make those decisions," he said.In an interview, Leonard said he thought the meeting went well. He said that during the meeting, CWDI discussed business deals they are working on."We're working through the strategy in our proposal process to get the next level of development," he said. "And so anything we discussed outside in public would adversely affect that. So we dealt with those aspects of where we're headed on the project." The Cambridge Harbor project will include creating public spaces like a promenade and parks, a boutique hotel that has a restaurant and bar, and residential and mixed-use spaces along the Choptank River. In an interview in September, Leonard said the goal is for the entire project to be complete in somewhere between five and 10 years from now.Leonard said CWDI's proposed tax increment finance district was discussed during the Nov. 13 meeting.In the the City of Cambridge's letter to CWDI, Carroll said this was one of the reasons City Council was concerned about the project. The letter said that the proposed TIF would take too much tax revenue from too large of an area for too long of a time, and the city and county would not receive a "meaningful" tax revenue benefit for decades.In an interview, Harrington said the proposed TIF is one of his biggest concerns with the project."It does not look viable," he said. "In the way it is structured, it seems like it would negatively impact the city as a whole." Harrington said the total new investment would be $113 million in one TIF district and $49 million in a second TIF district.Leonard said that the proposed TIF was discussed in the closed meeting, rather than publicly, because "it could negatively affect the strategy of our proposal for our future developers." He said that the TIF plans will be made a part of the public discussion when it won't "adversely affect our ability to get the best proposals." He expects CWDI to be able to bring all of this information to the public in the first quarter of 2024.Exactly how the TIF plan could adversely affect CWDI's ability to get the best proposals was discussed during the meeting, Leonard said.According to Cambridge City Council documents, the city had engaged outside counsel and received proposals from firms for an independent TIF analysis of the CWDI TIF.Along with the proposed TIF, Harrington said a lack of transparency is one of the biggest concerns with the Cambridge Harbor project."The Cambridge Waterfront Development project is probably one of the biggest deals that's impacted Cambridge," he said."So I think it's important that the public's informed on what's going on. I think Dorchester County and Cambridge itself have a history of a lot of behind the doors deals and that's not the way it should be done." Harrington said he thinks everyone wants a project that redevelops the waterfront and benefits the city and county."As it sits currently," he said, "it doesn't seem like it would do that."

title: Residents a No Show to Listening Session - Cambridge City Council to Vote on Ward Realignment
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Residents a no show to listening session - Cambridge City Council to vote on ward realignment

 October 19, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: A5 | Section: News

 Words

 CAMBRIDGE - Only city staff and committee members showed up to a Cambridge Ward Realignment Listening Session on Thursday, Oct. 12.The city's residents, who the informal meeting was intended for, were not present at the City Council Chambers that evening.Neither the Ward Realignment Committee members nor city staff were surprised by this, though."The people who aren't affected looked at the map, said 'That ain't me. Ok,"'Ward Realignment Committee member Lou Hyman hypothesized.The ward changes, which the committee proposes Cambridge City Council vote to make, would affect less than 3% ofCambridge's population.According to a news release from the city, the committee is proposing:⯀Moving the area bounded by Locust Street, Oakley Street, Park Lane and Willis Street from Ward 1 to Ward 3.⯀Moving the area bounded by Robbins Street, Maces Lane, Bradley Avenue and High Street from Ward 2 to Ward 4.⯀Moving the area bounded byVirginia Avenue, Peachblossom Avenue, Washington Street, Front Street, Brohawn Avenue and Perimore Street from Ward 3 to Ward 5.■ Moving the area bounded by Washington Street, Peachblossom Avenue, Boundary Avenue and Front Street from Ward 4 to Ward 5.These changes would make it so that each ward has a population size within the lawful plus or minus 5% range of the city's mean population.Wards must be within this range for elections.According to city council documents, there are currently more residents in Ward 1 than the range allows and fewer residents in Ward 5 than the range allows.At the end of the listening session, the committee voted unanimously to move forward with its proposal as is."Well, we did not hear anything in the listening session that would make me think we should change (our proposal)," Committee Member Tal-ibah Chikwendu said, referencing the absence of residents and causing those at the meeting to laugh."So I can't see a reason to make any additional changes."Following the committee's vote to move forward, the city will draft a resolution to be put on the City Council's next meeting agenda for a first reading. In November, the City Council will hold a formal public hearing for the the resolution.Ifthe City Council passes the resolution, the city will communicate the changes to the Board of Elections, who will then notify the residents affected.The majority ofthe meeting, however, was spent talking about how to achieve more engagement from residents on different city issues.Chikwendu said residents who would be affected by the proposed changes might have showed up to the listening session ifthey had been notified of the potential impact via mail."We could have gotten people here ifwe had been specific in the targets," she said.Chikwendu also said having more diverse wards could facilitate increased community engagement with the city, overall."It would have impacted a whole lot more people, but we could have actually created more diverse wards and still maintained the balance that we needed to to not be in violation," she said.Because the committee didn't have more time, it opted for the "next best thing," Chikwendu said, adding that there is nothing wrong with its proposal."But ifwe're talking about trying to get more and more people invested to show up for things like that and to do things that we talk about need to be done, we need to, first of all, give people reasons to start to talk to people who aren't like them," she said.Having grown up in Cambridge, Chikwendu acknowledged that there are other obstacles to increasing community engagement."In general, people who live here don't like people who came here later to tell us what to do," she said. "If they're people who aren't (lifelong) Cambridge residents saying it, it's going to be hard to get people to listen."Committee Vice Chair Greg Meekins said education is fundamental in growing engagement."We're not building up another set ofleaders," he said about Cambridge. "That's critical."Meekins also said marketing is important."We've got a large segment of the population in poverty," he said. "And ifwe are going to be intentional about reaching them, we've got to create the material that's going to hit them square in the face in a very positive way."

title: Cambridge, Dorchester Councils Discuss Working Together
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge, Dorchester councils discuss working together

 August 9, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 9 | Section: News 
 
 569
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - Cambridge City and Dorchester County councils discussed ways to join forces more often at a joint work session July 31."Where goes Cambridge, goes Dorchester County," interim County Manager Jeff Powell said about the county and city being in it together.At the beginning of the meeting, Cambridge City Manager Tom Carroll brought up the idea of sharing services.In a memo to the Cambridge City Council and Mayor Stephen Rideout, Carroll said sharing services might "save tax dollars, improve services, or both." The service that Carroll said both councils should consider sharing is central booking. In his memo, Carroll said a central booking service, which has been discussed over the years, would help keep staffing of officers on patrol at appropriate levels and not fall below the minimum.At the meeting, Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer expressed an interest in the service, but said "logistical issues" would need to be worked out first."We would love to be able to start doing the central booking," he said."For this to work best, the (court) commissioner would need to be at the detention center. We're trying to see whether we have the space to do that or if we can do video commissioner visits." Pfeffer talked about issues with personnel."Unfortunately, we have a high vacancy rate at the detention center, so we need to get our staff up," Pfeffer said.Powell said he thinks the county will be ready to discuss the possibility of central booking toward the end of the year.Carroll said he would reach out to Powell then to discuss options."If you have bandwidth before then," Carroll said to Powell, "you can reach back sooner." Carroll mentioned one other shared service idea for an agreement between IT staffs. He said the agreement would be for situations where the city or county has a special project and is in need or an extra IT staff member or two.Pfeffer said this is something that the city and county could look into doing, but reminded Carroll that the county doesn't have a surplus of IT staff.Toward the end of the meeting council members talked about getting to know each other."Soon, let's look at doing something together, bringing everybody together," Cambridge City Council Commissioner Sputty Cephas said. "Just to say, 'Hey I'm Sputty, and you're Ricky.' You know, learn more about each other." Cambridge City Council Commission President Lajan Cephas suggested having regularly scheduled events or dinners."Just so we can build that relationship, have that rapport and know that we are all on the same page," she said.

title: Tensions Flare Over Rezoning, Shoreline Project at Cambridge Council Meeting
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Tensions flare over rezoning, shoreline project at Cambridge council meeting

 October 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 622
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — There were a few tense moments at the Oct. Cambridge City Council meeting.During the open comment period, a resident called commissioners' discussions "spirited." At points during the meeting, commissioners spoke over each other and exchanged sharp words.
Tensions arose after Commission President Sputty Cephas made a motion to hear two rezoning ordinances together, meaning the vote for one ordinance would be postponed to another meeting. The applicant behind the delayed ordinance walked out of the meeting as a result, threatening to withdraw their application.
Jim Cheney with Quality Housing of Cambridge received approval from the Planning Commission to rezone three parcels into mixed-use Downtown Waterfront Development District zoning, opening those parcels up for potential commercial development.
Currently, two of the parcels are zoned as general commercial while the third is residential.
Cheney was represented by his attorney, Jesse Hammock, who came to speak during Ordinance 1255's public hearing Oct. 6 and did not seem pleased when the vote was taken off the agenda.
Cheney's neighbor, Benito Lake, is the applicant behind the other rezoning ordinance. Lake put in an application to rezone two of his parcels for the same use as Cheney.
Lake is a month behind Cheney in the rezoning process.
When the council decided to defer the second reading of Ordinance No. 1255 to be heard alongside Ordinance No. 1258, Cheney's attorney withdrew his client's application and walked out of the meeting.
City Attorney Patrick Thomas said with the applicant withdrawing, there may be no party to present the case, raising legal issues with approving the rezoning.
City staff and commissioners discussed whether they or the Planning Commission could initiate rezoning, and Thomas said they would need to research it but cautioned against rezoning a property without the owner's consent.
Commissioners and staff expressed intent to make contact with parties soon to align and potentially proceed collectively, acknowledging that delays could further complicate the multi-parcel rezoning.
Commissioners still held a public hearing on Ordinance No. 1255, though they did not hold a vote. Resident Sharon Smith expressed concerns over access to one of the parcels. City Planner Brian Herrmann responded, saying there is a paper street, a roadway that exists on city maps but has not been constructed.
Shoreline project debate
Tensions flared again when discussing renewing the consulting contract for Cambridge's shoreline project, which aims to thoroughly assess the factors and conditions that contribute to current and potential future flooding issues.
When speaking about the current consultant's contract, which has expired, some commissioners said they lacked a clear understanding of the project's deliverables and progress, hindering their ability to support the contract renewal.
But City Manager Glenn Steckman said delaying the shoreline project exposes the city to ongoing flood damage and potential catastrophe if there is a major storm.
Mayor Lajan Cephas, who is not able to vote on the matter, expressed agitation at the ongoing discussion and suggested Larry White, the current consultant for the project, come speak to the commissioners directly.
Sputty Cephas made a motion to defer the item so commissioners can have further conversations. He began speaking about why he made the motion, and Lajan Cephas cut him off, saying, "Well, I've attended the meetings."
Sputty Cephas asked, "May I finish?" Lajan Cephas responded, "No, I'm going to finish."
A few commissioners chuckled.
"I'm just to the point where I'm over talking about this, and Mr. White needs to come here and get the full opportunity to give a presentation, not shortened, not edited, so every single question can be asked, and then you can make that determination as commissioners whether you are going to save our shoreline or not, and let that be on the record," Lajan Cephas said, closing the discussion.
The specific terms of the flood mitigation consultants contract remain unresolved and will be the subject of a future meeting.

title: Cambridge Ordinance Proposes Updating Code on Group Housing
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Cambridge ordinance proposes updating code on group housing

 September 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 502
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Cambridge's Unified Development Code is "outdated," according to City Planner Brian Herrmann, who has proposed a new ordinance to align the city's code on group housing with state and federal laws.But rumblings on social media express concern over the proposed ordinance, saying it will lead to a proliferation of these types of residences if passed. Herrmann said that will not be the case.
A group home is a residential facility that provides supervised housing and support services for individuals who require assistance.
In the current code, group homes can have no more than eight clients and are allowed in every district. The new ordinance sets out to clarify where and what type of group homes are allowed.
The code only defines two uses: a group home and a set of institutional residential uses like nursing care, intermediate care and child care institutions.
The proposed ordinance would eliminate these two uses and replace them with four new categories: large group homes/large halfway houses, recovery residences, small group homes/small halfway houses, and commercial properties like assisted living facilities, residential care homes and nursing facilities.
The large group homes/large halfway houses, recovery residences and small group homes/small halfway houses will be regulated on the state and federal level.
"So we don't really have much say in it other than we do give a zoning certificate to say that, yeah, you do meet the zoning requirements and we're going to sign off on that," Herrmann said.
Herrmann clarified that the large group homes/large halfway houses would be primarily allowed in institutional, commercial mixed use and maritime resort zones, meaning few are likely to be in typical residential neighborhoods.
On social media, residents have expressed concerns over the ordinance out of fear the group homes will change the makeup of residential neighborhoods.
"I understand all of the concerns. I think everyone would probably have them with their own property. The issue is that we have to follow the rules and we can't just make them up," Herrmann said on aligning the city's code with state and federal regulations.
According to Herrmann, passing the ordinance will enhance the city's ability to register, track and inspect certain facilities, add enforceable conditions, and require a Board of Appeals review for some uses.
"It's a little stricter," he said.
Herrmann said in the past few years, the city has received far less applications to create these types of homes. He said they used to get 12 to 14 applications, but in his time as city planner, they have only received two.
Because downtown Cambridge has a form-based code, which puts more emphasis on what the homes look like rather than their use, Herrmann said the area is less attractive to applicants.
"I guess we just haven't seen as many applicants in the last couple years as we did in the past, which, to me, tells you that we're moving in the right direction. And then if we can get our code up to what it needs to be, and it's a little stricter, I think we'll be even better off," Herrmann said.

title: Cambridge Planning Commission Advances Community Garden Ordinance
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Cambridge Planning Commission advances community garden ordinance

 September 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 564
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — After three Cambridge Planning Commission meetings with public hearings, Blackwater Rising, a nonprofit organization that promotes nutritious food through community gardens, and planning commissioners have finally come to an agreement.Community gardens were not previously included in the city's code, prompting the need for an ordinance after gardens began popping up and being organized without clear regulation, according to Cambridge Director of Planning and Zoning Brian Herrmann.
Herrmann said it took three public hearings to get the language of the ordinance right and to provide the proper conditions without overstepping. "I find these regulations utterly confusing," co-founder of Blackwater Rising David King said on the second iteration of the ordinance during the Sept. 2 meeting.
"The fact that we had to have three hearings on the issue was that we had listed a number of things that we felt like either should or shouldn't be allowed in a community garden, but should have some sort of permission or oversight," Hermann said.
Those permissions or oversights are called conditions, and in the originally drafted ordinance, there were nine conditions. Herrmann said those conditions are likely what caused the three hearings.
He said the gardens were a conditional use because "we wanted to make sure that each garden had what we call a 'garden coordinator,' someone to kind of oversee the garden. And so we had to write that language and sort of specify that," he said.
In addition, there were nine items the garden coordinator had to get approved by city staff, then oversee the installation and use of these items.
Members of Blackwater Rising were against these conditions and expressed such during the public hearing.
The conditional items were one garden shed, benches and picnic tables, raised and or accessible planting beds, compost and waste bins, fences, signs, garden art, rain barrel systems and bicycle racks.
"So what I think the controversy was, you know, let's let each garden decide whether or not they want those things. And if they want them, they should be allowed," Herrmann said.
The ordinance applies to all land, not just city-owned property. This broad application made the drafting process more complex, Herrmann said. But he said it was worth it.
"I think the Planning Commission was a little upset with me that I kind of inferred that we should reopen the last meeting for public hearing," Herrmann said. However, he said without the public engagement, they likely would not have approved the ordinance for the City Council's review.
King said there are already three community gardens in town. He said to the best of his knowledge, they have not received any complaints about the gardens other than a hose that crossed the street.
King said Blackwater Rising is funded entirely by corporate grants, donations, fundraising and in-kind contributions, and it is run by volunteers. He said they are only asking the city "to not get in our way."
King said 30 residents showed up to the Sept. 2 meeting to express their support for the less restrictive community guidelines. King said a good compromise ordinance was reached, more in line with other jurisdictions that encourage community gardens.
"I think the process worked the way it's supposed to, so that's a good thing," Herrmann said.
The Cambridge City Council will have final say on the ordinance. It will be raised for a first reading at an upcoming City Council meeting, but Herrmann is not certain as to which meeting it will be.

title: Here's where Easton leaders stand on growth
author: Konner Metz
content:
Here's where Easton leaders stand on growth

 August 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Headlines 
 
 309
 Words 

 Read News Document

 It's a classic debate: build more housing or curb growth?Since joining the The Star Democrat in June 2024, I've seen the housing-growth debate consistently occupy the minds of elected officials, town planners, developers and residents. If you ask a Town Council member or a longtime resident the number one issue that Easton faces, I'd venture to say the answer will be growth-related more times than not.
There's hundreds of housing units in the town's pipeline — 1,127, to be exact. But at the same time, it's well-documented that Easton and Talbot County have an affordability problem, leaving many employees to commute daily from Caroline or Dorchester counties.
So what are the plans to pare down already-heavy traffic and keep the Easton Volunteer Fire Department from transitioning to a paid agency? And at the same time, how can the town still pursue some level of reasonably-priced housing for those that need it most?
It's a complex set of questions I asked the town's top officials, from the mayor, to elected council members, to a surprisingly powerful, six-member volunteer planning board.
The answers aren't clear. Some say slam the brakes. Others believe letting off the gas here and there will do.
There is, however, an approach gaining steam: focus on building from the inside-out, rather than annexing more county land into town or approving sprawling, single-family home developments. Most officials I spoke with endorse that strategy.
No "silver bullet" has emerged or will emerge, many town leaders told me. But a combination of items on the horizon — including a comprehensive plan update, zoning reform and a pause on annexations — will work to manage the town's growth without forgetting about those that seek an affordable place to live.
To hear specifics from town officials, or to find out where Easton's 1,127 units in the pipeline are located, check out my story below.
Thanks for reading.
— Konner Metz

title: New Comprehensive Plan Discussed in Cambridge
author: Lily Tierney
content:
New comprehensive plan discussed in Cambridge

 August 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 249
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Last week, the City of Cambridge hosted a charette to devise a new and improved comprehensive plan.The charette was a weeklong intensive and interactive public session where Planning Director Brian Herrmann, alongside a planning committee from consulting firm Able City, began to capture a vision of Cambridge's future.
The new plan outlined five main ideas: make downtown vibrant and multi-generational, encourage great places beyond downtown, reinvent lost Main Street areas, increase waterfront access and recreational amenities, and build a sustainable and equitable future.
The last time the city came up with a comprehensive plan was in 2011. They planned to re-address it in 2021, but due to the pandemic, that never happened.
Under Maryland law, cities must update their comprehensive plans every 10 years to reflect the community's current needs.
Individuals on the planning team specialize in a variety of development topics, ranging from economic development and housing to transportation.
During the weeklong session, there was strong community engagement, said Jason King, a city planner with Able City.
"This week, we started off with that hands-on design session — 135 plus people, 18 tables, two and a half hour event. It was an epic," King said. "For the city of 13,035 people, you know, we ran out of surveys, and we didn't have enough pens."
King said this kind of turn out is expected in a city of 100,000 residents.
Planners and city officials will continue to work on the comprehensive plan in the coming months before submitting a final version to the state.

title: Stakeholders Meet to Discuss Cambridge Waterfront
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Stakeholders meet to discuss Cambridge waterfront

 May 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: News 
 
 363
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Cambridge Waterfront Development, Inc. board, the Dorchester County Council and Cambridge City Council convened at their first quarterly stakeholder meetings Tuesday.The parties agreed to hold the quarterly meetings after convening in April. The meetings aim to repair relations between CWDI and the governments after years of contention including a lawsuit between CWDI and the city last summer.
Tuesday, county officials officials expressed lingering concerns CWDI won't attract a developer if it doesn't come up with a concrete project design soon.
During the open meeting, CWDI board members and Treasurer Frank Narr presented updates and working documents regarding the development of Cambridge's waterfront.
The team shared a revised version of the master plan introduced in 2023. The $3 million proposal laid out in the master plan includes a promenade (which is already under construction), two waterfront restaurants, townhomes, retail space, condominiums or a hotel, a facility for boat restoration and construction, two football fields' worth of public open space, and a fishing pier.
CWDI board member Tim Crosby said the goal is to create a vital, multipurpose space for the community that continues to honor Cambridge's maritime heritage.
According to County Council President Lenny Pfeffer, there have been multiple iterations of the design plan over the six years he's been on the council.
County Council Vice President Mike Detmer questioned the necessity of such a large amount of open space, saying residents have raised similar concerns.
Pfeffer, referencing CWDI's financial challenges without a secured developer. He said, "I'm real apprehensive about going forward without a buyer."
During the April meeting, Cambridge's Ward 1 Commissioner Brett Summers encouraged the board to hire a broker to support further development. Summers said a broker would offer valuable market expertise, assist with financial forecasting and modeling, and manage marketing and other critical functions.
During Tuesday's meeting, Narr expressed hesitation about hiring a broker due to previous legal issues with the city regarding a 2022 transfer agreement. However, Summers assured attendees that hiring a broker would not violate the agreement.
A decision on whether or not CWDI will hire a broker will be made at the next stakeholder meeting, which has not yet been set. Pfeffer hopes it will happen within the next three months.

title: Groundbreaking Ceremony Held for Tides at River Marsh Housing Project in Cambridge
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Groundbreaking ceremony held for Tides at River Marsh housing project in Cambridge

 April 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 547
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Local and state leaders mingled on the lawn in front of the Hyatt Regency Chesapeake Bay Golf Resort, Spa and Marina Tuesday for a long-awaited groundbreaking ceremony.A gentle breeze blew over those gathered, a contrast to the headwinds the project has faced in recent years.
"This has been a long haul, but we've done it," Fairchild Properties President Charlie Fairchild said about Tides at River Marsh.
Fairchild Properties is the developer behind Tides at River Marsh, a residential community located on the Hyatt property that is expected to bring 619 new townhomes, villas and single-family homes to Cambridge.
Mentioning rising interest rates, Fairchild said it took three "long" years to get a shovel in the ground for this project. Hyatt General Manager Shane Nicolopoulos said the addition of these homes to the Hyatt property has been in the works for decades.
"And how awesome is this?" he asked. "We are so excited, and I'm sure you felt it driving into the resort and seeing the progress that has taken place so quickly."
Although the groundbreaking ceremony was held April 29, the developers and builders started work on the project Dec. 30, Fairchild said. Currently, 75 homes are under construction with a plan to build 150 homes in the first phase and another 150 homes in the second phase.
In an interview, Fairchild said he expects in the next four months, about 80% to 90% of the first phase of homes should be built. He said they plan to begin the second phase in about two months.
Once complete, the first two phases of the project are expected to bring in roughly $2.5 million in property taxes for the city, county and state. Fairchild said the city is projected to bring in $1 million on the 300 homes, the county is projected to bring in $1.2 million and the state is expected to bring in $300,000.
This increase to the tax base is particularly significant for Dorchester County as it faces a difficult budget process.
"One of the biggest problems we have with Dorchester County is our failure to increase the tax the base, which is shown this year with us having to increase the tax rates," Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said. "And that's just what we need."
Fairchild said he expects the entire project of 619 houses to be completed in five years and be worth $300 million. He said approximately 40 houses have been sold so far, with the highest sale coming in at $580,000. Listing prices start in the low $300,000s for townhomes, at $400,000 for villas and at $450,000 and up for single-family homes.
The groundbreaking ceremony brought local and state officials to the Hyatt, including Maryland Housing and Community Development Secretary Jake Day, Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Cambridge Mayor Lajan Cephas.
Day said he is excited for families to move into these new homes, invest in the community and contribute to the economy.
"It's an incredible thing, and it's precisely what we need to be doing in every corner of this state," he said.
Hutchinson said his mantra as a state delegate is "to make a beautiful place to live even better."
"Oh my, have you made a beautiful place to live even better," he said to the developers and builders. "Congratulations."

title: CWDI board hears presentation about using brokerage firm
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
CWDI board hears presentation about using brokerage firm

 March 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 525
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — During the Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. Board of Directors meeting Wednesday, the board heard a presentation on the benefits of hiring a brokerage firm to market the Cambridge Harbor site.Cambridge Commissioner Brett Summers, who said he came to the board as a resident and not as a commissioner, presented on why he thinks hiring a national brokerage firm would help move forward the Cambridge Harbor project, which is a project to develop land along the Choptank River in Cambridge.
"I came to appreciate the value a brokerage firm can bring to a development site," Summers said after describing his 40 years of commercial real estate experience.
During his presentation, Summers told the board a brokerage firm would act as the marketing arm to help attract developers to the different sites at Cambridge Harbor.
"You have a mixed-use project here," he said. "And all these brokerage firms have different expertise. They have industrial brokers, they have retail brokers, they have office brokers, they have multi-family (brokers), restaurant (brokers). You need to find a brokerage firm that has those different expertise."
Summers said the brokerage firm could disseminate information about Cambridge Harbor to local and national developers.
During the presentation, the CWDI board brought up a city requirement that CWDI must use a request for proposals process to select developers to develop land conveyed to CWDI from the city. CWDI Board Treasurer Frank Narr said he was unsure if using a brokerage firm could serve as a replacement to the request for proposal process.
Narr asked Summers how CWDI could ensure the process of obtaining developers for the site stays public if CWDI uses a brokerage firm.
"Because I think that was always the intent," he said. "That this was a public process."
Summers said a brokerage firm can be "very public." He said the firm could come to CWDI board meetings and give updates.
CWDI board member Tim Crosby said the time to decide whether to hire a brokerage firm is now. Summers agreed, saying the sooner, the better.
"You've got a good concept," Summers said. "You've just got to get it out in the world and let people know about the opportunity with the math to back it up."
Summers said he expects it would take CWDI about three months to choose a brokerage firm. From there, he said CWDI would sign a listing agreement with the brokerage firm and the firm would begin putting together an offering memorandum, which includes detailed information about the property for the brokers to market it.
Later in the meeting, Cambridge resident Mary Ann McNamara thanked Summers for his presentation.
"Because I think that's what's needed," she said about his idea to involve a brokerage firm. "Something to get the project moving forward."
McNamara asked how the board plans to proceed. CWDI Board President Angie Hengst said the board will discuss the idea further and make a decision.
Doug Schuetz said he's "all for" Summers' idea, but said there should be a "sunset" on CWDI and the Cambridge Harbor project if CWDI can't get the ball rolling.
"Let's have a time frame," he said. "If these guys can't get it together in a year, let's start with the idea of a park."

title: Hearn Building Project Moves Toward Construction with Pivot
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Hearn Building project moves toward construction with pivot

 July 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 715
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Cambridge — Green Street Housing is adapting its design plans for the Hearn Building project on Race Street following concerns from Cambridge Planning and Zoning commissioners over ground-floor residential units.After a June 4 Planning and Zoning Commission meeting where Green Street — an affordable housing developer — presented its concept site plan for review, Cambridge City Attorney Patrick Thomas determined that placing apartment units on the ground floor of the Hearn Building does not comply with the city's Unified Development Code.
"So we will be adapting our plans accordingly to prepare for resubmission to the planning commission," Green Street Director of Development Chase Powell said in an interview.
Green Street hopes to have an updated concept site plan for the commission to review in time for the commission's August meeting, Powell said.
At the June 4 meeting, Powell presented his company's plans for 505 and 509 Race Street — a roughly 50,000-square-foot mixed-use development that would include 44 residential units and 4,000 square feet of commercial, office or retail space fronting Race Street.
Powell said Green Street is financing the project using funding through the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development's Low Income Housing Tax Credit Program and the department's loan resources.
"And with that comes a high commitment to designed quality and energy-efficiency," he said at the meeting.
Currently, there are two buildings on the land that Green Street plans to develop. Powell said they plan to raze 505 Race Street and build a new building in its footprint. For the Hearn Building at 509 Race Street, he said Green Street essentially plans to build a building within it.
"The Hearn Building is a shell, more or less, with a roof," he said. "So what we are proposing is what I would say, just a phenomenal feat of engineering to put a structure within a structure."
During the meeting, Commission Vice Chair William Craig brought up Green Street's plan to put apartment units on the ground level, behind commercial space. He cited a section in the city's Unified Development Code that states residential uses should be located on the upper floors of buildings in the "core" subdistrict, which the property is in.
Craig also pointed to the permitted uses table, which does not permit commercial apartments on the ground floor of a building located in the core subdistrict.
"That's what the ordinance says," he said. "And so I don't know how you're going to make it comply with that with this residential on the first floor."
Thomas said he hadn't looked into this before the meeting, but agreed with Craig's interpretation of the code.
NEXT STEPS
In an interview, Powell said since the city's determination that there cannot be residential units on the ground floor of the property, Green Street's architect is in the process of reconfiguring the plans to retain as many units as possible.
Although Powell suspects they will not be able to keep all 44 units in the property plans, he thinks the project will still be financially viable.
Cambridge City Planner Holly Baldwin said Green Street will need to come back to the Planning and Zoning Commission again with the project's preliminary site plan. Once the commission has approved the plan, Green Street will have to submit its final construction plans for review and approval by city engineering and the city's zoning official, Baldwin said.
Powell said Green Street has had to do a lot of work to help people understand Green Street's intentions with this project.
In October, Cambridge Commissioner Brian Roche sent a letter to Maryland Secretary of Housing and Community Development Jake Day requesting a revision to the Hearn Building project plans. Roche said the current plan would further concentrate poverty in an area without an excess of available jobs, would go against Cambridge's Neighborhood Revitalization Plan and its Comprehensive Plan goals and would be an "excessive" cost to taxpayers, among other things. Roche also brought up a concern for management issues down the line.
At the meeting on June 4, Powell said TM Associates Management, which manages Cambridge apartment New Horizons, will be managing the Hearn Building apartments once the project is complete. He said there shouldn't be concerns about poor management because Green Street is a local developer.
"So we're very driven to make sure that everything's being maintained and it's orderly," he said. "Because it's in my backyard, too."

title: CWDI, YMCA Say There Is No Cambridge Harbor Deal After Email Hints at YMCA Move
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
CWDI, YMCA say there is no Cambridge Harbor deal after email hints at YMCA move

 June 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 882
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Although a June 7 email sent by the YMCA of the Chesapeake made people think the organization had reached a deal with Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. to build a new YMCA on the Cambridge Harbor site, both CWDI Executive Director Matt Leonard and YMCA of the Chesapeake CEO Robbie Gill confirmed Tuesday that there is no deal."There has not been talk of a deal with the YMCA," Leonard said in an interview with the Star Democrat, adding that the two groups do have conversations from time to time about the YMCA's interest in being a part of the project to develop space along the Choptank River.
Leonard said CWDI has had those kinds of conversations with multiple respondents of a July 2022 request for proposals. The YMCA was one of the respondents of that request.
The June 7 email the YMCA sent out included a "facility update" about banners the organization is replacing at its current Cambridge location on Talbot Avenue.
"As we work to highlight all the positives that come with building a new Robbins Family Y at Cambridge Harbor, we wanted to give you a sneak peak of the new banners," the email reads.
After the email was sent out, people on social media shared concerns about the YMCA's plans. Cambridge Association of Neighborhoods President Chuck McFadden said in an interview that when he saw the email, he was "taken aback," and he said the news was "buried" in an email about banners.
Gill, who has received emails and phone calls from concerned residents since the email went out, said the YMCA is advocating the need to build a new YMCA. He said the existing site is not sustainable over the next two decades and can't provide certain programs, amenities and services.
"We are trying to help frame a narrative because, right now, you have other people that are framing narratives that are just wrong," he said.
Gill said the emails and phone calls expressing concerns with the YMCA's hopes to move to Cambridge Harbor have not made him reconsider those plans. He said the YMCA had a market study completed, which tested three sites for a new YMCA in Dorchester County, and Cambridge Harbor tested as the strongest site.
"We're trying to help people understand that if you did build a YMCA in the right location, that it could serve up to 7,000 people and 1,000 people a day," he said.
FUTURE PLANS
CWDI plans to issue another request for proposals in the fall for the second phase of the Cambridge Harbor project. Leonard said CWDI has made it clear to the respondents of the 2022 request for proposals that it will be issuing the new request in the fall.
"And if they're interested in having a place at Cambridge Harbor, they need to respond to that RFP," Leonard said.
Leonard said the YMCA "to some extent" fits the goal of having Cambridge Harbor benefit the community through offering things for the public to enjoy, like activity spaces.
"But we also understand there may be others," Leonard said about potential site partners.
The fate of the Cambridge YMCA has been a topic of conversation in the community for nearly a year. In July, Gill said that the YMCA began considering moving the facility following its market study. In late August, CWDI included a design for a new YMCA facility at the Cambridge Harbor site in its 2023 mid-year report, which sparked concerns from residents.
In October, the city council passed three ordinances that essentially limit institutional uses on the the YMCA's 201 Talbot Ave property in the event the YMCA were to move.
Gill and Leonard have both repeatedly said that there is no deal between CWDI and the YMCA to move the Cambridge facility to Cambridge Harbor. At a CWDI community update meeting April 18, Leonard said CWDI was not currently negotiating with the YMCA, and Gill said in an interview at the same event that there were no new developments with the Cambridge YMCA.
Although Leonard and Gill say there is no deal, Leonard said that CWDI paid for design plans to be drawn up of the YMCA's Talbot Avenue property if the YMCA were to move. He said that CWDI was asked by "some members of the community" what it would do with the Talbot Avenue property if CWDI received it. Leonard said CWDI would propose infill residential development to match the neighborhood.
"While we were having some of the Cambridge Harbor project design, we had our designer do a quick sketch of what that might look like," he said.
Though the Talbot Avenue property is not on the Cambridge Harbor site and CWDI's mission is to develop Cambridge Harbor, Leonard said CWDI is allowed to make deals to develop Cambridge Harbor "that sometimes might include other properties" per its charter.
Gill, who has seen CWDI's design plans, said the YMCA has not had any conversations with the city or potential developers about the redevelopment of the Talbot Avenue property.
"We just believe, based on the size of the site, it could be redeveloped to generate tax revenue that could be helpful," he said.
Gill said the YMCA will host Triangle2, the firm that completed the YMCA's market study, at its Cambridge location at 5 p.m. on June 18 to present data from the market study. The meeting will be open to Cambridge YMCA members.

title: Zoning Amendment Fails in Cambridge Council
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Zoning amendment fails in Cambridge council

 April 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 468
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — An ordinance that would have amended zoning to make four contiguous parcels at the corner of Washington and High streets the same zoning district was struck down by the Cambridge City Council before it could be voted on.The ordinance, brought to commissioners at a council meeting April 8, would have amended zoning for three parcels.
Jesse Hammock, an attorney representing the owner of the four parcels, said the parcels had once been owned by Cambridge resident Millie Lake and her family and were used as a bus lot.
Currently the four parcels are zoned three different ways. One is zoned Downtown/Waterfront Development District, one is zoned Neighborhood Conservation District and two are zoned General Commercial District.
The owner of the parcels, Quality Housing of Cambridge, asked that all of the parcels be zoned the same.
"Having disparate zoning classifications for those four lots makes it near well impossible to come up with a comprehensive development plan for the four lots that meets the requirements of the zoning code, comprehensive plan," Hammock said.
If it had been passed, the drafted ordinance would have made zoned the four parcels Downtown/Waterfront Development District.
At the April 8 meeting, City Attorney Patrick Thomas said the council had to make certain findings of fact before the council could vote on the ordinance.
"In order to grant the rezoning, you would have to find that all criteria had been satisfied," he said. "But even if you find that all criteria had been satisfied, you don't necessarily have to approve the amendment."
The findings Thomas listed included that the population of the area won't be substantially impacted by the amendment, that the amendment is unlikely to substantially affect traffic patterns and that two parcels were mistakenly remitted from a rezoning where one of the parcels was rezoned Downtown/Waterfront Development District.
Commissioners Brian Roche and Jameson Harrington voted in favor of all of the findings being considered fact. Commission President Lajan Cephas and Commissioners Sputty Cephas and Laurel Atkiss voted against it.
Lajan Cephas said she took issue with the statement that the parcels were mistakenly zoned.
"I believe it's possible that properties could be intentionally deadlocked so families can be stuck, and they don't have the ability of selling or developing," she said.
After the vote, Cephas said that her concern was whether the council could say it was a mistake.
"If it's intentional, is it really a mistake?" she said. "How do we determine what a mistake is?"
In response, Hammock said the only evidence available is a statement from a previous planning director saying that the two general commercial parcels not getting rezoned Downtown/Waterfront Development District was a mistake.
"Respectfully, there is no evidence that it was intentional," he said.
Without enough votes to consider the findings of fact, the ordinance could not be voted on.
The property owner could file an appeal regarding the council's decision.

title: Cambridge Establishes Land Bank Authority
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge establishes land bank authority

 March 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 373
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Cambridge City Council unanimously voted to establish the Land Bank Authority of Cambridge at a meeting March 25.With a land bank, the city hopes to advance its housing goals through taking an interventionist approach to the Cambridge housing market.
The land bank authority will have the power to take on, manage and sell vacant land in order to stabilize neighborhoods and encourage redevelopment.
The passing of this ordinance means the articles of incorporation for the land bank authority can now be filed.
The next steps to getting the land bank up and running will include deciding the structure of the board — including the number of representatives and how they are appointed — and searching for qualified residents to serve on the board.
In a Feb. 23 memo, Cambridge Program Specialist Gavin Woolford said city staff hopes to begin the search for residents who can serve on the board in the coming months.
At the meeting March 25, City Attorney Patrick Thomas said the ordinance identifies the mayor, city manager and himself by name as the incorporators for the original board before the actual board is selected.
"I would just ask that if there's a motion to pass the ordinance, that it just be clear that the articles should read the individuals holding those offices," he said.
Thomas said this is important due to Tom Carroll, the city manager having submitted his resignation. Carroll said his last day as city manager will be no later than May 17.
Commissioner Jameson Harrington made the motion to adopt the ordinance with a language amendment regarding the incorporators.
At a council meeting Feb. 26, Thomas said that to his knowledge, Cambridge would be the first municipality in the State of Maryland to establish a land bank.
He also said that because the land bank authority would be a corporation, it would be able to acquire and sell land "a little bit more nimbly" than the government because the authority wouldn't have to follow the same process outlined in Cambridge's charter.
Before the council voted unanimously to adopt the amended ordinance at the March 25 meeting, Harrington thanked Carroll and city staff for making the project happen.
"It's something I've pushed for since being elected," he said. "And it's really cool to see some progress."

title: Dorchester County Council Passes Property Registration, Accessory Structure Bills
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Dorchester County Council passes property registration, accessory structure bills

 March 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 396
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Dorchester County Council passed two housing-related bills at its meeting on March 5.The first bill establishes property registrations for vacant buildings, short-term rentals and rental units. These properties and units would need to be registered with the county annually.
Short-term rentals are defined as properties that are rented for more than 15 days and less than 30 days.
At a council meeting Feb. 6, County Planning and Zoning Director Susan Webb said the intent of creating these three different registrations is life safety and property maintenance.
She said with these registrations, the county would be able to contact property managers and owners in case of an emergency. Webb also said that the registrations would keep property owners accountable when it comes to property maintenance and following county codes and regulations.
The second bill the County Council passed on March 5 amends the zoning chapter of the county code to lessen restrictions on residential accessory structures.
The amendment makes it so that, for lot size of up to 1.99 acres, a residential accessory structure can't exceed 200% of the building footprint of the principal residential structure.
For a lot size of two acres to 4.99 acres, a residential accessory structure can't exceed 300% of the building footprint of the principal residential structure.
For a lot size of five acres or more, a residential accessory structure can't exceed 500% of the building footprint of the principal residential structure.
Before this bill was passed, for suburban residential, suburban residential-RCA, rural residential and rural residential-RCA zoning districts, the sum total of residential accessory structures on a property couldn't exceed the building footprint of the principal residential structure or 1,200 square feet, whichever is greater, without a special exception by the Board of Appeals.
For agricultural conservation, agricultural conservation-RCA, resource conservation, resource conservation-RCA and rural residential-conservation zoning districts, the sum total of residential accessory structures on a property couldn't exceed the building footprint of the principal residential structure or 1,600 square feet, whichever is greater, without a special exception by the Board of Appeals.
At the Feb. 6 council meeting, Webb said the amendment would provide relief to both property owners and county staff. She said 75% of the county's Board of Appeals cases in the past two years have been for accessory structures that are greater than what is allowed by county code, which has incurred more legal fees for the county and made meetings longer.

title: Dorchester County Council Tables Solar Bill
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Dorchester County Council tables solar bill

 March 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 513
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Dorchester County Council voted to table a bill that would amend a part of the Dorchester County Code that deals with utility-scale solar energy systems at a council meeting March 5.Specifically, the legislation would put a cap on how many aggregate acres in the agricultural conservation zoning districts of the county can house utility-scale solar energy systems. This would mean that up to 1,800 acres of land in the agricultural conservation zoning districts of the county could be used for utility-scale solar energy systems.
The legislation would also make it so that a 75-foot-wide alive and maintained vegetated buffer must surround the solar energy systems.
This legislation was introduced at a council meeting Feb. 6.
At the meeting March 5, County Planning and Zoning Director Susan Webb said the county recently learned the state could be adopting new solar legislation.
"That should be approved or disapproved sometime in April," she said. "Not sure if that would affect anything that we have in this document."
Following a public hearing for the bill at the meeting March 5, Council Member Ricky Travers motioned to table the bill until the council sees what happens in the state legislature.
"I'd really like to defer this bill until we see exactly what Annapolis passes in this session," he said. "I like some of the things that are in it, but I can't see us passing it right now."
Before the county voted to table the bill, three people spoke in opposition of it.
Cambridge resident Charles "Chad" Edmondson said the bill would restrict or hinder the implementation of some solar energy sites "drastically." He said the the aggregate acreage cap didn't seem equitable for the county and for the property owners and tax payers interested in investing in renewable energy.
Leah Meredith, Mid-Atlantic senior manager of the Solar Energy Industries Association, listed multiple factors that a solar developer has to consider when determining where to place a grid-scale solar project. This includes access to a proper power connection, the availability of a utility connection and flood vulnerability.
"Solar development is thus naturally limited by these technical and practical considerations," she said. "And the additional red tape created by (this bill) will make it difficult to economically develop grid-scale solar projects in the county."
James McCullough, a utility scale development manager at RWE Clean Energy — which is currently developing a utility-scale solar project in the county — said the bill would make it difficult to construct projects like theirs.
"(It) would also discourage other companies from investing in the county," he said.
Before the vote at the meeting, Council Vice President Mike Detmer addressed the commenters, saying that he appreciated what they had to say. He said the reason he has been pushing for this legislation is not to prevent solar, but to prevent bad solar.
Detmer said government decisions at the state level could take away the county's ability to consider solar projects on a case-by-case basis.
"That's what we're concerned about," he said. "Is that we're not going to be able to have that case-by-case consideration. That's what we're afraid of. We're afraid of the bad actors."

title: Dorchester County Council Introduces Rental Registration Legislation, Zoning Code Amendment
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Dorchester County Council introduces rental registration legislation, zoning code amendment

 February 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 614
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Dorchester County Council introduced two housing-related pieces of legislation at its meeting on Feb. 6.The first piece of legislation deals with rental properties. If passed, vacant buildings, short-term rentals and rental units would need to be registered with the county annually.
Short-term rentals are defined as properties that are rented for more than 15 days and less than 30 days.
County Planning and Zoning Director Susan Webb said the intent of creating these three different registrations is life safety and property maintenance. She said that with this registration, the county would be able to contact property managers in case of an emergency.
"Right now we don't have anything," she said. "If there's a vacant property out there, and there's a fire and the person lives out of state or out of the area, we have no way of contacting them."
Webb said the registration would also keep property owners accountable when it comes to property maintenance and following county codes and regulations.
"We don't get a lot of complaints about rental properties, but when we do, they're deplorable," she said.
Webb said although code enforcers aren't firemen and policemen, creating these registries and being proactive can help save lives.
Currently, the county doesn't know how many vacant and rental properties there are in the county, Webb said.
"We need to see how many we do have, and how much time and manpower we have to put into these properties," she said.
Because of this, Webb said the Council might have to revisit this legislation in the future to make it stronger.
The second piece of legislation would amend the zoning chapter of the county code to lessen restrictions on residential accessory structures.
Webb said 75% of the county's Board of Appeals cases in the past two years have been for accessory structures that are greater than what is allowed by county code. She said this has incurred more legal fees for the county and made meetings longer.
"We need to make a difference," she said. "I mean we've had some meetings that have gone later than 10 o'clock at night because the agenda's so big."
Webb said she thinks this amendment would provide relief to both property owners and county staff.
If passed, the amendment would make it so that, for lot size of up to 1.99 acres, a residential accessory structure could not exceed 200% of the building footprint of the principal residential structure.
For a lot size of two acres to 4.99 acres, a residential accessory structure could not exceed 300% of the building footprint of the principal residential structure.
For a lot size of five acres or more, a residential accessory structure could not exceed 500% of the building footprint of the principal residential structure.
According to current county code, for suburban residential, suburban residential-RCA, rural residential and rural residential-RCA zoning districts, the sum total of residential accessory structures on a property cannot exceed the building footprint of the principal residential structure or 1,200 square feet, whichever is greater, without a special exception by the Board of Appeals.
For agricultural conservation, agricultural conservation-RCA, resource conservation, resource conservation-RCA and rural residential-conservation zoning districts, the sum total of residential accessory structures on a property cannot exceed the building footprint of the principal residential structure or 1,600 square feet, whichever is greater, without a special exception by the Board of Appeals.
At the meeting, Council Vice President Mike Detmer verified the amendment would not give anyone permission to use the residential accessory structure for commercial use.
"Absolutely not," Webb said in response. "Every permit that comes into the office, I review and sign off on use to make sure that is compliant with zoning."
Council President Lenny Pfeffer said public hearings will be held for both of these pieces of legislation.

title: Planning and Zoning Commission Approves Plans for Cambridge Harbor Promenade Extension
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Planning and Zoning Commission approves plans for Cambridge Harbor promenade extension

 February 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 491
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Cambridge Planning and Zoning Commission approved the preliminary and concept plans for an extension of the wharf promenade at a Commission meeting Feb. 6.The application was submitted by Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc.
The promenade extension is part of a larger project to develop space along the Cambridge waterfront, known as Cambridge Harbor. Plans include public spaces, a boutique hotel and residential and mixed-use spaces along the Choptank River.
This extension is the first construction phase of the Cambridge Harbor project. It will make it so that the existing promenade along the wharf, next to Yacht Maintenance, stretches around what is known as Lookout Point and to the Franklin Street boat ramp.
CWDI Executive Director Matt Leonard said the promenade will be 20 feet wide with a 6-foot band of landscaping and bio-retention swales on the sides of the path.
In a memo about the design, City Planner Emeritus Pat Escher expressed concern with the width of the promenade and planters. She wrote that she believes the design should be wider.
"The promenade may be used for craft fairs, art and music events, etc.," Escher wrote. "The additional width will provide the vendors and performers with an adequate width to set up their venue."
Escher also said in the memo that the promenade could become part of a city-wide bicycle route, and if it does, a wider promenade would accommodate pedestrians and cyclists safely.
During the Commission meeting, Leonard said the width of the promenade cannot be changed because it has already been agreed to by the U.S. Economic Development Administration. The EDA has awarded CWDI for $2.4 million for the promenade extension.
"If we try to change it now, we can't get the funds and we can't do the project," Leonard said about the width of the promenade.
Leonard also said that CWDI's designers believe a 13-foot-wide path is wide enough for two-way traffic, both biking and walking. He said this makes the plan for a 20-foot-wide path "more than enough."
After Leonard and CWDI's civil and coastal engineer, Ken Usab of Morris & Ritchie Associates, spoke about the project, Commission Chair Mary Losty asked if the city engineer had reviewed the plans.
City Planner Holly Baldwin said the city engineer's comments had been addressed with CWDI during the creation of the plans. Usab said he and Leonard had met with the city engineer and will continue to meet with him.
"We're trying to be proactive and have very clear communication with the city engineer as we go along instead of submitting a plan and having a big issue," Usab said.
The Commission voted to approve the plans with a condition that the plans be subject to any additional comments from the city engineer.
Leonard said that per CWDI's contract with the EDA, CWDI will need to have the bids out for this project in April and have a contract for construction by July.
"So we've got a couple of months to get this (project) through the process of approval," he said.

title: City of Cambridge Confirms Dri-Dock Recovery and Wellness Center Can Be in New Location
author: Maggie Trovato Mtrovato@Chespub.com
content:
City of Cambridge confirms Dri-Dock Recovery and Wellness Center can be in new location

 February 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 856
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Cambridge — The City of Cambridge has determined that, under the city's zoning requirements, Dri-Dock Recovery and Wellness Center is allowed at its new location on Maryland Avenue.The center's move from 524 Race St to 103 Maryland Ave caused city officials and Cambridge residents alike to question whether the new location is consistent with the city's zoning code.
The Dorchester County Health Department, which runs the center, did not receive a zoning certificate from the city before moving to 103 Maryland Ave.
The center provides recovery support, advocacy and a substance-free environment. According to the County Health Department, it is a place that those recovering from a substance use disorder or mental health disorder can go for voluntary and free services.
"We're there to help people and to try and help resolve problems that arise in the area," Donald Hall, the county's director of behavioral health, said about what Dri-Dock does.
Hall said Dri-Dock opened its doors on Maryland Avenue on Jan. 22. The center plans to have a grand opening, where people can come in and ask questions, once it is fully unpacked.
While Dri-Dock settles into its new digs, the city has been reviewing whether the Health Department properly followed the city's zoning requirements.
Cambridge City Manager Tom Carroll said that although the Health Department shouldn't have moved without a zoning certificate, the city believes the center is permitted in its new location.
To come to this answer, Carroll said it was a matter of determining exactly what the space is used for and whether it complies with the city's zoning requirements.
If the city had determined the center was not in compliance with zoning requirements, Carroll said the city would have taken action.
Gene Lauer, who is on Cambridge's Planning and Zoning Commission, said he was surprised to learn that Dri-Dock had moved its location.
Before learning of the city's determination in regard to zoning, Lauer said in an interview that he had looked through the permitted uses for the district that the new location of Dri-Dock is zoned in. He said he did not see that clinics or treatment clinics were permitted.
Carroll said that after the city met with the Health Department, it became clear that the center is essentially being used as an office for peer counseling.
Hall said the center does not keep medications on the premises or give medications out on-site.
Lauer said checking zoning should be one of the first steps when it comes to moving a business.
"Because there are no guarantees after that," he said.
Hall said the Health Department had reached out to the city before moving, providing its license and asking what it needed to do to "expedite the situation."
"That response was a little slow getting back to us," he said. "So we ended up having to move."
Being a part of government, the Health Department did everything they could to meet all the laws and regulations, Hall said.
The move to Maryland Avenue has been two years in the making for Dri-Dock. Because the center was on the second floor at its Race Street location, it didn't meet Americans with Disabilities Act requirements, Hall said.
Along with that, the center experienced issues with leaking, heating and cooling and plumbing at the Race Street location.
CONCERNS FROM THE COMMUNITY
Hall said he has heard concerns from residents that Dri-Dock's move to Maryland Avenue could affect property values. He said that he understands the concern, but doesn't think this will be an issue.
"We are very conscious that we are in a community," he said.
In a Jan. 22 letter to his constituents, Commissioner Brian Roche expressed concerns with the new location's "visibility and exposure," bringing up the city's comprehensive plan — a plan that establishes the city's goals to guide growth and development in an "environmentally sustainable manner" in Cambridge.
Roche said the comprehensive plan discourages facilities like Dri-Dock from being in retail storefronts on the city's gateways and in its "downtown commercial core."
Carroll said the comprehensive plan guides the city's Unified Development Code.
"If there is a disconnect between the Unified Development Code and the Comprehensive Plan, then we need to amend the code to line up with the comprehensive plan," he said. "The plan is on top, the code follows. And so if there's any inconsistency, you amend what follows."
In his letter, Roche said the exposure might also be unwanted by those utilizing the center.
"I question that the most highly visible public storefronts in our city are suitable locations for those seeking medically and behaviorally sensitive, personal treatment," he wrote.
Roche also mentioned crime as a concern, saying that there had been a "significant number" of complaints and criminal activity at the center's prior location of 524 Race Street. He attached a police report to his letter that lists the 30 calls for service from Aug. 1, 2021 to Nov. 30, 2023.
Acknowledging the move was a recent one, Hall said that since Dri-Dock has moved to Maryland Avenue, people haven't been "lingering in the area." He said the goal of Dri-Dock is to help the community.
"Our target population is Dorchester County residents," he said. "These aren't folks who are being bussed in. These are people who live in the community, who walk those streets everyday."
