title: CWDI to give monthly updates to public on Cambridge Harbor project
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
CWDI to give monthly updates to public on Cambridge Harbor project

 January 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 456
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — In an effort to keep the community up to date on all things Cambridge Harbor, Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. will be putting out letters to the public every month.The letters will detail what the CWDI board is working on with Cambridge Harbor, a project that will create public spaces like a promenade and parks, a boutique hotel that has a restaurant and bar, and residential and mixed-use spaces along the Choptank River.
"We plan to keep the public informed on our progress and what you can look forward to in the coming months/year," the Jan. 29 letter, signed by CWDI President Angie Hengst, said.
Along with these letters, the public will also have the opportunity to attend CWDI's meetings. According to Hengst's letter, all of CWDI's meetings for 2024 will have an open session that the public can attend.
In the January letter, Hengst shared the results of the board's January 2024 officer election and gave updates on the project's progress.
She said board officers were elected at the board's annual organizing meeting. Hengst was elected president of the board, Shay Lewis-Sisco was elected vice president of the board and Frank Narr was elected secretary and treasurer of the board.
Dion Banks, Rich Zeidman and Mike Frenz are CWDI's other board members. Currently there is one vacant seat on the board that needs to be filled via an appointment made by the Dorchester County Council.
Hengst said board members serve on different committees including a Planning Committee, a Finance Committee, a Communication and Outreach Committee, a Government Relations Committee and a Hotel Development Committee.
When it comes to the project's progress, Hengst said CWDI is currently negotiating a $30 million deal with a boutique hotel developer. She said CWDI hopes to finalize this deal and announce it to the public in the coming months.
In the past year, Hengst CWDI has purchased the Richardson Maritime Museum property. The private nonprofit is helping the museum expand and advance its mission to preserve Cambridge's Maritime heritage and history.
CWDI is also working with Yacht Maintenance to facilitate the company's $25 million expansion.
This year, CWDI plans to break ground on a portion of the Waterfront Promenade, a multi-lane trail that will line the riverfront.
Hengst said the Waterfront Park, which borders the current boardwalk, is available for public use.
"We welcome organizations that would like to have an event here to please reach out to us," she said in the letter.
CWDI will hold its meetings at 4 p.m. in the Dorchester Chamber of Commerce Conference Room at 306 High St on March 20, May 22, July 31, Sept. 25 and Nov. 20.
In the letter, Hengst said people can reach out to her, at Angie.hengst@cwdimd.org, or CWDI Executive Director Matt Leonard, at matt.leonard@cwdimd.org, with any questions or concerns.

title: Zoning Commission Splits on YMCA Recommendation - Cambridge Y May Stay Where It Is If Recommendation Adopted
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Zoning commission splits on YMCA recommendation - Cambridge Y may stay where it is if recommendation adopted

 September 8, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: A4 | Section: News 
 
 561
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - The Cambridge Planning and Zoning Commission voted four to three in favor of recommending to the City Council a companion ordinance to a proposed YMCA overlay ordinance Tuesday, Sept.5.The proposed companion ordinance is a zoning text amendment that would add an additional category within the table of permitted uses in the overlay ordinance, which the commission voted to recommend to the City Council Aug. 1."This should ensure that the YMCA is allowed to stay in its current location and operate in all the ways YMCAs on the Eastern Shore might be called to do," City Planner Steve Kaii-Ziegler said at the Sept. 5 meeting.The amendment would "create a definition for a non-commercial community recreational facility in institutionally zoned districts that better describes the current YMCA's use of the facility," Kaii-Ziegler said.Planning and Zoning Commissioners George Brown, A.C. Alrey, Eugene Lauer and Chair Mary Losty voted in favor of making the recommendation.Commissioners Chantay Nelson, Theresa Stafford and Vice Chair William Craig voted against making the recommendation.The original drafted ordinance, which was already introduced to city commissioners for first reading Aug. 14, would put an "institutional overlay district" on the YMCA at 201 Talbot Ave. If passed by City Council, the overlay would limit the institutional uses the parcel could be used for in the event the YMCA were to move. It would remain in effect for five years or until the city's next comprehensive rezoning - whichever comes first.At the Aug. 1 meeting, YMCA of the Chesapeake CEO Robbie Gill asked for a third party to review the language in the drafted ordinance to make sure the YMCA will be able to continue providing all of its programming and services.Kaii-Ziegler said city staff and the city attorney considered "several different approaches" to address the YMCA's concerns. The discussions resulted in this companion ordinance submitted to the Planning and Zoning Commission for review and recommendation, he said."This definition specifies that a non-commercial community recreational facility may have ancillary uses that address the concerns the YMCA has expressed," Kaii-Ziegler said.At the Sept. 5 meeting, Gill said he wanted to thank city staff for working with the YMCA to make sure the nonprofit can continue to serve Dorchester County. He said that the proposed overlay, without the companion ordinance, could jeopardize the YMCA's programming."There needs to be an added use that represents the organization's work that it's doing," he said.Kaii-Ziegler said the city received a letter, dated Aug. 25, from the YMCA that confirms the nonprofit's support for the original proposed overlay with the companion ordinance. He said the YMCA also sent a letter, dated Aug. 13, that states the YMCA won't enter any agreements to "sell or convey" the 201 Talbot Avenue property until the end of 2023.Ward 1 Planning Commissioner William Craig said he took issue with the wording of the companion text amendment."This needs more work as far as I'm concerned," Craig said. "I don't think this wording is accurate." Craig said he didn't agree with the description of uses for the overlay companion ordinance."I think we need to get an accurate description of what the local YMCA does and then we'll deal with where it goes in the table," he said.No residents spoke for public comment before the commission voted on the amendment.

title: Cambridge Planners Recommend YMCA Overlay to City Council
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge planners recommend YMCA overlay to City Council

 August 4, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 3 | Section: News 
 
 752
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - The Cambridge Planning and Zoning Commission voted Tuesday night to recommend to City Council that an "institutional overlay district" be put on the YMCA at 201 Talbot Avenue.Following a public hearing, the commission voted 4 to 3 on the matter. Planning and Zoning Commissioners Theresa Stafford, Chan'tay Nelson and A.C. Alrey voted against recommending the overlay.Cambridge City Council will schedule a public hearing for comments from residents before making a final decision on whether to institute the overlay.Currently, the YMCA property is zoned as institutional. The parcels surrounding the property are residences zoned as NC-1.If passed by City Council, the overlay would limit the institutional uses the parcel could be used for in the event the YMCA were to move.The drafted ordinance for the overlay states the YMCA of the Chesapeake would be able to "engage in all uses on the real property to the same extent that it could prior to the establishment of the Institutional Overlay District." In the event the YMCA were to move, the drafted ordinance lists 13 uses that would be prohibited with the overlay. These uses include homeless shelters, boarding houses, airports, day care centers and nurseries with more than 30 clients, medical treatment facilities, nursing care institutions, colleges, museums or cultural centers, fire stations, rescue squads and public utility buildings.The overlay would remain in effect for five years or until the city's next comprehensive rezoning - whichever comes first.City staff began looking into updating the property's zoning after hearing concerns from residents about the possible relocation of the YMCA to the Cambridge Harbor area.YMCA of the Chesapeake CEO Robbie Gill said in an interview that the nonprofit organization is in an exploratory phase with no formal plans to relocate its Cambridge location. The organization said it began considering moving the facility following a market study that surveyed Dorchester County residents.With residents concerned about the fate of the property if the YMCA does move, city staff recommended the institutional overlay to the Planning and Zoning Commission.At the public hearing preceding the vote Tuesday, residents asked questions and voiced their concerns.Judd Vickers, who is a board member of the Cambridge Association of Neighborhoods, said he supports the overlay. He talked about the importance of neighborhood input."If this overlay doesn't pass, many of those (prohibited) uses will not require a public hearing," Vickers said. "So the public would have no further input. And that's really the crux of my concern." Ken Smith, who lives across the street from the YMCA, said he uses the facility twice a week.Smith shared his concern about the five-year limit on the overlay."I think there should be no limit," he said "These guys could wait you out. Five years from now you could all be gone. You could be replaced with business-friendly people who would not take the interest of the neighborhood into consideration." Planning and Zoning Commissioner George Brown, who voted in favor of the overlay recommendation, said recommending the overlay now makes the most sense."If we wait, we're going to lose the opportunity to do so," Brown said. "To me, it's not even a difficult question." Alrey, who voted against the overlay, said he would be comfortable with prioritizing the comprehensive rezoning plan rather than instituting an overlay."If the Y is not going anywhere, the Y is not in a hurry, I am comfortable with waiting a little bit longer," he said.Cambridge City Manager Tom Carroll said the comprehensive rezoning plan is half-funded, with $50,000 in the budget for the current fiscal year.Stafford, who voted against the overlay, said she doesn't think the city should rush into the overlay. She said she thinks the city should consider the YMCA's opinion more than they currently are."I don't feel that we're giving their opinion the weight that we should be giving it," she said.Gill said that if the facility does move, YMCA of the Chesapeake thinks the property should be rezoned residential. However, Gill said the nonprofit is "comfortable" with the overlay recommendation.He said the YMCA would like a third party to review the language in the drafted ordinance - specifically, the part that says the YMCA will be able to continue providing its programming and services."We would like third-party administrative review of that to make sure that, legally and judicially, it would hold up in a court of law," Gill said.

title: Sewage Seeping onto Streets Sparks Cambridge Flood Debate
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Sewage seeping onto streets sparks Cambridge flood debate

 October 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 506
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Cambridge city commissioners met for a work session Monday to review a presentation from the "Make Cambridge Resilient" team and to ask questions about the project — and there were many.The initiative is a shoreline and stormwater flood risk-reduction project, but some commissioners and elected officials have expressed concerns about its scope and goals. The design phase is now 30% complete, but without secured funding and support from the city, county and elected officials, the effort may stall.
Current goals include:
Designing and constructing a living shoreline.Creating a stormwater system with nature-based water storage and control features.Gathering public comments.Institutionalizing floodplain management and flood risk reduction.Developing a green infrastructure plan.Implementing additional nature-based solutions.Reactivating and maintaining the stakeholder group.Providing support to property owners to identify risk-reduction strategies.
During recent City Council meetings, Commissioner Brett Summers raised concerns about toilet paper in the street, an issue caused by floodwater entering the sewer system through manhole defects. Director of Public Works Wayne Suggs said during the meeting that three spots remain where sewage and floodwater are still connected.
Suggs said three elements must be addressed to control these issues: top-down flooding, pump station capacity limits and creek water entering the system.
The Trenton Street Pump Station, which takes in most of the city's stormwater, is 97 years old and failing. When floodwater enters wastewater lines, it is pumped to the nearly century-old station, which doesn't have the capacity to handle it. As a result, toilet paper and sewage rise onto the streets.
"So can this project help us with that problem — and when?" Summers said.
Project Manager Larry White responded that adding pumps at the end of streets, repairing older infrastructure and constructing a living shoreline will help with sewage issues, but the project itself does not cover wastewater.
The city has published a bid to rehabilitate the Trenton Street Pump Station, but it's a $7 million project.
"Even if we moved and we awarded the bid tomorrow for Trenton Street, it will be 18 months before that system can be brought online," City Manager Glenn Steckman said.
Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) said a mutual understanding of the project's goals is lacking and needs to be developed.
Del. Tom Hutchinson (R- Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) expressed concerns about the project, saying there has been mixed feedback from constituents and comparing the initiative to the "failing" Strand Beach project in Oxford.
Other concerns included insufficient outreach — particularly to Black and Hispanic communities and city park users — a lack of coordination with state agencies such as the Department of Natural Resources and the Maryland Department of the Environment, and long-term maintenance responsibilities.
Hutchinson said he contacted stakeholders listed on the project's website and many raised similar concerns.
"I had the opportunity to talk to DNR Secretary Kurtz, and he wasn't aware of the project," he said.
Some stakeholders, including Debbie Cornwell with the Maryland Department of Planning, expressed concerns about transparency.
Commissioners agreed to make the council chambers available for future public "Make Cambridge Resilient" meetings to improve transparency, but no further action was taken during the work session.

title: Transportation Officials Tour Eastern Shore to Discuss Funding and Project Statuses
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Transportation officials tour Eastern Shore to discuss funding and project statuses

 September 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: News 
 
 975
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Members of Maryland's Department of Transportation came to the Eastern Shore on Tuesday to meet with county and city officials and give updates on current projects.MDOT officials traveled through the Mid-Shore to discuss the agency's Draft Consolidated Transportation Program for fiscal years 2026 to 2031, which details a $21.5 billion, six-year capital budget investment in the state's transportation network.
Three separate meetings were held with MDOT officials Tuesday, one each in Talbot, Dorchester and Caroline counties. The meetings are part of the department's tour visiting every Maryland county.
TALBOT
Meeting with local officials at the Talbot County Community Center, acting Secretary of MDOT Samantha Biddle presented a draft of the Consolidated Transportation Program, emphasizing efforts to enhance safety, maintain systems and drive economic growth.
Biddle and other MDOT representatives shared status updates for several transportation projects in the county.
The Route 50 corridor project from Dutchman Lane to Lomax Street in Easton is in the final design stages, with construction expecting to begin in 2026, Biddle said. This project includes signalized pedestrian crossings at the Route 50 intersections with Dover and Matthewstown roads.
State Highway Administrator Will Pines reported that the State Highway Administration upgraded and improved 38 crosswalks across Talbot County in fiscal year 2025.
The county will receive a Kim Lanpheir Bikeways Grant for bike racks as part of the Easton Community Bicycle Parking Initiative. Director of Local Transit Support Travis Johnston said that MTA will provide Talbot County with $1 million in operating grants and preventative maintenance for local transit operations.
St. Michaels Town Manager Don Richardson requested the restoration of two crosswalks, which District Engineer Kenny Fender said would be completed in the next two weeks.
Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) raised concerns over a funding issue for the Oyster Recovery Program, which he said is designed to mitigate damage from port activities and has been the backbone of oyster restoration.
Biddle responded to Mautz's concerns with good news, saying funds are secured for this fiscal year to continue that work. But the conversation escalated at the Dorchester County meeting later Tuesday, when Mautz expressed he felt the secretary had presented conflicting answers throughout the day.
DORCHESTER
Mautz worried transportation officials weren't following through on the details of the contract between MDOT and the Department of Natural Resources. That contract outlines that the agencies together will provide $2 million in funding this fiscal year for the oyster program, Mautz said, among other specifics.
Biddle ensured that the departments would hit the $2 million "target," adding that she will "stay very close" on the matter as her agency works with DNR.
Meanwhile, transportation officials told the Dorchester County Council and residents on Tuesday that a long-awaited roundabout project in East New Market is moving forward.
During MDOT'S stop in Dorchester, Pines said the department's six-year capital funding plan fully supports the roundabout design for the intersection of Routes 392 and 14 in East New Market next to Dockins Service Station.
According to the draft plan, estimated cost is $4.65 million for the improvement. Pines said Tuesday the design should be completed in 2026.
Dawn Stanley, who was in an accident at the intersection two years ago and pushed transportation officials on the matter at last year's annual meeting, clapped when Pines spoke and thanked him.
"Knowing that that roundabout is coming is really essential," said Dorchester County Council Vice President Mike Detmer. "Talking with responders from Station 21, this has always, always been a problem. This is gonna be a triumph of making the roads safer."
SHA District Engineer Mark Crampton touched on efforts to fix culverts at Route 336 as it goes over Worlds End Creek. The road is one of limited access points for residents in southern Dorchester County.
Crampton said temporary improvements have been done and estimated a three-week construction timeframe to begin this summer once school is out. State transportation leaders will meet with the county next week to look at the detour route, Crampton said.
Other areas discussed included:
Warwick Elementary School. Biddle said officials have worked to improve safety on the roads in front of the school in Secretary.Route 392 sidewalks. Biddle said the sidewalks on the portion of the state road in Hurlock were completed this year.
CAROLINE
MDOT came to the Health and Public Service Building on Tuesday morning to hear Caroline County's requests for projects and answer questions from the County Commissioners.
The commissioners also listened to MDOT's plans to ensure federal funding possibilities are still available for the county.
"Our team specifically at the State Highway Administration is looking for opportunities to look where we can apply federal funds for critical safety and state of repair projects here in the county," Biddle told the Star Democrat in an interview after the meeting.
"So, as many projects as we can identify that are federally eligible, it allows us to stretch limited state resources even further to be able to do more projects such as, the intersection improvements referenced by the commissioners today or just safety and resurfacing project where those are helpful and necessary parts of keeping our system in a state of good repair," Biddle said.
Here are the current projects in the county under construction, in progress or requested:
Bridge replacement and rehabilitation at Maryland Route 16 and Harmony Road. The project is already under construction.Intersection capacity improvements from Maryland Route 16 and Harmony Road to Greenwood Road. A planning study is underway.Additional striping or re-striping at the intersection of Maryland Route 317 (Burrsville Road) and Maryland 313 (Greensboro Road). This was requested by the county.Signal change for the traffic lane at Maryland Route 16 (Harmony Road) and Maryland 404. This was requested by the county.Additional lighted intersection at Maryland 404 and Gay Street. This was requested by the county.Consideration of the 16 E school in Greenwood and 404 as a major breakout point. The commissioners requested this change, calling the road as a "major disaster."
Reporters Ahmad Garnett, Konner Metz and Lily Tierney contributed to this report.

title: Cambridge Harbor Promenade First Phase Over Halfway Done
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Cambridge Harbor promenade first phase over halfway done

 July 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 335
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. board of directors and the Cambridge and Dorchester County managers met on Thursday to discuss updates on the Cambridge Harbor project.These meetings, which aim to streamline communications between project stakeholders, come after years of tension between CWDI and the city slowed Cambridge Harbor's progress.
According to updates given at Thursday's meeting, phase one of the project's promenade is officially more than half finished.
"So phase one of the promenade is over halfway done," said CWDI President, Angie Hengst. "We should have that completed, hopefully, by the end of the summer for people to use."
The promenade is part of an ongoing project aimed to develop Cambridge's waterfront similarly to Baltimore's Inner Harbor.
In addition to the promenade, Hengst said board members have met with Department of Natural Resources Secretary Josh Kurtz to discuss plans for a fishing pier.
"DNR Secretary Kurtz seemed excited about the plans we drew up. Obviously funding is a question now," Hengst said.
DNR has earmarked funds for the demolition of the city's old pier. Hengst said the new fishing pier will be owned by DNR and managed in partnership with the city, not CWDI.
"It would not be something privately owned by CWDI," Hengst said.
The board gave several other updates at the meeting.
The city filled the final CWDI board seat last month, appointing Bernard Brathwaite. "He's up on the website for people, you know, if they want to see a little bio about him," Hengst said.
The city-appointed board members are meant to get everyone on the same page about project movement and financial concerns.
According to Frank Narr, head of the financial committee, the year to date financial reports appear to be on budget for the remainder of the year.
Hengst said moving forward, CWDI will put out two monthly newsletters to update the community. In addition, there will be a community informational session held on July 31 at the Pine Street Elk Lodge at 6 p.m.
"You know, just another way to keep people informed on what's going on," Hengst said.

title: 'Light at the End of the Tunnel': Cambridge Sink Hole Repairs Finishing Soon
author: Lily Tierney
content:
'Light at the end of the tunnel': Cambridge sink hole repairs finishing soon

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News

 CAMBRIDGE — A car sized sink hole swallowed part of Cedar Street on Tuesday, July 8, the result of a failing storm drain pipe.Sink holes are not a new phenomenon in Cambridge, according to Public Works Director Wayne Suggs, who has been in this position for two years.
Suggs said during his time with the town, it's experienced about half a dozen small "ankle twisters" but nothing of this magnitude.
"You know, your foot might go in, but not your car," he said.
Suggs said the repair job has been a complicated process because crews had to dig 11 feet deep to avoid a 27-inch sewer line and a tightly packed bundle of Verizon cables. Public Works needed a specially made trench box to do it safely.
The failed pipe section was not replaced during a previous upgrade around a decade ago, according to Suggs.
"This was a man-made problem, not naturally occurring," he said, adding that the failed pipes were removed in 2-foot by two-foot sections and were significantly deteriorated.
The city received the pipes necessary to complete the work on Thursday morning and installed them Friday. On Monday, the repaving process will begin.
Residents can expect Cedar Street to remain closed over the weekend and should plan accordingly. Cedar Street will fully reopen by Tuesday morning.
"We can see light at the end of the tunnel now," Suggs said.

title: Broadband Service Expands in Dorchester County
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Broadband service expands in Dorchester County

 June 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester

 Historically, those living down long lanes and private roads in Dorchester County have struggled to get broadband access. However, a state funded program is working to expand high speed internet access to these areas."One of the cool things about this is that a majority of the people on this list, except for the people who came forward, don't even know they're getting broadband coming to their homes," said Dorchester County grant writer Marylin Williams.
The Maryland Homestretch — Difficult To Serve Properties Program is administered by the Maryland Office of State Broadband and provides funding for internet installation in areas where it can be particularly expensive. The program is also referred to as the Long Driveway Internet Program.
Williams referred to the program as "ever changing," saying the state modified the grant program as recently as this spring.
This came in handy when the amount initially awarded to the county was not enough to cover projected costs for the project.
Initially, the county was granted $1.1 million, but the project is estimated to cost $2,422,493. The county was recently awarded with a higher grant after Williams advocated for more homes to be covered.
However, The grant still will not cover all of the 299 homes approved to be serviced, so energy companies Bay Country and Choptank Electric are investing in the county to ensure access, Williams said.
Choptank Electric spokesperson Valerie Connelly and Williams requested two action items from the Cambridge County Council at the June 3 County Council meeting.
The first item is accepting the higher grant award of $1,217,852. The second is having the county sign a memorandum of understanding with Choptank Electric and Bay Country. The Commissioners unanimously agreed, with County Commissioner Ricky Travers leading the motion.
According to Connelly, broadband will be installed at no cost to the homeowners and all construction must be completed by Dec. 31, per the grant.

title: Cambridge Amends Paving Contract to Address ADA Requirements
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Cambridge amends paving contract to address ADA requirements

 March 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 324

 CAMBRIDGE — During a Cambridge City Council meeting March 18, the council voted unanimously to amend a paving contract to include updating intersections so they are compliant with the Americans with Disabilities Act.In September, the City Council awarded David A. Bramble Inc. with a $447,150 contract to resurface three miles of roads at various locations in the city. City Manager Glenn Steckman said the contract was approved before city staff was made aware that if the city paves through intersections that are not up to standard with Americans with Disabilities Act, it has to update those intersections.
"So to pave through the intersection, you have to improve the intersection," Steckman said.
During the council meeting, Steckman told commissioners the city could either spend approximately $125,000 more to address the intersections as the city paves the three miles or reduce the scope of the project and pave less road in order to address the intersections with the money already budgeted in the contract.
Steckman said the city is estimating intersection updates would cost about $6,000 per intersection. He recommended the council vote to spend additional money to complete the three miles of paving. He said the city had originally budgeted $600,000 for the project.
Before the council took a vote, commissioners asked questions about prioritizing certain streets and areas for paving.
According to City Council documents, the city used a 2018 pavement condition study for the project to determine which streets are in most need of being repaved. Commissioner Brian Roche said it would be a waste of money to ignore the study.
"You have to be careful because we could end up having roads that fall further into disrepair just because someone thinks that their road is in worse shape when in fact an engineering analysis has determined where (is in worse shape)," he said.
After discussion, the council voted to increase the cost of the contract to include updates to the intersections without reducing the scope of the project.

title: CWDI Breaks Ground on Cambridge Harbor Promenade
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
CWDI breaks ground on Cambridge Harbor promenade

 December 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 555
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — After a tumultuous year — complete with a lawsuit and mediation with the City of Cambridge — Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. has taken a significant step forward in bringing life to the city's waterfront.Thursday, CWDI and the Dorchester Chamber of Commerce, held a groundbreaking ceremony for the Cambridge Harbor promenade. Once complete, the project will extend the existing promenade along the wharf, next to Yacht Maintenance, so that it stretches around what is known as Lookout Point and to the Franklin Street boat ramp.
For CWDI Board Secretary-Treasurer Frank Narr, who has been involved with the Cambridge Harbor project for almost 32 years, it felt "unbelievable" to witness the ground breaking.
"You know, it's funny, 32 years ago Gov. Schaefer said we're going to get this done in three or four years," he said. "But the reality is — as political climate changes, as things like the hospital, changes in health care, things like that — you start to realize these things take time and you have to have patience."
Narr said passion has kept him involved with the project for all these years.
"I'm just passionate about making sure what we do here is right for the community," he said. "Because you only get one chance to do it right."
Although the groundbreaking was held Thursday, the work to extend the promenade has already started. Narr said CWDI expects the project to be finished by the end of June.
Once the promenade project is complete, CWDI plans to put out a request for proposals for Cambridge Harbor's developable parcels. Narr said the community will have the opportunity to offer input once CWDI has received proposals.
The ground breaking on Thursday brought together a variety of local and state representatives, including members of the Cambridge City Council.
In the last year and a half, tensions between the city and CWDI bubbled to the surface, culminating in a lawsuit filed against CWDI by the city regarding a transfer agreement. In August, the groups settled the lawsuit, with both city officials and CWDI board members expressing hopes for a stronger relationship moving forward.
During the groundbreaking, Cambridge Commission President and Mayor-elect Lajan Cephas acknowledged the hard work of CWDI's board.
"They've experienced a lot of abuse over the last couple years," she said, adding that it's important trust is rebuilt.
"So I think this is a wonderful opportunity for us to take the next step forward," she said about the promenade. "The best step forward."
CWDI Board President Angie Hengst said the board hopes this promenade will be enjoyed by the entire community and "will be just the beginning of creating a waterfront area and experience that is accessible to all."
Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer called Thursday "a great day" for the community.
"This is a clear canvas now that we're going to start building up from," he said. "And this is a great project to start with."
Chesapeake Conservancy's President and CEO Joel Dunn, called the day "bittersweet." He said it's his second to last day at the Chesapeake Conservancy, which is a project partner of Cambridge Harbor.
"I've helped create a national wildlife refuge, a national park, two national monuments, expand Blackwater Refuge, create local parks, state parks," Dunn said about his time with the organization. "But I've got to tell you, this is one of my favorite parks that I've ever been a part of."

title: Dorchester County Talks Road Projects with MDOT
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Dorchester County talks road projects with MDOT

 October 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 702
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Cambridge — During an annual transportation meeting, the Dorchester County Council pushed Maryland Department of Transportation officials on two issues: the current paving project on U.S. Route 50 and the intersection at Maryland routes 14 and 392.At the outset of the meeting, Deputy Secretary of Transportation Samantha Biddle acknowledged the department's budgetary challenges. She said the $18.9 billion Consolidated Transportation Program for fiscal years 2025 to 2030 has $1.3 billion less than the last program.
"But even with these reductions, we are committed to using those resources to advance the state's priorities," Biddle said. "And that number one priority that you always hear from us is safety."
County Council member Ricky Travers questioned the department's commitment to safety after hearing about an intersection project whose timeline is being stretched due to the budget.
"You stood up and you said your number one priority for MDOT was safety," he said to the officials. "It's not there."
INTERSECTION PROJECTState Highway Administration District Engineer Mark Crampton told the council at the meeting that the timeline to put in a roundabout at the intersection of Maryland Route 14 and Route 392 in East New Market will need to be stretched for budgetary reasons.
Crampton said the survey for the project has been completed, and a 30% plan is scheduled for January. He said the final design for the project isn't expected until fiscal year 2028 due to the extended timeline.
After Crampton spoke, Council President Lenny Pfeffer introduced the MDOT officials to Dawn Stanley, who was in an accident at the intersection last year.
"We want to put a human element to this," Pfeffer said. "I know that you aren't the ones deciding about the budget here, but we need you to be able to take these stories back with you."
Stanley said she was on a motorcycle when she collided with a car that didn't see her. She said the accident caused seven breaks in her back, two breaks in her shoulder, eight broken ribs and a broken finger. A retired EMT, Stanley said she has also "cleaned up many" people off that intersection since the '80s.
"This place needs to be fixed, and it needs to be fixed now before someone gets killed," she said. "Or is it going to take the family member of a higher up to get killed for the state to do something?"
After Stanley spoke, Crampton said he was sorry for what happened to her.
Travers told Crampton it is frustrating that the council has presented the need for the project many times and the issue hasn't been fixed yet.
"We've been through the study, we've done all this stuff," Travers said. "And then you stand up here tonight and say, 'well we're looking at 2028 or ...' It's unacceptable."
PAVING PROJECTMDOT is in the midst of a project to resurface Route 50 between Bucktown Road and the Frederick C. Malkus Jr. Bridge. Because the asphalt mix used for the project requires the temperature be at least 50 degree Fahrenheit to place it, there have been some days where MDOT has had to do work on the project in the daytime, which has caused significant traffic.
Travers said that along with increased traffic, there were accidents. He said more consideration should have gone into what time of the year to do this project.
"Nothing against the job," he said. "It's needed, and we thank you for that. But we got to figure out a better way to do this."
State Highway Administration Administrator Will Pines said that due to beach traffic in the summer, SHA had a tight window for the project. He said the project should be complete by the end of the year, weather permitting.
Pines said the westbound part of the project, which has not yet begun, could be postponed until the spring, but that could affect funding. He said if they begin other projects before finishing this one, the funding for this project could be used for other projects if there are change orders.
Council Vice President Mike Detmer said there needs to be more communication when it comes to this project.
Biddle said they will work on getting the word out better when it comes to communication and will look into short-term solutions for increasing visibility at the East New Market intersection.

title: Property Owners Learn About Potential Compensation for Rails to Trails
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Property owners learn about potential compensation for Rails to Trails

 October 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 694
 Words 

 Read News Document

 HURLock — Landowners with property adjacent to future Rails to Trails projects may be entitled to compensation, according to attorneys from Missouri-based law firm Lewis Rice.The law firm is representing about a dozen Mid-Shore residents who have signed onto a lawsuit seeking compensation from the federal government for potential trail projects.
A handful of people sat in the Unity-Washington United Methodist Church on the evening of Oct. 14 to learn about what this effort looks like in Dorchester County.
The county is in the process of obtaining the rights of way for rail lines from Preston to Hurlock and Linkwood to Cambridge. When the state grants them these rights of way, the county will be able to implement Rails to Trails on those pathways.
In an interview Tuesday, Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said the county has no immediate plans to implement Rails to Trails in those places. He said the county hasn't even started to discuss implementation and would need to seek public input first.
"It would be a community process," he said. "And again, we don't have any money to do anything like that. So it's nothing that's going to happen in the near future."
But during the event at Unity-Washington United Methodist Church, attorneys gave a presentation to inform landowners with property adjacent to the rail lines about potential compensation from the federal government.
Attorney Meghan Largent led the presentation, which detailed the process of making a claim. She said neither the government, nor the railroads, nor the trail groups involved are required to notify landowners when a certificate of interim trail use is issued by the Surface Transportation Board.
"We have challenged that," Largent said. "What the courts have found is that publishing it in the federal register is effective notice."
Largent said landowners usually don't know what's happening or what their legal rights are until lawyers show up.
Pfeffer said in an interview that in this particular situation, the state had made notice of the easements, but he was unsure of the exact status. He said his understanding is that the state published a press release and then law firms directly contacted property owners of land adjoining the rail lines.
Largent said that once the certificate of interim trail use was issued on Aug. 30 for this potential project, it triggered a six-year statute of limitations. This means property owners have six years to file a claim for compensation. She said that although six years seems like a long time, it can sneak up quickly.
Largent said that within a week of the issuance of the certificate, Lewis Rice filed a lawsuit seeking this compensation for residents. The U.S. Department of Justice has 60 days from the filing of the lawsuit to answer.
Lewis Rice is currently representing about a dozen local property owners, but there are more than 50 property owners who they believe have a good claim. Largent said they have sent mail to property owners who they believe will be successful in receiving a claim.
"We do have to follow the solicitation rules in the state, which require us to market as an advertisement," she said in an interview. "So, whether everybody got that information, I can't confirm, but we certainly sent it."
Currently, Lewis Rice can still add landowners to the lawsuit. Largent said she doesn't have an exact date that this period of adding landowners will end. She said that if property owners don't file a claim, they won't be compensated.
"It's not a class action," she said. "Government's not going to reach out to them and offer them money."
After the presentation, one resident said he appreciated the attorneys reaching out because neither the federal government nor county government notified him of the turning over of rights of way.
Largent said she wanted to make it clear that Lewis Rice wasn't there to advocate for or against the trail. She said compensation to property owners doesn't mean less funding for the trail.
"We might have clients that love the trail," she said. "We might have clients that really dislike the idea of a trail. Some that are ambivalent. But that's not what we're here to do. They'll be hosting the trail through their property, and they should be compensated."

title: West End Sewer Project Showing Improvements, Completion Expected in January
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
West End sewer project showing improvements, completion expected in January

 September 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 561
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — With the West End sewer project more than halfway complete, the city and its residents are noticing improvements.The project aims to address sanitary sewage overflow in the lowest lying area of the city at Water Street and Hambrooks Boulevard.
Lou Hyman, a resident of Ward 1 — the ward in which the project is located — said that sewage overflows mean brown water flooding the streets and people's yards.
"It was just really nasty when you're trying to walk your dog," he said.
Cambridge City Engineer Carl "Bucky" Jackson said as the cracks and leaks in the sewer system along Hambrooks Boulevard from Choptank Avenue to Somerset Avenue are repaired, less ground water and tidal water is flowing into the sewers. This means that the sanitary sewer flow is lower, so there aren't as many overflows during rain and high tide events.
"The tidal influence we've had just recently in the last five days, we more than likely would have had a sanitary sewer overflow prior to this project," Jackson said in an interview with the Star Democrat on Sept. 24. "But we have not experienced it in the last week."
Hyman said while there is still flooding, the water is now clean.
As the project progresses, Jackson said the sewer lines between Glenburn and Somerset avenues still need to be completed, along with "some minor work along the way." Jackson said after repairs have been made to the sewers, the next step will be to pave the entire stretch of road from Somerset Avenue to Choptank Avenue.
Jackson said completion of the project is expected in January, as long as they are able to get asphalt before the asphalt plant closes for the winter.
Although the project is currently slightly ahead of schedule, Jackson said it's too early to say if the project will get completed earlier than planned. He said that some bad weather is typical for the months ahead and so the project might not remain ahead of schedule.
The $3.8 million West End sewer project is the first of four projects part of a five-year, $20 million capital program to address water and sewer infrastructure. Jackson said the $4.1 million Trenton Street pump station replacement, also part of the capital program, is currently awaiting permitting.
Cambridge Ward 1 Commissioner Laurel Atkiss said that along with sewage overflowing onto the street, some residents in her ward have had issues with their drains and with flushing their toilets in instances when the tide is high and the streets are flooded.
"That's definitely a problem," she said. "Everybody needs to be able to use their facilities."
She said she has heard from residents who live along the waterfront that they are feeling relief from the West End sewer project.
Hyman said there is still more work to do.
"But we're not getting the sewer line overflows that we were getting," he said.
Atkiss said that many of the city's current projects are to correct mistakes made in the past. She said some of the plumbing practices used 100 or 150 years ago aren't environmentally sound or don't have "effective, long-term results."
"When they get into some of these streets, they're unearthing a puzzle — almost at every intersection — of what was done over the years and how they have to untangle it and correct it," she said. "So they don't even know what they're getting into until they get to each block."

content:
Residents get update on Cambridge flood mitigation project

 August 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 587
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The City of Cambridge held the first of what it says will be multiple "periodic" public meetings to share progress and get feedback on its flood mitigation project along the shore of the Choptank River.The city's Make Cambridge Resilient Flood Mitigation Project Manager Larry White said the city will continue to reach out to the public throughout the entire design process of the project.
"This is the kickoff," he said. "There'll be other meetings where we get you up to date on what's transpired and what's come out of our studies."
The presentation, which was held at the Cambridge branch of the Dorchester County Public Library on Aug. 21, brought many residents who had questions about how the project, which will stretch from Gerry Boyle Park at Great Marsh to the mouth of Cambridge Creek, will affect their properties and the city in general.
The plan for the project includes three main elements: a living shoreline, earth and rock embankments and stormwater management to alleviate flooding.
The city is funding the two-phase project through the grants from the Federal Emergency Management Agency, a grant from the Maryland Department of Natural Resources, the Resilient Maryland Revolving Loan Fund and city budget funds. In June, it announced that the FEMA had awarded the city $1.7 million for the first phase of the project.
The city said FEMA is also reserving $16 million for the second phase of the project. The total $17.7 million in grant money is being awarded through FEMA's Hazard Mitigation Assistance grant.
During the meeting, representatives from the city, the state, the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science at Horn Point, and BayLand Consultants and Designers spoke about climate change, flooding and the project itself.
Maryland Secretary of Emergency Management Russell Strickland talked about the importance of mitigating disasters prior to them occurring. He said mitigation cuts down on the need for response and on the costs associated with recovery.
"So this would be what I would call a transformative mitigation project for the city," he said. "And it's important that it be projects like that because that will have a greater result and a greater benefit for more people."
Horn Point Lab professor Ming Li talked about sea level rise across the Chesapeake Bay and increases in flooding. He said working with nature can be better than fighting with it.
"So that's why there's a lot of interest in a lot of places all around the world to look at nature-based solutions," he said.
Megan Barniea, a BayLand senior project engineer, said no design decisions have been made yet, but the plan is to build upon those three main project elements of a living shoreline, embankments and stormwater management.
Horn Point Lab, which is supporting the project, will help to optimize the living shoreline design, assess flood risk reduction, monitor living shoreline performance and evaluate ecological co-benefits of the project.
Barniea said the project partners will be coming back to the public to get feedback on a 30% design plan. The plan, which she expects will be ready to show in early 2025, will include the footprint of proposed features, elevations and dimensions, and a construction cost estimate.
After the presentation, residents asked questions about the project, including how the project will affect private docks and public access to the waterfront.
White said the city and its partners will work with each property owner, and residents will keep access to their docks. He said there will be some public access to the living shoreline.
"I mean it can't be everywhere, but there will be access," he said.

title: Cambridge Makes Switch to Stop Signs at Some Downtown Intersections Permanent
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge makes switch to stop signs at some downtown intersections permanent

 July 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 317
 Words

 CAMBRIDGE — About five months after the City of Cambridge began turning off certain downtown traffic lights and replacing them with three- and four-way stop signs, the traffic lights are officially coming down.At a City Council meeting on July 8, the council voted unanimously to remove the traffic lights at six intersections where stop signs have been installed.
In a July 1 memo addressed to the City Council, Cambridge City Engineer Carl "Bucky" Jackson shared some background on this project. Last summer, the city contracted with The Traffic Group to complete a downtown traffic study, according to the memo. In December, the City Council voted to temporarily — pending feedback — replace the traffic lights with stop signs at certain intersections.
Since February, the city has replaced six intersections with stop signs over three phases. Those intersections are:
Spring Street and Gay Street.Muir Street and Race Street.Muse Street and Gay Street.
High Street and Glasgow Street.
High Street and Locust Street.
Gay Street and Poplar Street and Race Street.
At the City Council meeting on July 8, acting City Manager David Deutsch said the city found no negatives associated with the study. He said there wasn't an increase in traffic accidents, and neither the city nor police department received "feedback of any significant nature."
In the memo, Jackson said the city received both positive and negative feedback about a week after each phase of the project was completed.
At a City Council meeting in March, Cornelia Turner expressed concerns about the switch from stop lights to stop signs.
"It's a mess," she said at the meeting. "I've almost been rear-ended."
Jackson said that since all three phases were completed in mid-April, the city has received little to no feedback on switch to signs.
With City Council's approval, Deutsch said the city would get started on taking down the traffic lights as quickly as possible. It will cost the city about $4,000 to remove the traffic lights and poles.

title: Choptank Fishing Pier Plans Still TBD
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Choptank fishing pier plans still TBD

 June 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 737
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Maryland Department of Natural Resources is continuing to determine the best place for a new fishing pier on the Choptank River between Talbot and Dorchester counties.The search for a location began in 2021 with closure of the Bill Burton Fishing Pier.
Gregg Bortz, media relations manager for DNR, said in an email that the department is working with both counties, as well as the City of Cambridge, to find "the best option for access" to the Choptank. He said the department is considering a few sites that are "in the general vicinity of the current pier."
Bortz said after this process is complete, DNR plans to move forward with creating that access.
In late December 2021, the fishing pier was closed due to structural safety concerns. A February 2022 underwater inspection revealed crumbling concrete in multiple areas of the structure below the water's surface.
Although Joe Brooks — who lives a few houses down the road from the Dorchester County side of the fishing pier, on Radiance Drive — was sad to see the fishing pier close, he was happy that it would put an end to the trash in his front yard and illegal parking on the street.
"It was just out of control for many years," he said. "Everyday you get up and walk and pick up trash out in the front yard. ... And it's all kinds of trash."
Brooks helped petition the City of Cambridge to get no parking signs put up on the street, but he said there were people who parked there anyway.
"There's not adequate parking for a fishing pier there," Brooks said about where pier's former location. "I mean, there's a very small parking lot for the use of the pier."
As DNR looks for the best spot for a new fishing pier, Brooks thinks it should go somewhere other than where it currently is. He said the Talbot County side of the river has many acres of land with ample space for parking. Brooks said if the fishing pier must go on the Dorchester County side, the county Visitor Center is on the other side of U.S. Route 50, and would make more sense as the pier's location.
"It's not trying to fit a square peg in a round hole," he said.
Parking and accessibility are primary concerns for DNR when it comes to deciding on a location for a new pier, Bortz said.
Brooks said he doesn't know anyone else in the neighborhood who wants a new fishing pier to be built in its current location.
"Pretty well everyone in my area had issues with parking and sometimes (dis)respectful people on the pier," he said.
American Legion Post 91 Commander-elect and former Maryland Sen. Rich Colburn said he estimates there is room for 12 cars in the parking lot for the closed fishing pier. He said a new fishing pier on the other side of Route 50 or on the Talbot County side would have more room for parking.
The American Legion Post, which is directly across the street from the closed fishing pier on Radiance Drive, has been interested in leasing the fishing pier parking lot from DNR since the pier closed. In a May 24 letter, DNR Secretary Josh Kurtz told Colburn in response to the reuqest that DNR was unable to lease the parking area at that time.
Bortz said the lot is not for sale because it could be part of the department's plans for future park access. Colburn said he understands DNR will need the parking lot when it demolishes the current pier, but until that happens, he believes DNR could easily lease the lot to the American Legion.
Mid-Shore Fishing Club President Tom Wilkison thinks the closed pier should be replaced with a new one in the same location.
"Because the community needs it," he said. "There are so many people that used to use that pier, especially from the Cambridge side."
Wilkison, who has never fished off the pier but has walked on it, said the current location of the pier is accessible. He acknowledged it could use a little more parking on the Dorchester side.
"I just hope that the state puts something back there," he said.
Brooks said when DNR does construct a new fishing pier, it's important that it also maintains and polices the pier.
"That's the best way to keep people — in my mind — respectful, is have a respected place and have a presence of people to enforce that," he said.

"The City of Cambridge is committed to the 'Make Cambridge Resilient Initiative' and views this project as a major step forward," the press release states.

title: County Hopes Taking Control of Sanitary District Will Solve Resident Concerns
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
County hopes taking control of sanitary district will solve resident concerns

 April 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 784
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Still in the process of taking back control of its sanitary district, Dorchester County sees the planned transfer of power as a solution for certain issues faced by residents.At a County Council meeting April 16, two residents came to speak about issues relating to water and sewers. Council President Lenny Pfeffer asked for their patience.
"I know this is not the answer that you want to hear at this exact moment," he said to one resident.
Pfeffer said the county is in the process of taking back the Dorchester County Sanitary District to provide the best service for county residents.
"The sanitary district unfortunately grew to much larger than a voluntary board of members could handle, including the day-to-day," he said.
For decades, a volunteer six-member Sanitary District Commission has governed the Dorchester County Sanitary District, which includes the county's water and sewage systems. The commission is appointed by the County Council to six-year terms.
With more resources to manage the sanitary district, the county has been working for the past year to take control of it. At the meeting April 6, Pfeffer said the county expects this change in power will take place in July.
RESIDENTS' CONCERNSCounty resident Jerome Harris, who lives west of Vienna, expressed his concerns with the current setup of Vienna's water treatment plant. The plant serves the residents of Vienna as well as residents of the area known as "West Vienna," including Harris. The plant, set up in the late 1990s, is owned by the Town of Vienna.
Harris said it is unfair that that residents of Vienna and residents of West Vienna get treated differently when they don't pay their quarterly water bills. He said that residents of West Vienna who don't pay are charged for it via the county property tax.
Interim County Manager Jeff Powell said that for those residents who don't pay, the county essentially foots the bill so that their water stays on. County Council Vice President Mike Detmer, who represents Harris' district, said that in the Town of Vienna, residents who don't pay get their water turned off.
Harris said he was not aware of the town shutting off water for town residents.
Powell said the sanitary district could help resolve this issue once the county has regained control of it.
"Sanitary districts have some powers that don't exist otherwise that maybe can help be a solution in this thing," Powell said.
County Attorney Chip MacLeod said a grant for the treatment plant — issued in the 1990s — drove the current setup of the plant.
"It's time to really rethink what this arrangement is," MacLeod said. "And the property owners deserve certainty about what happens if they don't pay their bill. And there should be equal treatment among utility users."
MacLeod said there needs to be a discussion with the Town of Vienna.
Detmer said his personal view is that the residents of "West Vienna" aren't being harmed for not paying their bill.
"This should be resolved so we're not relying on an old agreement," he said. "I think we all can agree on that."
Detmer said other than the West Vienna area being annexed by the Town of Vienna, the main route to solving this issue is through the sanitary district.
Cambridge resident Phil Cecil spoke during public comment about a permit request that the Dorchester County Sanitary District has not acted on since it was submitted in September 2022. The request is to connect his property to the sanitary district sewer line. Cecil said there was nothing "special or unusual" about the request.
Cecil said that when he asked the Sanitary District Commissioners what was being done, and when he could expect action, they said his request had been discussed at a meeting this month, and the commissioners decided that someone from the county office would respond to the connection request.
"What is happening here is a deliberate and intentional delay of assuming the responsibilities delegated to this agency and cannot be tolerated," Cecil said.
Powell said this is a matter of the commission making a decision. He said some of it is because things with the sanitary district are "in the air" right now.
Cecil said he understood and sympathized with that, but things weren't up in the air in 2022 when he applied for the permit.
Powell said he would see if the county could arrange to make an agreement with Cecil that states the county will get him that permit when it has taken control of the sanitary district so that Cecil can start building on the land.
Cecil said he has concerns about falling through the cracks.
"Whenever things change, whenever the powers that be change from one section to another, people like me get lost in the cracks," he said. "And I don't intend to get lost."

title: Sewage Overflows in Cambridge, City Prioritizing Improvements
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Sewage overflows in Cambridge, city prioritizing improvements

 January 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 779
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Harford County resident Jayne Ash saw more than she expected on Jan. 13 when she brought a group of people to Cambridge to look at birds.The end of Oakley Street, near the Choptank River, was flooded that day, Ash said.
"And the overflow was not draining," she said.
The group began to notice a white residue on the sidewalks, which seemed to have been left by the water, now below the curb but still flooding the street.
"The longer we stood there and the longer we looked, we just realized that this was just really nasty sewage water," Ash said, adding that she saw what looked like human feces floating in the water.
As the group was leaving the area, Ash said she could see a leak "coming out of the street," bubbling up six to eight inches.
The entire experience worried Ash.
"We figured we probably shouldn't be walking in the water," she said. "So we were kind of tiptoeing around the edges of where we normally would have gone."
Ash said the city should have roped off the area, posted signs and pumped up the flooded water to transport it elsewhere.
"It's just so many things that they could have done, but I guess they weren't keeping aware of it," she said.
According to the Code of Maryland Regulations, the owner or operator of any sewer system is required to report any overflow — defined as a loss of wastewater or discharge from a sewer system — to the Maryland Department of the Environment and local health department. This report must be made no later than 24 hours after the owner or operator becomes aware of the overflow.
COMAR also states that unless advised otherwise by the state or local health department, the owner or operator of the sewer system must notify the public no later than 24 hours after they become aware of the overflow if it enters shellfish harvesting waters, drinking water sources, waters used as public beaches or waters used for public recreation.
They must also notify the public if the state or local health department has reason to believe the overflow is a public health risk
The public must be notified via a public service announcement or paid advertising in a daily newspaper, radio station, or television station. According to COMAR, if appropriate, the public should be notified of larger overflows with potential environmental or health impacts through posted signage, as well as through the media.
On Jan. 17, the city submitted a telephone report to MDE. In a letter attached to the report, signed by Cambridge City Engineer Carl "Bucky" Jackson, Jackson said that high tides caused the sewage overflow event on Jan. 13.
According to the report, the city was informed of the overflow by MDE on Jan. 17 following a complaint from a resident. No personnel from the city observed the overflow.
Jackson said in the report that based on the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Cambridge tide gauge, the overflow is estimated to have begun at 8 a.m. and stopped around 11:59 p.m on Jan. 13.
Jackson wrote that discharge from the overflow wasn't observed, but paper products were discovered around the manhole where the overflow occurred. Once notified, the street and storm drains were cleaned and disinfected.
In an interview, Jackson said signage notifying residents and visitors of the overflow were placed at the location of the event within four hours of the city learning about it.
Jackson said it was surprising that high tide was the sole cause of this incident. He said that, usually, the cause is a mix of high tide and heavy rains.
Water and sewer infrastructure improvements are one of the city's priorities this year.
Cambridge City Council has set out a $20 million capital program over the next five years for water and sewer infrastructure. The city has budgeted $8 million for fiscal year 2024.
During a meeting between Cambridge City Council, city staff and local state legislators last Monday, Jan. 22, City Manager Tom Carroll said Cambridge annually gets fined for violating the Clean Water Act.
"We are focused on fixing the sewer issues and reducing or eliminating overflows," he said at the meeting.
Earlier this month, the City Council awarded a contract bid to replace the West End sewer, located in the lowest lying area of the city at Water Street and Hambrooks Boulevard.
"Routinely, we have elicit discharges when we have wet weather events," Carroll said. "We have sewage overflows. And we're hoping that this project will fix that."
Jackson said the West End sewer replacement will benefit Oakley Street near the river.
Carroll said there are three other major sewer projects planned that are in "various stages of design" as well as a water booster station to accommodate new development.

title: County Council Approves Vehicle Weight Limit On Black Dog Alley
author: Natalie Jones; Njones@Chespub.Com
content:
County Council Approves Vehicle Weight Limit On Black Dog Alley

 December 14, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; Njones@Chespub.Com | Page: B3 | Section: News 
 
 426
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - The Talbot County Council on Tuesday approved legislation establishing a vehicle weight limit on Black Dog Alley to reduce heavy truck through traffic.Resolution 351, which received unanimous support from council members, will prohibit vehicles over 17,000 pounds from traveling on Black Dog Alley, which runs between Cordova Road and Dover Road.
Some vehicles are exempt from the restrictions, including vehicles owned or operated by government entities and their employees, vehicles involved with agricultural production or operations, emergency vehicles, vehicles belonging to those whose land is located on or is only accessible via Black Dog Alley and vehicles providing services like heating oil delivery, trash pickup or property improvement.
Vehicles over the weight limit can use U.S.
Route 50 as an alternate route, which is better equipped to handle oversized vehicles and higher traffic volume.
The need for the legislation stems from maintenance and safety issues along the narrow roadway.
The concept of a weight limit on the road has previously been considered by the county.
The council introduced similar legislation in late 2019, but the resolution did not progress.
During the legislation's public hearing Tuesday, Talbot County farmer Keith Shortall, who lives off of Black Dog Alley, said while he does utilize the road for agricultural purposes during harvest season, he's noticed many trucks hauling grain from the Port of Baltimore down into Hurlock in Dorchester County year-round.
Shortall emphasized the need for advance signage for the change in vehicle allowance.
He also stressed the need for other improvements on the narrow parts of the road that don't have shoulder lanes.
" Regardless of what you do with this, the work that needs to be done on Black Dog Alley still needs to happen," he said.
Design for improvements to parts of Black Dog Alley is in progress, said Ray Clarke, the county engineer.
Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble echoed safety concerns, noting that Black Dog Alley is the most accident-prone road in the county.
Gamble also raised a flag to future traffic problems once the new regional medical center is constructed, saying Black Dog Alley will likely see more emergency vehicles coming from southern Caroline County utilizing the road.
Gamble said the sheriff 's office would start enforcement of the new restriction on Black Dog Alley in an educational way at first.
Citations are more likely to be handed out after an adjustment period.
John Trax, a Talbot County farmer and the "self-proclaimed mayor of Black Dog Alley," expressed full support for the resolution. He adding that he wished more could be added to it, namely ways to further address traffic and speeding.
The resolution took effect upon adoption.

title: Commissioners Prioritize Roads, Bridges Projects
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
Commissioners prioritize roads, bridges projects

 November 22, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 3A | Section: News 
 
 666
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - A list of projects to repair and maintain the county's dirt roads and to open closed bridges was presented to the Caroline County Commissioners Oct. 24 by then-Caroline County Director of Public Works Ryan White and Roads Superintendent Bryan North.As of Nov. 8, White was no longer the director, but no further information was available as of press time.The number of houses on the roads determined the priority of attention to them.Applying that standard, Commission President Travis Breeding set aside Alms House, County Farm and Dead End roads east of Denton as low priority.Concerns about the amount of traffic and the distance road crews must travel to maintain the roads were also considered, along with the amount of truck traffic and school bus routes."A truck on a muddy road, it just kills it," White said. "So that's also something we took into account when we figured this out.Breeding and Commissioner Frank Bartz agreed that Mitchell and Wolf roads were priorities because of the number of houses. White said he considered property density rather than the number of houses.Participating remotely, Commission Vice President Larry Porter suggested beginning work on Wolf Road east of Henderson and reaching out to residents for feedback on Mitchell Road south of Denton, who had expressed concerns in the past about increased traffic if the road were tar-and-chipped.Tar-and-chip paving increases the speed on those roads about 10 to 15 miles per hour.Beck Road connecting State Routes 404 and 313 (Federalsburg Highway), Trunkline Road north of Henderson and Jones Corner Road between Concord and American Corner were also considered.Dirt roads are inspected about once a month and scraped as needed, White said.The commissioners determined that Beck and Wolf roads were priorities, which are in line for gravel, then tar-andchip paving, with Mitchell on the list after calls to residents.White said he's reached out to the Maryland State Roads Administration about funding the culvert pipe replacement on River Road.In the meantime, White has "given (SHA) the green light to go ahead and try to get us at least an 80-20 (state and county funding) split on Bloomery Road" north of Federalsburg Road, he said. "That does not sound like it's going to be an issue at all." Issues concerning the approach to the bridge on Long Swamp Road generated some discussion about the extent of the county's ownership of certain rights of way, something County Attorney Stewart Barroll suggested discussing in a closed session."If we can get 100% funding, are we interested in having a discussion about reopening some of the older bridges that have been closed?" Breeding asked. Bartz and Porter agreed.Regarding reopening bridges, property owners will be contacted for their opinions.The attention turned to River Road west of Denton. "I don't think anybody misses that bridge being closed from a traffic standpoint," Porter said."No, but where I'm coming from is the proximity to the high school, the waterfront and the potential for economic growth out there," Breeding said. "It's close to our growth area in the county, it is waterfront property with higher potential property values and it's right in the center of the county as well. If we have a discussion about opening one, i think that one makes sense to talk about.Other closed bridges are on Poplar Neck Road west of Preston, Bloomery Road and Back Landing Road which runs from Preston into Dorchester County. White said he was waiting to hear back from SHA about available funding for reopening the bridge on Gregg Road.According to the county's website, the roads division "is responsible for maintaining over 450 miles of roadway and 39 bridges or crossings in Caroline County." Over 70 miles of those roads are dirt roads.

title: County to Consider Vehicle Weight Limits on Black Dog Alley
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
County to consider vehicle weight limits on Black Dog Alley

 November 16, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 4 | Section: News

 EASTON - The Talbot County Council on Tuesday introduced a resolution that would establish a vehicle weight limit on Black Dog Alley to reroute some of the road's through traffic.According to Mike Mertaugh, the assistant county engineer, Black Dog Alley has essentially become a bypass around Easton for traffic going to and from southern Caroline County and Dorchester County.That traffic volume, along with heavy trucks, are causing maintenance issues along the roadway, Mertaugh said. Restricting heavy trucks from traveling on the road would extend its lifespan and improve safety on the road.Some parts of the road are narrow, and the southern part of Black Dog Alley does not have a shoulder lane.While the county roads department has worked to keep it maintained, heavy vehicles on the edge of pavement without support can cause the road to "crumble away," Mertaugh said.The restriction wouldn't burden trucks, he said - U.S. Route 50 almost runs parallel to Black Dog Alley, and the highway is designed for that type of traffic.The legislation, if passed, wouldn't impede local traffic or farmers, and exceptions would be made for agricultural businesses and government vehicles.The county already has a similar weight restriction in place on Dover Neck Road, which experienced similar issues.The council unanimously introduced the legislation, known as Resolution 351. A public hearing will be held on Tuesday, Dec. 12, at 6:30 p.m.

author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: News
