 CAMBRIDGE - During a council meeting recently, the Dorchester County Council was given an update by Maryland Department of Transportation officials on different projects and programs affecting the county.The council heard from Maryland Transportation Secretary Paul Wiedefeld as well as representatives from the Maryland State Highway Administration, Maryland Motor Vehicle Administration, Maryland Transportation Authority, Maryland Transit Administration, Maryland Aviation Administration and Maryland Port Administration.Matt Baker, state highway deputy administrator for project development, talked about a traffic signal project affecting U.S. Route 50 and Maryland Route 750 that will enhance safety for pedestrians and bicyclists. The $208,000 project includes the implementation of countdown pedestrian signals.Baker also mentioned the new sidewalk on Bayly road, which runs between Maces Lane and Governors Avenue, that will make the road safer for pedestrians and bicyclists.Currently, the State Highway Association is doing an intersection study at Maryland Route 343 and Maces Lane to see what safety enhancements it might need to employ at that intersection, according to a press release from MDOT.Bob Munroe, Maryland Port Administration deputy executive director of administration and environment, talked about the Mid-Chesapeake Bay Ecosystem Restoration project. The project, in partnership with the U.S.Army Corps of Engineers and located in Dorchester County, will create shoreline protection for the county by using dredged material from shipping channels to rebuild James and Barren islands."On a macro-level, this project will give the state much needed Chesapeake Bay sediment replacement capacity for the next 30 years," Munroe said during the meeting. "Locally, we believe that the MidBay island restoration will help reduce storm-related shoreline erosion for up to 30% on the upper Hoopers Island area and the areas north of Fishing Creek." Munroe added that he believes the project will also increase overall property values in the county by more than $1 million.This is in part due to a reduced rate of energy and improved water quality.Barren Island construction has already begun and James Island construction is set to begin in 2025, Munroe said.These projects are a part of MDOT's six-year draft Consolidated Transportation Program, a $21.2 billion investment plan for the state's transportation system. According to the press release, the plan will be finalized and submitted in January for consideration of the General Assembly. MDOT is meeting with all of Maryland's counties and Baltimore City to discuss the plan.According to the press release from MDOT, allocations for Dorchester County in the draft Consolidated Transportation Program also include $919,000 to support local transit operations provided by Delmarva Community Transit, $123,000 to help Delmarva Community Services install a propane station for propanepowered vehicles and $337,000 to help fund HVAC improvements at the Cambridge-Dorchester Regional Airport terminal.During the meeting, the County Council presented a list of priorities it hopes MDOT can address, including traffic improvements, pedestrian and safety improvements around the county.These include:▪ Traffic and geometric improvements at the Maryland Route 392 and Route 14 intersection.▪ A pipe replacement on Maryland Route 336.▪ Pedestrian improvements on Maryland Route 392 through Hurlock.▪ Railroad crossing improvements at Indiantown Road and Maryland Route 331.▪ Turn lane improvements to Maryland Route 16 at Mount Holly Road.▪ Pavement marking updates in Cambridge.▪ Painting the jersey walls on Malkus Bridge.▪ A full-function intersection on westbound U.S.50 at Chateau Road.▪ Rumble strips on Mount Holly Road.▪ Visibility improvements on the drawbridge in Cambridge.The city of Cambridge and town of East New Market also submitted a list to the county to be presented to MDOT. Their lists include changes to the intersection at Maces Lane and Washington Street in Cambridge and assistance with speeding in East New Market, among other items.After hearing the presentations from MDOT officials, council members shared their comments with the officials.Council member Ricky Travers talked about the change in road width on Maryland Route 335.He said the road width changes by about 2 or 3 feet on either side."I really think the state needs to take a strong look at that," he said.Council President Lenny Pfeffer and Vice President Mike Detmer thanked the State Highway Administration District Engineer Mark Crampton."I wanted to thank you so much for answering emails and questions and concerns of the council in general and our citizens when they talk," Pfeffer said. "Mark has been phenomenal in customer service [and] getting back to us with answers, whether it's something we like to hear or something we don't." Detmer said the work Crampton and his team have done means a lot to him and to the residents of Dorchester County."From the little to the big, your local team here has been very exemplary in helping us," he said to the MDOT officials.

title: Broadband Internet Project Ahead of Schedule
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Broadband internet project ahead of schedule

 September 28, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 4 | Section: News

 Words

 CAMBRIDGE - Choptank Electric Cooperative and Choptank Fiber presented the Dorchester County Council last Tuesday evening on the broadband internet project that will bring broadband to about 704 locations in the county."We believe that this entire project will be done by the end of 2024," Valerie Connelly, vice president of government affairs and public relations for Choptank Electric, said. "We are moving much faster than we thought." Choptank Fiber, a broadband internet company, is a wholly-owned subsidiary of Choptank Electric. Its goal is to "serve the unserved." Connelly said a broadband project of this kind is often expected to take about three years."The first year is all engineering and design, the second year they start to do the construction, the third year [is] connecting members," she said. "We've been able to build out most of what we're doing in 14 months or so. We're very pleased." The $8.3 million project, which runs below Federalsburg and into Northeast Dorchester County, builds on a recently finished broadband project in Caroline County. Funding for this Dorchester project comes from the Maryland Office of Statewide Broadband, Choptank Electric and Choptank Fiber and Dorchester County.The Office of Statewide Broadband is contributing $4.08 million, Choptank Electric and Choptank Fiber is contributing $3.7 million and Dorchester County has pledged $500,284 of American Rescue Plan Act funds."The grant money that was contributed by the county and by the state allows us to bring on contractors and keep them working continuously," Connelly said. "So we're moving them from one project to the next trying to get to everybody who is unserved here on the shore." Connelly said construction has started for the project and most of the engineering has been completed. She added that because the project has been divided into zones, some areas are opening up for service as the project continues."We're not waiting until the entire project is built out," she said. "We're, weekly, announcing areas that we're opening for service for members who live there." Connelly said the question everyone asks as soon as they hear about the project is, "How much is it going to cost?" Choptank Fiber offers different speed packages. These include: Up to 100 Mbps for $84.95 per month Up to 450 Mbps for $99.95 per month Up to 1,000 Mbps for $139.95 per month Up to 2,500 Mbps for $279.95 per month Connelly added that there are three affordability programs that could bring down these prices for customers. The first program is a $15 discount per month if the customer qualifies for energy assistance.The second program is a $30 discount per month if the resident is eligible for certain programs, like income programs.Connelly said residents must log onto the Federal Communications Commission website to get qualified for this program.The third program is an additional $15 discount per moth for those that qualify for the second program."They automatically get the state program," Connelly said.Connelly said Choptank Electric thinks these programs are important."We don't want anyone to have to make the decision not to take broadband when we get there because of an affordability issue," she said. "We are doing more this fall to really promote that and make sure that families know that all these options are available." After Connelly's presentation, council member Ricky Travers asked what the company needs from the county to continue moving forward with this project - "other than money," he joked.Connelly said council members should continue to keep track of residents that reach out to say they don't have good service or they don't have any service.Council Vice President Mike Detmer called some of the areas in the county "drastically unserved." "So I know that it's going to be a very welcomed thing for the citizens of this county," he said of the project.

title: Dorchester County Public Schools Faces Budget Deficit
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Dorchester County Public Schools faces budget deficit

 January 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 636
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — As Dorchester County Public Schools prepares to submit its fiscal year 2026 budget to the county, it is also preparing for some tough conversations.With $86 million in expected revenues and $97.5 million in estimated expenses for fiscal year 2026, the district is facing a deficit. Currently, with carryover in funds from previous years, the estimated deficit is at $10.19 million.
"We've just got some difficult decisions to make as a district on how we're going to move forward with the current budget crisis that we're in," DCPS Superintendent Jymil Thompson said during a Dorchester County Board of Education budget work session Thursday.
Jodi Colman, district assistant superintendent of academics and student services, said the budget increases for fiscal year 2026 make it possible to keep the district's current staff in place.
"This would just be to basically maintain the programs that we have right now," she said about the draft budget. "All of those increases were due to just keeping our staff that we have for the most part."
Thompson said "a whole host of things" has caused the deficit, mentioning fixed costs and unfunded mandates from the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, a plan passed by the Maryland General Assembly in 2021 that aims to improve student outcomes and the quality of education across the state.
Board of Education Member Brandy Dawson Cumberland said that although the board likes a lot of what the Blueprint aims to do, there are "certain unfunded mandates that are going to cut other things."
Thompson said the district is still waiting on exact numbers from the state and county. He said once they have those numbers, it is possible the deficit could be lower than $10.19 million.
"But I don't think that it will be higher than that," he said.
So far, the district has taken a number of actions to reduce the deficit, Thompson said. This includes:
Reducing some positions added with Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief fundingSending emails about non-essential spendingDeciding not to hire for vacated positionsReducing the central office custodian scheduleReducing student support monitorsMerging some job dutiesEliminating the education specialist position
"We did try to make some significant changes," Thompson said. "And there's more that I didn't put up that we have done. But the reality is it's not enough."
The district is looking into more actions that can be taken to reduce the deficit. Some possible actions include revisiting who should have board vehicles, auditing and reducing the number of programs and platforms the district uses, revising overtime policies, sharing resources with the county and reducing staff.
"No one wants this one," Thompson said about reducing staff.
While listing different "cost containment options" Thompson and board members made it clear that the district hasn't made any decisions yet, and is just looking at potential cost-cutting options.
"We are just at the beginning of starting to think about what things we can do to attack that number," Board of Education Vice President Talibah Chikwendu said.
"And that's why we really would like to have public input to know what the public feels are areas we should focus on if possible," Board President Sheri Hubbard said. "Because we want to do what's best for kids, bottom line."
The Dorchester County Board of Education will host another budget work session on Feb. 13. It will also hold one in March. The district's proposed budget must be submitted to the county in June.
Board Member Chris Wheedleton said that if community members are able to do anything, they should talk with their representatives in Annapolis.
"Because we need their help," he said.
Thompson urged that this is the time to work together and not be divided.
"Because at the end of the day, we know that $10 million deficit that we're in, that's going to hurt the kids," he said. "That's going to have a profound impact on how we can provide resources for our students."

title: Cambridge City Council Passes Fiscal 2026 Budget
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Cambridge City Council passes fiscal 2026 budget

 June 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 395

 CAMBRIDGE — The Cambridge City Council adopted its fiscal year 2026 budget Monday night after a contentious discussion over whether or not they would hold a vote or defer the budget adoption.After hearing public comments, council members considered whether or not they needed to make further amendments or deletions that would require deferring the vote.
Council member Brett Summers suggested deferring the vote because council member Brian Roche was not in attendance.
"I just want to remind you all, we're here to do the city's budget not to make sure commissioners have their camera time," said Mayor Lajan Cephas in response.
Council President Sputty Cephas pointed out that two council members will be absent at the next meeting and that deferring budget approval again would push the budget adoption very close to the start of the fiscal year on July 1.
The discussion of whether council members' schedules aligned and if they would discuss budget approval continued for several minutes.
"I just want to make you all aware, I'm very disappointed right now," said Lajan Cephas, who is not able to vote on council matters except in the event a tiebreaker vote is necessary. "I know my opinion doesn't matter, but we're here to do the city's business, and that should always matter."
Summers made a motion to defer the vote, and council member Frank Stout seconded. Sputty Cephas was joined by council member Shay Sisco-Lewis in opposition the motion. Lajan Cephas broke the tie, also voting in opposition of the motion. The council then began discussing the proposed budget.
Eventually, council members approved the budget unanimously.
The council also passed an ordinance establishing a maintenance reserve fund, which transferred $500,000 from the general fund to the maintenance reserve. Steckman and Director of Finance Perry Peregoy will maintain the reserve and deposit a minimum of $50,000 each fiscal year. No money will be withdrawn from the maintenance reserve fund until July 1, 2036.
The FY26 budget established the property tax rate of $1.69 per $100 of all assessed value, the same tax rate as the previous year.
The City Council was presented with a comically large check from representatives of Chesapeake Employers Insurance totaling $174,000 from a 2022 dividend. Steckman said the city has been working with Chesapeake Employers to help control workplace accidents and that the money will go into the general fund.
The city's FY2026 budget will go into effect on July 1.

title: Dorchester County Council Approves 2026 Budget
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Dorchester County Council approves 2026 budget

 May 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 434
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DORCHESTER — After receiving community feedback over removing the tax differentials for Cambridge and Hurlock, the Dorchester County Council worked with each other, County Manager Jerry Jones and county staff to modify the proposed county budget.The differentials, which lower tax rates in the municipalities to account for duplicated services, remain intact in the fiscal year 2026 budget passed by the County Council Tuesday.
Rather than removing the differentials, the county made adjustments to its budget including deferring all nonprofit funding to a later time.
The county's real property tax rate will increase by 3 cents across the board, bringing the overall tax rate to $1.03 per $100 of assessed value. Cambridge residents will pay 95.67 cents per $100 of assessed value, and Hurlock residents will pay 94.79 cents per $100 of assessed value.
"We came up with a product. Is it the best product in the world? Heck no. But it will suit the needs of the people in the county," said council member William Nichols in reference to the budget.
As Nichols voted in favor of the budget bill, he made a point to explain to the community that this was the worst budget he has seen in the 30 years he's sat on the council. Nichols said that there have been no hidden agendas and that he appreciates all the feedback.
Council President Lenny Pfeffer is concerned the council will end up in the same position next year, with the state of Maryland expecting to reach a $6 billion deficit in the next two years if there are no significant changes.
Council member Rob Kramer agreed with Nichols, saying this was the worst budget he's seen in the 20 years in his seat, but "we made lemons out of lemonade."
Contention between the state capital and rural Maryland was brought up often. Kramer said he doesn't think Annapolis has any hope in rural Maryland, but at the same time, he doesn't have any hope in Annapolis.
Maryland Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) attended the meeting Tuesday, assuring residents they have a voice in Annapolis. Hutchinson echoed the sentiments of the council members, saying there's a major disconnect between what happens in the capital and what happens in the community.
"I just ask you, please, when you hear us talking about this stuff next year, please, I ask you to write letters, please make phone calls, please be as active as possible in your community to relay to Annapolis that Dorchester County cannot continue to take the economic hits it has been," Pfeffer said before opening up the floor for comments.
The budget bill will take effect on July 1.

title: Residents Frustrated with Dorchester Budget Proposal
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Residents frustrated with Dorchester budget proposal

 May 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: News 
 
 611
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The sign-in sheet to speak was as full as the room at Tuesday's public hearing on Dorchester County's proposed budget for fiscal year 2026.In the packed council chambers, residents brought concerns over the looming possibility of losing their tax differentials.
Cambridge Mayor Lejan Cephas walked up, shook each council member's hand and stepped to the podium. She encouraged the council to think about the ramifications of this decision and pleaded to keep the tax differential for city residents.
Cephas then read a letter from the Mid-Shore Board of Realtors.
"In Dorchester County, 33% of homeowners and 30% of renters are already cost burdened, spending more than 30% of their income on housing," she said. "Increasing property taxes would further strain these households potentially leading to displacement or severe financial hardship."
In the letter, the board articulated that getting rid of the tax differential will disproportionately affect senior citizens and low-income households while simultaneously unfairly burdening Cambridge and Hurlock residents.
Concerns largely centered on a proposal in the county's draft budget to remove tax differentials, a move suggested among multiple tax increases in an effort to address a $6.2 million deficit.
The tax differentials, introduced in Dorchester County in 2007, lower property taxes in Cambridge and Hurlock to offset the cost of providing duplicate services like zoning and policing in the surrounding municipalities.
The county raised its overall tax rate by 3 cents in its budget proposal, a 3% increase. That increase would be more steep for Cambridge and Hurlock residents if the differentials are removed.
In the current fiscal year, Cambridge residents pay the county 92.67 cents per $100 of assessed valuation of property. Hurlock residents pay 91.79 cents per $100 of assessed value. If the differential is removed, these residents will pay the county's proposed rate of $1.03 per $100 of assessed value.
Some residents, such as Tom Hannon, advocated for a more equitable tax increase. Hannon noted that higher taxes are inevitable but do not have to be inequitable. Seated residents nodded their heads and echoed his sentiments with a "mhm" and "that's true."
Several more county residents came up to speak. A majority remained on theme, condemning the council for the proposed budget plan and begging for their voices not to fall on deaf ears. The room was tense. Residents and council members alike hung their heads and let out frustrated sighs throughout the 45 minutes of open session.
Council member Ricky Travers was the first to comment. He insisted the council give staff direction on changing the budget to better reflect the residents' voices before signing it on May 20.
"That would mean, you know, we're talking, everyone in the county is taxed the same," he said. The room erupted in applause.
Council Vice President Mike Detmer appeared visibly frustrated throughout the evening. When asked if he had a comment, he said, "I have a lot to say actually."
Detmer expressed that this is painful for him for two reasons: the first being that he dislikes taxes and the second being that this is not his doing.
"This entire imbalance was foisted upon us by a supermajority from somewhere else," he continued.
"It's extremely painful to have any implication on things originating in this county. This is all from the state," he said. As Detmer concluded, a few residents walked out in frustration.
At prior meetings, Dorchester County officials have placed some blame for the $6.2 million deficit with state mandates for education funding and cost shifts from the state for things like teacher pensions.
Council member Rob Kramer did not make a comment and council member William Nichols stated he is waiting until the budget vote next week to comment. That meeting will be held on May 20 at 6 p.m.

title: Cambridge, Hurlock Speak Out Against Dorchester Tax Differential Cut
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Cambridge, Hurlock speak out against Dorchester tax differential cut

 May 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 655
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Leading into the first public budget hearing for Dorchester County's proposed fiscal year 2026 budget, Cambridge and Hurlock leaders made their appeals for a reinstatement of tax differentials."We beg you to pull out a pencil and make some changes," Hurlock Council President Earl Murphy Jr. said at the Dorchester County Council meeting May 6.
During the standing-room-only meeting, the council heard from municipal leaders as well as residents about their concerns with the state of the draft budget.
Concerns largely centered on a proposal in the county's draft budget to remove tax differentials, or lower property tax rates, for Cambridge and Hurlock residents. The proposal was one of multiple tax increases suggested in an effort to address a $6.2 million deficit.
The differentials aim to address services paid for by the municipalities instead of the county.
In the current fiscal year, Cambridge residents pay the county 92.67 cents per $100 of assessed valuation of property. Hurlock residents pay 91.79 cents per $100 of assessed value. If the differential is removed, these residents will pay the county's proposed rate of $1.03 per $100 of assessed value.
At the meeting May 6, Cambridge Mayor Lajan Cephas said the removal of the tax differential would only be acceptable if the county planned to provide the services to Cambridge and Hurlock residents that the municipalities currently provide.
"Let's be real, the county does not have the capacity to fulfill these necessary service needs," she said. "Therefore, why remove the differential?"
Cephas proposed the county should instead take out a loan on its reserve fund and pave three less miles of roads in fiscal year 2026. She said doing this would save the county enough money to keep the differentials.
Hurlock Town Manager John Avery suggested keeping the tax differentials in place and imposing a higher tax across the county. He said that would be more equitable.
Cephas also mentioned an idea to create a Dorchester County Revenue Options Task Force. She said those in the task force would be charged with locating potential additional revenue streams. She said she would sign up to be on the task force if it was created.
"A loss for Dorchester County is a loss for Cambridge," she said. "And we're in this battle with you."
In an interview May 7, Hurlock Mayor the Rev. Charles Cephas said the duty of elected officials is to make life better for their constituents. He said with other financial concerns like inflation, the removal of the tax differential could be devastating for residents.
Charles Cephas said after the county meeting, he is still "very concerned" and "very wary" the county's budget difficulties will be an annual issue. "And the residents are unable to financially support this type of increase," he said.
In recent months, the county's budget woes have created an atmosphere of concern, frustration and, at times, despair during meetings. The council has said its budget problems have largely been brought on by cost shifts from the state.
Former Cambridge Mayor Cleveland Rippons argued the county is doing the same thing to its residents that the state is doing to the county with cost shifts.
"Is that not the same?" he asked.
At the end of the meeting, Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said the council hears what everyone is saying and understands this is hard for residents.
"We lose sleep over this," he said. "Everybody says that we don't care. We do care."
Pfeffer said the council has made efforts to address budget problems without raising taxes, but those efforts have not been fruitful.
"If we don't pay the bills, they'll withhold our income tax," he said about the state. "That is why this is so hard for us to deal with."
The Dorchester County Council will hold its next budget public hearing May 13 at 6 p.m. The final budget hearing and budget adoption is slated for May 20. Pfeffer said the council cannot make any changes to the draft budget until after the next public hearing on May 13.

title: Caroline County Retains Tax Differentials, at Least for This Year
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County retains tax differentials, at least for this year

 May 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 546
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners held their last fiscal year 2026 public budget hearing Tuesday evening.While the commissioners received multiple recognitions for balancing the budget, municipalities brought questions about property tax rates and real property tax differential rates.
Ridgely Commissioner Brad Sears asked the county commissioners what the extended outlook was for municipal tax differentials.
"Just in terms of looking forward from my town's perspective, I would like to get your overall sense of where this might be headed, if that's appropriate," Sears said.
In Caroline County's proposed budget, the property tax rate sits at 98 cents per $100 of assessed value. For towns incorporated within the county, tax rates can sit between one cents to six cents lower than the county's rate.
The differentials were put in place to keep resident of towns from being taxed twice for services provided to these residents by the municipality instead of the county.
"This is something that was in play when I came into office, and it's been a real subject that I battle with over the years," County Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter said. "What this means is it does not affect the town's budget, it affects the money the county collects in their county property tax rate.
"I will say tonight that this will be the last year I would support the property tax differential, I know its gonna be a very controversial subject... In this year's budget, we did not collect about $600,000 in the property tax differential. We're able to balance the budget this year. Going forward, I don't have a clue."
Porter advocated for eliminating the differentials in coming years, pointing to cost shifts from the state that he says will make it more difficult for the county to balance future budgets.
"We will not be able to forgo $600,000 revenue in the next year, I don't think we will," Porter said. "I see nothing but cost being shifted every year, the Blueprint number just keeps exponentially going up every year... I'm not sure where the road is going to take us."
The situation is similar to one being seen in Dorchester County this fiscal year.
In an effort to address a $6.2 million deficit, Dorchester County has proposed multiple tax increases in its draft fiscal year 2026 budget, including the removal of tax differentials for Cambridge and Hurlock residents.
The Cambridge City Council has voiced opposition to the county's elimination of the differentials. In a unanimous vote Monday, the City Council voted to adopt a resolution that requests the Dorchester County Council "develop and implement an annual tax differential or rebate model" to address the "tax burden" of county property taxes on Cambridge residents.
While Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding does not fully agree with Porter, he said he understands Porter's point.
"My position is a little different than Commissioner Porter. I believe that there are redundant services that are provided by the municipalities," Breeding said. "I know the formula that generated the tax differential was generated for police protection.
"....I don't know what the fiscal situation is going to be next year, we may find ourselves in the same dilemma that Dorchester county is in this year, I don't think we will…. I am still at the maintain point, but I certainly understand Commissioner Porter's position. That's where I'm at right now."

title: Cambridge City Manager Presents Balanced Draft Budget
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Cambridge city manager presents balanced draft budget

 April 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 442
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — A few sentences into introducing Cambridge's proposed fiscal year 2026 budget, City Manager Glenn Steckman told those at a Cambridge City Council meeting April 28 that the city is financially stable."And I think that's very important," he said. "That does not mean that challenging times may not be in the city's future. However, we should look at the glass as half full."
During the meeting, Steckman detailed the city's proposed balanced $18 million general fund budget and discussed the city's four enterprise funds, which include sewer, marina, water and special projects funds.
Steckman called the fiscal year 2026 budget a "transitional budget" as COVID-19 relief funding through the American Rescue Plan Act comes to an end.
"This year's budget preparation included transitioning away from the ARPA funds," Steckman said. "These are once-in-a-generation funds that allow the city to pay salaries, support capital projects and fund nonprofit donations."
GENERAL FUND
According to the draft general fund budget, the city expects to bring in $9.84 million in taxes at the same tax rate it did last year, 80 cents per $100 of assessed value. With no plans to raise taxes, the city's budget stands in contrast with the county's.
In mid-April, the Dorchester County Council introduced a $91.96 million proposed operating budget for fiscal year 2026 with proposals to increase property taxes, remove the municipal tax differential, increase local income tax and eliminate tax rebates offered to municipalities.
In Cambridge, the proposed general fund budget includes a 3% raise for all city employees except Steckman and additional $3,000 raises for those in the police department so the positions stay competitive in the marketplace.
Steckman said the budget includes four new positions: a public information officer, code officer, housing adviser and GIS technician.
Steckman said the housing adviser will act as an advocate for renters in Cambridge.
CAPITAL PROJECTS
Although the city is not facing the same kinds of budget concerns the county is facing, Steckman said the city has $23 million in capital needs. He said the city will seek grants to help address this but that probably won't be enough.
Currently, the city has budgeted $2.1 million for capital projects in fiscal year 2026.
Steckman said the mayor and commissioners will "seriously" have to look into borrowing or obtaining a bond of $1.5 million to replace the HVAC system at the city's public safety complex on Washington Street and at least $8 million to renovate the historic city hall on Gay Street.
"We cannot get grants or anywhere enough grants to offset these costs," Steckman said. "And these costs are only rising each year that we don't address them."
Steckman said the city will begin setting times to meet with City Council about the budget.

title: Cambridge City Council Calls on County for Tax Differential
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Cambridge City Council calls on county for tax differential

 April 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 489
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Following the introduction of Dorchester County's draft fiscal year 2026 budget, the Cambridge City Council is requesting a more equitable approach to taxes.In a unanimous vote Monday, the City Council voted to adopt a resolution that requests the Dorchester County Council "develop and implement an annual tax differential or rebate model" to address the "tax burden" of county property taxes on Cambridge residents.
In an effort to address a $6.2 million deficit, Dorchester County has proposed multiple tax increases in its draft fiscal year 2026 budget, including the removal of tax differentials, or lower property tax rate, for Cambridge and Hurlock residents.
During the meeting, Cambridge Commissioner Brian Roche said the council understands the county is facing budget problems that have been brought on by "unfunded mandates" from the state.
"We're sympathetic to those challenges," Roche said. "However, the solution cannot be to place an even greater burden on Cambridge."
In the current fiscal year, Cambridge residents pay the county 92.67 cents per $100 of assessed valuation of property and Hurlock residents pay 91.79 cents per $100 of assessed value. If the differential is removed, these residents will pay the county's rate of $1.03 per $100 of assessed value.
Roche said the tax differential is essentially the county acknowledging Cambridge and Hurlock pay for many of their own services — like public safety and water and sewer — so the county doesn't have to.
Roche estimated that with the county's budget proposals — which include an increase of 3 cents to the real property tax for all county residents — Cambridge residents would face a 11.15% increase on their county tax bill. He said Hurlock would face an increase of about 12%.
Roche said county residents who do not live in Cambridge or Hurlock would face a 3% increase.
"It's not equitable to ask for us to take a bigger slice of this pie when there's other areas they're not asking for them to do their share," Cambridge Mayor Lajan Cephas said.
Before the City Council voted to adopt the resolution, Commissioner Brett Summers said he has been talking about the tax differential since his campaign. He said he has been advocating for the hiring of a consultant to determine what the "right" tax rate is.
"And I think what that'll result in doing is reduce the tax rate that city residents pay but ... increase the tax rate that county residents pay," he said, "... because we're not trying to reduce the revenue coming into the county, we're just trying to have a fair and equitable allocation of taxes bases on services provided."
Commission President Sputty Cephas agreed with Roche and Lajan Cephas, saying that he understands the county's situation, but the city is providing services that would otherwise fall on the county's plate. He said there needs to be a "fair and equitable" solution.
"So how we get there, I'm open to it," he said. "But as of right now, I'm in support of (the resolution)."

title: Dorchester County Makes Its Way Through Grueling Budget Process
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Dorchester County makes its way through grueling budget process

 April 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 694
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Over the past four months, an atmosphere of concern, frustration and, at times, despair has colored budget meetings in Dorchester County.In mid-April, the Dorchester County Council introduced a $91.96 million proposed operating budget for fiscal year 2026 with proposals to increase taxes. The introduction came after months of work by county staff to eliminate an estimated $6.2 million deficit.
At the same time, Dorchester County Public Schools has been working to eliminate a multi-million dollar deficit of its own. At an April budget work session, DCPS Superintendent Jymil Thompson said the district is still $5.59 million in the hole. The district hopes to eliminate the deficit by the Board of Education's May meeting.
To balance and pass these budgets, difficult decisions — like the school district canceling summer school for 2025 and the county increasing 911 fees from $1.50 to $4.25 — have already been made.
"We hate to have to put any of this on the backs of our citizens, but these are state laws that are being passed down as a bandaid for us to pay," County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said in an interview with The Star Democrat. "And unfortunately we're having to pass it down onto our citizens because we have no other revenue to pay these bills."
WHAT MAKES FY26 DIFFERENT
Dorchester County's proposed operating budget is $10 million more than the fiscal year 2025 budget passed last May. County Manager Jerry Jones said the increases are in part due to new education requirements from the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, the state's education plan.
Jones said another reason the county has had to increase spending include cost shifts from the state to the county for things like teacher pensions.
In an effort to lessen budget costs, the county sought a waiver for the maintenance of effort for education, which is a law that requires counties to provide as much funding per pupil as was provided in the previous fiscal year. But with a narrow window between the state passing a budget and the waiver's due date, the county had to ask for an extension, which was denied.
"It's disappointing," Jones said. "But at the end of the day, we've got to keep moving forward."
Thompson said Blueprint requirements, like increasing teacher starting salaries, are part of the reason why the school district's budget — which is separate from the county's — has been difficult to balance this year. He said inflation and recurring program costs have also hindered the process.
"No decision is easy," he said. "But I think we're all trying to make the best decision for our students."
Both Jones and Thompson said they don't see the annual budget process getting easier any time soon. Jones said he doesn't see things getting easier unless change is made at the state level.
"I don't see (the budget) easing up in years to come unless some big changes are considered at the general assembly and future sessions," he said. "We'll see how it plays out."
TAX DIFFERENTIALS
One of the proposed changes to balance the county's budget is to remove the tax differential, or lower property tax rate, for Cambridge and Hurlock. This would mean Cambridge and Hurlock residents would have to pay the full property tax rate.
Cambridge Mayor Lajan Cephas said although the county is trying its best to balance the budget, she believes this measure is unfair to Cambridge residents. She said the tax differential essentially returns money to tax payers for "duplicated" services.
Cephas also said Cambridge is growing, which will increase the tax base and bring in more revenue for the county. She said the county should instead look into raising taxes in unincorporated areas that are "a little bit better off."
Jones said he doesn't know what the final budget will look like, but said the council welcomes input.
"We want people to come forward and contribute to this conversation," he said.
Adoption of Dorchester County's budget is slated for May 20. The county's first public budget hearing will be held May 6.
Thompson said the Dorchester County Board of Education has to pass the budget by the end of June, but he hopes the board will pass the budget in May to give staff time to make necessary preparations.

title: Counties Approve Chesapeake College Budget Request, Shift Cost of Tech Center
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Counties approve Chesapeake College budget request, shift cost of tech center

 April 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 526
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WYE MILLS — In a joint meeting Thursday, officials across Caroline, Dorchester, Kent, Queen Anne's and Talbot counties approved a shift in county cost shares for Chesapeake College's new technical building.During the meeting, which was held at the college's main campus in Queen Anne's County, the five counties approved a total $9.02 million budget request made by the college for fiscal year 2026. The school's budget is $1.31 million higher than its fiscal year 2025 budget.
Part of the $9.02 million budget request included a $952,560 request for the design of a new technical building. Chesapeake College Vice President for Administrative Services Karen Smith said the new building will have areas for a variety of programs, including agriculture, electrical, welding and fabrication, construction trades and advanced manufacturing. She said the cost for the design phase could be lower depending on state approval.
Although the five counties approved the request for funding for the design, the decision came with a shift in contributions toward the project.
Dorchester County's share of costs for the design phase will be taken on by Queen Anne's County. This means Queen Anne's County's responsibility for the project will jump from 28.9%, or an estimated $275,290, to 47.8%, or an estimated $455,324.
During the meeting, Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer and Vice President Mike Detmer outlined their council's concerns regarding paying for the project.
Although other counties hope to use the new technical building for career and technical education at the high school level, Dorchester County has a career and technology center it is still paying off, they said.
Through its budget process, Dorchester County has struggled to eliminate an estimated $6.2 million deficit.
Pfeffer said Dorchester County takes in about $45 million in property and income taxes and will have to give Dorchester County Public Schools $26.6 million for fiscal year 2026.
"So we're trying to run the rest of the county on half of that," he said. "So while in conceptual context, we believe in the project, fiscally our citizens and our staff are saying we don't know how we're going to be able to participate."
At the Chesapeake College meeting, Queen Anne's County Commissioner Jack Wilson Jr. shared his county's decision to cover Dorchester County for the project design costs.
"We all know what happens if we let this money go back to the state," Wilson said. "It's going to go somewhere else in this state, and it's not going to be here. We got this far. And Lenny, listen, I feel for you guys. I know what you're going through. But I think we just need to keep it on the rails at least through the design phase and see what the state's going to help with."
According to documents from the meeting, the state will support 75% of project costs, and the counties will support the remaining 25%.
After the counties voted to approve the amended capital budget, Kent County Commission President Ron Fithian said he understands the position Dorchester County is in, mentioning the Blueprint for Maryland's Future and "unfunded mandates" by the state.
"I think we all understand any one of us could be in your same position very easily," Fithian told the Dorchester County Council members.

title: Dorchester County Proposes Tax Increases to Balance FY26 Budget
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Dorchester County proposes tax increases to balance FY26 budget

 April 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 633
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — In an effort to address a $6.2 million deficit, the Dorchester County Council introduced a draft fiscal year 2026 budget that raised taxes.The $91.96 million proposed operating budget presented Tuesday includes proposals to increase property taxes, remove the municipal tax differential, increase local income tax and eliminate tax rebates offered to municipalities.
The council will consider these proposals through the remainder of the budget process, which concludes May 20.
The balanced draft budget comes after months of work by county staff to eliminate an estimated $6.2 million operating budget deficit, which the county has said was brought on by cost shifts from the state.
"These are painful decisions," County Manager Jerry Jones said in an interview with The Star Democrat. "But at the end of the day, given the climate and what's being pushed down from the state for us to absorb, sadly it's one of those things we have to do."
GETTING INTO THE NUMBERS
In the draft operating budget, the county is proposing an increase of the real property tax by 3 cents so county residents would pay a rate of $1.03 per $100 of assessed valuation of property.
The proposal to remove the tax differential, or lower property tax rate, for municipalities would mean Cambridge and Hurlock residents would have to pay the full tax rate of $1.03 per $100 of assessed valuation of property.
In the current fiscal year, Cambridge residents pay the county $0.9267 per $100 of assessed valuation of property and Hurlock residents pay $0.9179 per $100 of assessed value.
On properties with a semi-annual tax payment option, the proposal would add a service charge based on a rate of 0.02% applied to unpaid real property taxes due in December.
With the proposed property tax changes to the budget, the county expects to bring in an additional $2.15 million.
The proposed budget would raise the county's income tax rate from 3.2% to 3.3%, generating $600,000 more in revenue.
In another effort to increase revenue, the county voted April 15 to increase its 911 fee to $4.25 per month. This is the second time the rate has been raised this year.
In early March, the council passed a resolution to increase the county fee that residents pay on their cell phone lines from $1.50 to $2 per month. Council Vice President Mike Detmer said in March that he introduced the legislation to increase the fee to $4.25 as a potential way to reduce a budget deficit.
To alleviate the tax and fee increases' impact on seniors, the county is considering expanding its senior tax credit, which offers a 5% deduction on the county tax bill for those who are at least 70 years old and receive the Homeowners' Property Tax Credit. If passed, the expansion would increase that deduction to 10% and expand eligibility to Homeowners' Property Tax Credit recipients who are at least 67 years old.
Proposed expenditure increases include 3% salary increases for airport, solid waste, water and wastewater, courthouse maintenance, courthouse security and Eastern Shore Innovation Center personnel and an increase in spending on the county's 14 volunteer fire companies. The proposed $35,000 total increase to fire companies would add to the county's $1.22 million expenditure on fire companies and advanced life support services.
Proposed cuts to expenditures include the delaying or eliminating funding to nonprofits that request money from the county.
According to the draft grants budget, the county expects to receive a total of $9.78 million in state and federal grants.
At the end of the council meeting April 15, Detmer encouraged residents to come to council meetings or reach out to council members and make their voices and concerns about the budget heard. He said he is available to discuss the budget or just listen.
"It's your budget too," he said.
The first public budget hearing, as well as a meeting with municipalities, will be held May 6.

title: Cambridge Moves Portion of Funds to State Investment Pool
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Cambridge moves portion of funds to state investment pool

 March 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 346
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — In an effort to grow its funds, the City of Cambridge is putting a portion of its money into the Maryland Local Government Investment Pool.The city expects to make between $175,000 and $200,000 in interest annually by moving some of its funds to the local government investment pool, an investment fund available to local communities in the state.
According to a March 19 memo to the City Council from Cambridge Finance Director Perry Peregoy, this plan is part of an effort to "streamline administrative tasks and benefit from a broader suite of treasury services and capital market opportunities." The memo the city would like to put "idle" funds, or money available for investment, into the Maryland Local Government Investment Pool to increase interest income.
Peregoy said about $8 to $10 million of its current deposits in five different financial institutions could be considered "idle."
During a Cambridge City Council meeting March 24, the council authorized moving that money into the fund. Peregoy said at the meeting that the local government investment pool offers the highest interest rate the city can earn with minimal risk.
"It's really what I would refer to as almost as risk-less an investment as you can find in today's environment," he said.
Peregoy said the city is currently making about 2.5% interest on all it's money. He said the local government investment pool is currently offering a 4.4% interest rate.
Cambridge City Manager Glenn Steckman said with interest rates up right now, this move will be a "revenue generator."
Peregoy also talked about the city's relationships with local banks. He said the city won't "materially alter" its local banking relationships.
"I've had preliminary conversations, and they all understand and they realize they can't match," Peregoy said about the seven banks the city currently deals with.
Peregoy said the city will continue to keep a "substantial amount of money" in banks in the community in order to maintain its relationships with those banks.
"This will just be part of that ongoing cash management and treasury function that I hope to expand over the next year within the city," he said.

Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. passes budget

 CAMBRIDGE — During a board meeting March 19, the Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. Board of Directors passed its budget for the 2025 calendar year.CWDI Board Treasurer Frank Narr said that although the budget is a "barebones" one, it takes into account the money CWDI has leftover from 2024 and what it projects for 2025.
Narr said CWDI — which is spearheading a project to develop land along the Choptank River in Cambridge — expects to bring in $182,000 and spend $308,000 in 2025. Although that would create a budget deficit of $126,000, Narr said CWDI had $139,000 surplus from the 2024 calendar year budget.

After Narr presented the proposed budget, Cambridge City Manager Glenn Steckman expressed concern the board might be creating a false narrative that CWDI is in financial trouble with this budget.
"I just want to state as the city manager, I still see a very financially sound community development board," Steckman said. "It's just the way the numbers are reflecting right now. And that could change dramatically in five months."
Steckman shared other opportunities where CWDI could gain more income, including potential city and state tax breaks and additional funding in the new fiscal year.
"While this looks kind of negative, it really isn't," Steckman said, later adding, "So please don't post on 'Destination Cambridge' the world is ending for CWDI."

title: Dorchester County Council Introduces Bill to Raise 911 Fees More

Dorchester County Council introduces bill to raise 911 fees more

 March 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 CAMBRIDGE — The Dorchester County Council will consider raising its 911 fee more after passing legislation to increase it by 50 cents earlier this month.On March 4, the council passed a resolution to increase the county fee that residents pay on their cell phone lines from $1.50 to $2 per month. During a County Council meeting March 18, the council voted to introduce legislation to further increase the fee to $4.25.
Currently, the county is going through the process of preparing its budget for fiscal year 2026. At a budget work session Feb. 28, County Manager Jerry Jones said the county is facing a deficit of $6.2 million, with $87.7 million in estimated revenue and $93.9 million in estimated expenditures.
At the council meeting March 18, Council Vice President Mike Detmer said he wanted to introduce the legislation to increase the 911 fee because he thinks it is necessary.
"Unfortunately, because of the budgetary mandates that have been passed down to us and the need for us, as we discussed, to look to other sources to raise revenue, unfortunately I believe it's my duty to introduce another increase from $2 to $4.25," he said.
Detmer said the county's Emergency Communications Division has a budget of about $1.9 million. He said the $1.50 fee raised about $660,000 for the county last year.
"If we increase it out of necessity to $4.25 per line per month, it would bring fees to a total of $1.8 million, which would be a large part for funding that budget," he said.
The council will need to hold a public hearing before it can vote. Detmer said he thinks it's the county's duty to consider the bill and hear residents' opinions on the matter.

title: Mid-Shore Counties Advocating Against State Cost Shifts
author: Konner Metz
content:
Mid-Shore counties advocating against state cost shifts

 March 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 371
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council sent a letter this week to the Maryland General Assembly expressing its concerns regarding more than $1 million in county money impacted by the state's Budget Reconciliation and Financing Act."The proposal to shift costs onto counties by sending invoices simply places the State's fiscal problem into other hands and threatens local services," reads the letter, which was unanimously approved by the council Tuesday.
Cost shifts are expected as the state aims to balance a budget with a nearly $3 billion deficit. Specific costs include contributions to teacher pensions and the state Department of Assessments and Taxation.
Council Vice President Pete Lesher said it's "simply a poor and inappropriate strategy for resolving the very real state budget crisis."
Lesher noted Tuesday that Talbot County isn't seeing the worst of the cost shifts — Dorchester County may be looking at more than $3 million affected, he said.
Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said he testified at a Senate budget committee meeting in Annapolis and talked with members of the governor's staff.
Pfeffer says Department of Legislative Services recommendations to double the costs for counties to pay toward teacher pensions is particularly alarming. For Dorchester, it would cost $1.1 million compared to the previously estimated $550,000.
Gov. Wes Moore has said solving the budget crisis is an "enormous task" only made more difficult by constraints from the federal government. At a Feb. 28 Senate budget committee hearing, he emphasized that the budget bill is nowhere near final.
"While I still remain locked in on the destination, I come in moving in partnership to be flexible on the journey," Moore said.
Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding said the county may lose $1.1 million in income tax revenue if Moore's tax cut plan is approved.
Moore has maintained that giving middle-class families tax relief is a critical component to the budget and state's economic growth plan.
"Marylanders are being squeezed. They're being squeezed by rising prices," Moore said Feb. 28. "They're being squeezed by the rising cost of groceries, they're being squeezed by the rising cost of energy."
As session continues, Breeding says Caroline County has representatives in Annapolis fighting for relief from the potential cost shifts.
"We have a lot of heartburn with the proposed budget," Breeding said.

title: Dorchester County and DCPS Working to Reduce FY26 Budget Deficits
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Dorchester County and DCPS working to reduce FY26 budget deficits

 March 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 573
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Dorchester County Manager Jerry Jones considers the fiscal year 2026 budget a moving target."There are a lot of things that are changing," he said about predicted state funding during a Dorchester County Council budget work session Thursday. "This is not a weekly thing, but almost a daily thing. ... We just don't know how this is going to unfold."
County staff has been going through the operating and capital budgets line by line to find efficiencies, Jones said.
"We are constantly working on solutions," he said. "We're finding those efficiencies. We have made substantial changes already."
During the work session, Jones detailed estimated revenue and expenditures for fiscal year 2026. According to Jones' presentation, preliminary projections for the budget show a deficit of $6.2 million, with $87.7 million in estimated revenue and $93.9 million in estimated expenditures.
Jones outlined a list of mandates from the state that contribute to the county's deficit. These include reductions in grant funding, losses from proposed property tax deductions, an increase in state education maintenance of effort costs and increased financial responsibilities for things like teacher retirement.
Both Jones and County Council members said the budget would look a lot different without these mandates. Jones said that without the mandates, the county would not be facing a deficit. He said he county would instead have had $200,812 more in revenue than expenditures.
The council and county manager also talked about significant budget cuts made two years ago. Council Vice President Mike Detmer said the fat had already been trimmed from the budget at that time.
"At this point, we're trying to keep the ship from sinking," he said.
Council President Lenny Pfeffer said he and Detmer have plans to go to Annapolis to testify in front of the Maryland General Assembly on legislation that would negatively affect the county's budget.
EDUCATION FUNDING
Detmer said the decrease in state funding and increase in the county's fiscal responsibility is largely driven by the state's goal to meet its financial obligation to the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, a state plan that aims to improve student outcomes and the quality of education.
Dorchester County Public Schools, which has its own budget separate from the county, also is facing a deficit. The deficit, which was estimated to be $10.19 million in January, is now estimated to be $5.59 million.
During a Dorchester County Board of Education budget work session also held Thursday, Dorchester County Public Schools Superintendent Jymil Thompson shared refinements the district has made to the budget since the board's work session in January.
He said the $4.6 million in additional cuts to to reduce the deficit were made through reductions to alternative education programming, supplies costs, travel costs, contracted services and fixed charges as well as expanding the district's understanding of Blueprint guidance to better match funding with expenses.
"We are taking it serious, and we are trying to make the changes we can to reduce our budget in a smart way," Thompson said.
At the County Council work session, council member Ricky Travers said other counties are having the same budget problems.
"Rural Maryland is the worst right now because the bigger counties, you just add another zero to it, but they've got a little bit more ability to garnish more money per penny (on taxes)," he said. "But this big number is astronomical."
Jones said the county will play it by ear on when it holds its next budget work session. He said when it is held will be announced to the public.

title: MACo Officials Say Cost Shifts from State to Counties Are 'Absurd,' Unfair
author: Konner Metz
content:
MACo officials say cost shifts from state to counties are 'absurd,' unfair

 March 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 647
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Representatives from the Maryland Association of Counties minced no words when speaking to the Eastern Shore's state legislators Friday morning about the expected cost burdens being placed on counties this budget cycle."Shifting these costs onto counties at this point is absurd," said Kevin Kinnally, the association's legislative director.
Earlier this month, the Department of Legislative Services told the Eastern Shore Delegation that local governments across the state may have to pick up around $144 million in costs as the state legislature and Gov. Wes Moore grapple with tackling a near $3 billion deficit.
The governor's proposed fiscal year 2026 budget would shift costs in a number of areas, including teacher pensions and property assessments, according to MACo officials.
In Caroline and Talbot counties, projected local cost shifts are in the $700,000 range, per legislative services projections. Dorchester County is at $830,000, while Queen Anne's County leads the pack for the Mid-Shore at $970,000. Kent is the lowest of the five counties with a $300,000 projection.
Friday at the Eastern Shore Delegation meeting, Kinnally said the Shore's poorer counties, like Caroline and Dorchester, are being "railroaded."
Kinnally claims the state budget leaves counties with no choice but to raise property tax rates, going so far as to deem it a "state-mandated property tax increase."
"Two-thirds of Marylanders live in counties at the maximum local income tax rate, so the only place to go is to the property tax," Kinnally said. "Which is regressive, which everybody hates. But they're pushing us into a corner here, and that's not fair."
Michael Sanderson, executive director of MACo, said the organization took a closer look at how cost shifts would impact Dorchester County's fiscal situation.
After running the numbers, Sanderson said he believes Dorchester County may have to raise property taxes, a result he called "absolutely bonkers."
"I have no idea how Dorchester County manages this year's budget," Sanderson said.
SOLAR COMPROMISEAs legislators and industry leaders have eyes on a joint hearing Friday regarding the state's solar legislation, MACo is opposing Senate Bill 931 and its paired House bill.
The legislation is designed to expand solar energy across the state, a measure intended to work toward accomplishing Moore's clean energy goals for Maryland. If passed, the bill would give the state authority to approve solar energy projects — a significant harm to local siting authority, critics say.
Dominic Butchko, MACo's intergovernmental relations director, said the association opposes the legislation based on five impacted areas: safety, livability of rural areas, concerns for local taxpayers, affordable housing opportunities being stripped and inefficiencies in the legislation's requirements.
Butchko said the legislation strays from compromises MACo thought it reached last November.
But through recent discussions with solar industry leaders and environmental advocates, Butchko still sees a path to compromise.
"Those efforts have started to yield some fruit," Butchko said. "We believe we actually have amendments that revert the legislation back to where we were at or pretty close to where we were at in November."
MUNICIPAL LEAGUE
Friday, the Eastern Shore Delegation heard a brief update from the Maryland Municipal League, an organization representing local municipal governments.
The group has two legislative priorities this session: Senate Bill 390, which would allow local governments to have trained civilians issue speed camera citations instead of police officers; and House Bill 991, which would allow local governments to institute food and beverage fees.
Justin Fiore, the league's deputy director of advocacy and public affairs, said House Bill 991 could give flexibility to governments that are "heavily dependent on property taxes as (their) only revenue."
"We have 43 million visitors annually to the state of Maryland, and while they do pay a hotel tax if they stay, we really don't capture revenue from the services that they utilize," Fiore said.
The food and beverage fee bill is still waiting committee review and House approval before it moves to the Senate, while the speed camera citation bill was passed by the Senate earlier this month and currently sits in the House.

title: Dorchester County Braces for Budget Season, Asks Residents to Participate
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Dorchester County braces for budget season, asks residents to participate

 February 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 549
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — During a County Council meeting Feb. 4, Council President Lenny Pfeffer said that based on preliminary numbers, the county is in need of an estimated $3.5 to $4 million to balance its budget for next fiscal year.With significant concerns, the County Council is encouraging residents to participate in the budget process and reach out to elected officials.
Pfeffer said there is no fat left to trim, and so it is searching for ideas on how to balance the budget. "All of our departments are cut down to bare bones," he said.
Council Vice President Mike Detmer called the county's preliminary budget numbers "extraordinarily drastic."
"There's no cutting, in my view," he said. "There's no navigating through it. There's no weathering the storm. ... This is a breaking point type of moment."
Pfeffer said Blueprint for Maryland's Future mandates are the reason for these shortfalls. The Dorchester County Board of Education is facing a $10.19 million deficit going into fiscal year 2026.
"We don't want to put the kids at risk here," he said. "We just can't afford this Blueprint program that exceeds our revenues by drastic numbers."
Detmer said tough decisions might need to be made this year and residents should be paying attention to the budget process.
He brought up a June 2024 Board of Education decision — which was ultimately reversed — to remove media specialists from libraries, redistributing them to other positions in the school system. The move, which did not have to do with Blueprint requirements, would have saved the district more than $313,000 this school year.
"What else do you think might be on the chopping block for them to be able to balance?" Detmer asked.
Pfeffer said not paying for the Blueprint is not an option. He said the state will withhold the county's income tax revenues if it doesn't pay.
"It keeps all of us up at night trying to figure out ways to fix this," Pfeffer said, "and we just don't have all the answers. So, please, help us think of ideas. Send us emails."
During public comment, resident Sharon Smith said the county needs to "inundate" Gov. Wes Moore (D) and other state leaders with emails and phone calls. She suggested the County Council take out ads in local newspapers that ask residents to do the same.
Resident Morgan Tolley asked the county to post contact information for state legislators and leaders on social media so that residents can reach out. "Because this is a dire situation," Tolley said.
Detmer said although residents might be hesitant to reach out to their representatives because they don't want to complain, it is helpful when they do.
"You're not chewing them out," he said. "To me, you're arming them with evidence that their voters feel a certain way."
Resident Bucky Jackson said the county is cutting "pennies on the dollar" and recommended it look at the number of schools in the district. He said the district has too many schools considering its number of students.
Detmer said Jackson was right about his "pennies on the dollar" comment, adding that if the county were to eliminate its Economic Development, Tourism and Recreation and Parks departments, it would only save about $1 million.
The county will host its first budget work session on Feb. 25 at 6 p.m. The budget adoption schedule can be found on the county's website.

Dorchester County Council stresses need for conservative budget in FY2026

 December 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 CAMBRIDGE — As Dorchester County begins preparing for budget season, "conservative" is the name of the game.During a Dorchester County Council meeting on Dec. 3, council members stressed the importance of the county being conservative and efficient with how it spends its money in the upcoming fiscal year.
In response to County Manager Jerry Jones' question of whether the council has any priorities for the fiscal year 2026 budget, Council Member Ricky Travers said he wants to "hold the status quo" without raising taxes.
"My goal would be to be very conservative because we don't know where we're going to be at, what money we're going to have to spend," he said.
Council President Lenny Pfeffer brought up the budget deficit facing the state.
"With the state facing a $2.7 billion deficit, we're not sure exactly what the governor's going to cut," Pfeffer said. "So I think we're going to have to be very dynamic and make changes on the go as we go through this next budget cycle."
According to Dorchester County's budget adoption schedule, the County Council will begin holding budget work sessions in late February. Following public hearings, the adoption of the budget is scheduled for June 10.
The county's fiscal year 2025 budget, which included a 5% raise across the board for county employees, totaled $86.52 million. The operating budget increased by about $2.5 million, or roughly 3%, compared to fiscal year 2024, and the capital budget decreased by about $6.3 million, which is roughly 58%.
During the meeting on Dec. 3, Council Member William Nichols and Council Vice President Mike Detmer both agreed that not raising taxes — particularly for seniors — is important.
"It would be the last thing I would do," Nichols said about taxing seniors.
Detmer said he values the county manager and county staff for being consistent and increasing efficiency in county government. He said that along with being conservative and consistent, the county should also make sure it remains creative when it comes to the budget.
"We can't just be in shutdown mode, you know?" he said. "There's low-hanging fruit out there that we've got to be able to convert little things and enrich the life here."
Pfeffer said that the county's budget goals will be discussed more during the upcoming budget workshops.
"We're going to hear from all our department heads and see what the real needs versus wants are going to be from the county," he said.

title: Legislators Talk State Budget Before Heading Back to Annapolis in January
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Legislators talk state budget before heading back to Annapolis in January

 December 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 557
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The state of the state's budget took up a large part of the conversation at a Dorchester Chamber of Commerce luncheon with state legislators on Dec. 4.The Lower Shore delegation answered questions from chamber members regarding concerns about Maryland's fiscal health, with a looming $2.7 billion state budget deficit predicted in fiscal year 2026.
"The reality is that if you continue to do the things that have gotten us into this deficit, it's only going to take us back there again," Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) said. "There needs to be a structural, fundamental change."
Mautz and Dels. Sheree Sample-Hughes (D-Dorchester, Wicomico), Chris Adams (R-Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) all spoke at the chamber lunch. They, along with the rest of the state's legislators, will head back to Annapolis in January for the 447th session of the Maryland General Assembly.
In talking about the state's budget, Mautz also said there should be incentives in place to try to drive state agencies to save money.
Sample-Hughes said the state should do its fiscal homework and find out what it "really (has) to work with."
"But I do believe that we can still address and attack some of these goals that we have, whether it's education, whether it's climate, whether it's criminal justice," she said. "We can do it in a pragmatic way."
Adams said to solve the budget problem, the state has to leverage and grow its private sector.
"You do not do what we've done for the past two years," he said. He said the state and its leadership need to stop spending so much, own up to the problem and stop blaming it on COVID-19.
Hutchinson expressed his concerns with the transportation budget and the lack of funding for many infrastructure projects across the state.
"We've got to pay attention to our transportation budget," he said.
BLUEPRINTThe legislators also talked about the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, a plan passed by the Maryland General Assembly in 2021 that aims to improve student outcomes and the quality of education across the state through increasing education funding by $3.8 billion over a 10-year period.
Sample-Hughes said although Blueprint's goals are important, the General Assembly's decision to pass the plan has contributed to the state's budget deficit. She later advocated for giving more resources to the nonprofits that already serve 3 and 4 year olds, rather than putting money toward expanding early childhood education in the state's public school systems.
Mautz said he thinks the project needs to be paused so that the plan's strengths and weaknesses can be better evaluated.
JUVENILE CRIMEThe legislators also talked about the state of juvenile crime in Maryland, with Sample-Hughes calling for the removal of Department of Juvenile Services Secretary Vincent Schiraldi.
Hutchinson said that with recent juvenile justice reforms going into effect Nov. 1, he doesn't think a lot of legislators are going to want to discuss juvenile crime this upcoming session.
"Because they'll say, 'We just put that in place. We haven't even been able to see the results,'" he said.
Adams said law enforcement is needed now more than ever and officers need to be able to do their jobs.
"If you want a society, if you want a City of Cambridge, if you want an Eastern Shore (or) State of Maryland, if you want a United States that is civil, there have to be consequences," he said.
