title: Cambridge City Council Approves Obligation of Remaining ARPA Funds
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Cambridge City Council approves obligation of remaining ARPA funds

 November 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 504
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The City of Cambridge is reallocating $1.39 million in non-obligated American Rescue Plan Act funds in order to meet an end-of-the-year deadline.The decision to reallocate the city's remaining ARPA funds was made during a Cambridge City Council meeting on Nov. 12. With this decision, those funds can be obligated, and the city will be protected from having to return that money to the U.S. Department of the Treasury.
According to a Nov. 6 memo to the City Council from Cambridge City Manager Glenn Steckman and Finance Director Perry Peregoy, the city received $12.08 million in COVID-19 relief funding through the American Rescue Plan Act. The memo states $10.68 million of those funds have been spent or obligated.
The remaining $1.39 million in funds has to be obligated — meaning there is an executed contract or issued purchase holder — by Dec. 31 to ensure no money has to be returned to the federal government.
At the meeting Nov. 12, Steckman talked about what the city recommends obligating those remaining funds to. He talked about three potential Department of Public Works purposes: a bucket truck, a Vac-Con trailer and a sweeper to clean sidewalks.
He said the sweeper would be beneficial when it comes to the areas where people take out their trash.
"It will help especially with the fall now coming and leaves are blowing into areas where our storefronts, the doors are set back," he said. "We'll be able to get in there and clean it up. So it should be able to make the downtown area, especially, look nicer while we have tourists coming into town."
According to the Nov. 6 memo, the remaining funds would also go to Rescue Fire Company for fire apparatuses, the Economic Development Division for the Hyatt Bridge, Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. for the Cambridge Harbor project, Cannery Park for lighting and the Engineering Division for GIS equipment.
The commissioners voted to approve the obligation of the remaining ARPA funds to these recommended projects and purchases with a unanimous vote. Commissioner Jameson Harrington was absent from the meeting.
At the end of the meeting, Commissioner Brian Roche thanked city staff for making sure the money will be spent and not sent back to the federal government. He said COVID-19 has had a significant negative impact on the youth in Cambridge.
"And one of the things (the city) did, which is not obvious, is they've actually saved the money that we wanted to allocate for a new park, Leonards Lane, and a brand new (one) which is slowly developing by the Packing House, Cannery Park," he said.
Roche said this ensures the city will be able to move forward with the creation of these two brand new parks.
"I just want to applaud staff for making that happen, making sure that could happen," he said. "Because I think the development of those two parks, connecting them in safe ways, is going to be just tremendous for the youth of this community to continue to have green space and enjoy outdoor recreation for their health and well-being."

title: Dorchester Finance Director Gives Update on County Audits, ARPA Money
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Dorchester finance director gives update on county audits, ARPA money

 October 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 355
 Words

 CAMBRIDGE — At a Dorchester County Council meeting Tuesday, county Finance Director Karen Tolley gave an update on the status of the county's audits and the remainder of the county's American Rescue Plan Act funds.Tolley said the Finance Department has wrapped up its work on the fiscal year 2022 audit. She said the audit is currently under external review.
As soon as the audit is released — which Tolley anticipates will be in the coming days — it can be published and will be put on the county website.
In September 2023, a WHCP reported the county's failure to submit financial reports and audits since 2020. That month, Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said county staff had been working "tirelessly" with independent auditing firm UHY to complete the missing audits.
At the meeting this week, Tolley said the county finance department had done a lot of work internally to help move the process along.
"I couldn't be more proud of our finance team that we're building out here in the county," she said.
Tolley said she expects to see repeat recommendations in the fiscal year 2022 audit because it is from years go, but she expects "the gray clouds" will "start clearing" for the fiscal years 2023 and 2024.
Council member Ricky Travers said it is important the auditors release the fiscal year 2022 audit as soon as possible because it is holding up county projects.
"We need to keep pushing (the auditors) every single day to make this happen so that we can get these projects moving that are on hold because of this," he said.
Tolley said that with the audit in the hands of the auditors, all the county can do is wait for the release.
Tolley also talked about the county's remaining $1.4 million in ARPA funds at the meeting. She said the county received a total of $6.2 million in ARPA funds.
The remaining $1.4 million will need to be obligated by the end of the year. To consider the funds obligated, there will need to be a contract or memorandum of understanding with a vendor, Tolley said.
The deadline to spend the ARPA money is Dec. 31, 2026.

title: Talbot County Proposes Hotel Tax Increase to Local Delegation
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County proposes hotel tax increase to local delegation

 October 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 589
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County leaders met with the local delegation Tuesday afternoon to discuss creating legislation during the upcoming General Assembly to raise the county's hotel taxes.Talbot County's current public accommodations tax rate, or hotel tax rate, is 4%, the lowest of any county in the state. The tax is levied on those staying in hotels or short-term rentals in the county, collected by the business and then paid to either the county or one of three towns.
Easton, Oxford and St. Michaels collect revenues from such properties within one mile outside town limits. The county collects revenue from all other properties not within those boundaries.
A potential increase to 6%, which would increase total revenue collected by around $1 million in fiscal year 2024, requires approval from lawmakers in Annapolis.
Cassandra Vanhooser, the county's director of tourism and economic development, along with Talbot County Council members briefed Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), Del. Christopher T. Adams (R-Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) on the proposed increase.
"I'm anticipating that this is going to be our principal legislation request for the delegation this year," council Vice President Pete Lesher said.
Adams and Mautz explained that state lawmakers will be tasked with addressing significant budget problems in the upcoming session. Adams said it's likely lawmakers will try to pass the budget by voting for state tax increases that were not passed last year.
He said it's probably the first year he will vote against the budget. Any tax bill will require his careful consideration, Adams noted, saying he'd like to hear the council's opinions on potential hotel tax legislation.
Council Member Keasha Haythe said the spike would help "level the playing field" for the county, as well as increase funding for the tourism and economic development department. Revenue the county collects from the accommodations tax goes to that department.
"This particular tax I do believe is necessary for Talbot County and tourism and (the) hospitality industry," Haythe said.
Mautz agreed with Haythe's points but brought up the benefits of Talbot County's low accommodations tax rate.
"I also agree with the perspective that would say, if your accommodation tax is lower than the neighboring county, then you have an advantage as far as attracting (people)," Mautz said. He added that the council should take into consideration that it may make the area more attractive for investors.
Jessica Bellis, CFO at the Avalon Foundation and a member of the Talbot County Tourism Board, expressed her support for the increase. She said the taxes benefit her organization since they are cycled back into Talbot County's and Easton's respective economic development and tourism departments.
"We can't market in the big world, as tiny little Avalon Foundation or as a small Airbnb in Talbot County," Bellis said. "We really rely on that tourism office for its marketing power."
Hutchinson said the county should ensure business owners are on board and lay out to the delegation how the taxes collected cycle back into the local economy.
Council President Chuck Callahan said it's important for the county to do its "due diligence" and gather feedback from businesses before voting on the topic as a council. While the bill could be pre-filed by the local delegates in November, January was agreed upon as a deadline for the county to have a draft bill ready for the legislators.
"This is a really important issue," Mautz said. "We definitely don't want to be in a situation where we go up to Annapolis and are not prepared."
"It's a different discussion when you go across the bridge," he said.

title: Dorchester County Purchases Race Street Property for Health Department
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Dorchester County purchases Race Street property for health department

 August 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 452
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Dorchester County Health Department is moving.At a Dorchester County Council meeting on Aug. 6, Council President Lenny Pfeffer announced the county has purchased the former Department of Social Services building, located at 627 Race St., for the health department.
In his announcement, Pfeffer said this has long been a wish of the department's health officer, Roger Harrell. Pfeffer said the current building, located at 3 Cedar St., has had mold and mildew issues, and the department has dealt with windows falling out.
"I know you've done interviews in mop closets over there," Pfeffer said to Harrell, who was at the meeting. "So hopefully now we can get you into a facility that's great for the citizens and their employees."
Harrell said in an interview with the Star Democrat that the department needed more space. He said the building on Race Street has about three times more square feet than the department's current building. He said the new building also has up-to-date heating, air conditioning and ventilation.
The Race Street property was purchased for $6.1 million from Leeward Holdings LLC. Pfeffer said they went to settlement the week before the County Council meeting.
Harrell said he was "very appreciative" of county officials for making this happen. "It's going to be nice to have more room to provide the services we provide for our community," he said. "It's exciting times."
When the department moved to Cedar Street in 2000, the plan was to stay for a couple of years, Harrell said. He said for various reasons, the department stayed longer than planned.
According to an Aug. 9 news release from the county, next steps for the move include "minor renovations" to meet the needs of the department as well as the transfer of technology and infrastructure from Cedar Street to Race Street. The release said the start date of when the department will begin offering services out of the Race Street building is "fluid and largely dependent on when the aforementioned next steps are completed."
Harrell said the minor renovations include putting in exam rooms and fiber internet.
In an interview with the Star Democrat, Pfeffer said that once the health department has moved out of the Cedar Street property, that property will be surplussed.
At the end of the Aug. 6 meeting, Council Member Ricky Travers said he was glad and said this move is long overdue.
"I'm sorry your agency's had to work in this situation it's been (in)," he said. "And I'm glad to see it move forward in the right direction."
Council Vice President Mike Detmer said moving the facility to Race Street puts it "in the heart" of the community. "And I think it's going to be a great thing," he said. "It's well-deserved by your team."

title: Dorchester County Council Passes Budget, Looks Ahead
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Dorchester County Council passes budget, looks ahead

 May 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 698
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Cambridge — The Dorchester County Council unanimously passed its balanced fiscal year 2025 budget at a meeting on May 28, acknowledging what it took to get the budget across the finish line as well as what challenges are likely coming down the pike."Next year's going to be bad," Council President Lenny Pfeffer said at the end of the meeting. "This year we made it by the skin of our teeth to balance this budget."
The fiscal year 2025 budget — an $81,938,414 operating and $4,584,711 capital budget — includes a 5% raise across the board for county employees. The operating budget increased by about $2.5 million, or roughly 3%, compared to fiscal year 2024. The capital budget decreased by about $6.3 million, which is roughly 58%, compared to fiscal 2024.
The county's tax rates are the same as the fiscal year 2024 budget. The real property tax is $1 per assessed $100 of value. The personal property tax is $2.44 per assessed $100 of value.
Council member William Nichols said a lot of cuts had to be made to get the budget to where it is.
"We went through H-E-double-L to complete this budget," he said. "A lot of people gave up a lot of things to make this work."
Nichols said he hopes that next year the council can be extra generous with the departments that gave up a lot to allow for a balanced budget.
"For those who gave so much to make this work, we've got to go back and pick them up," he said, adding that there are three specific departments he has in mind. He did not name which departments those are.
Although Council Member Ricky Travers doesn't think this budget was easy to get to the finish line, he said they were able to give all county employees a raise without raising the tax rates.
"That was our number one priority going into this," he said. "Trying to take care of our employees that are taking care of us."
Travers said that of the 18 budgets he has passed in his time as a council member, the fiscal year 2025 budget ranks in his top two of being the worst to do.
"I need the public to understand that it's not this group's spending habits that's causing this problem," he said. "We need to go across the bridge there to Annapolis, and it's their spending habits that are coming back on us."
Travers said that when the General Assembly passes bills for things like the Blueprint for Maryland's Future without knowing how those things will be paid for, it has a "devastating effect" on rural Maryland.
"I can tell you that I hope that it gets better," he said. "But when you're sitting on the side of the bank in the boat and you see the sky is getting cloudy, you know what's coming. You better get in the boat and head to the shore."
Before the council passed the budget, it amended the budget to allot about $28,000 more to the volunteer fire departments and companies from the county's contingency fund. The volunteer departments were originally budgeted a total of $1.06 million in the fiscal year 2025 budget.
Pfeffer said this modification to the budget means that each fire department or company will receive roughly $2,000 more than originally allotted in the budget.
At the end of the meeting, Pfeffer brought up a story he heard on the news about another county on the Shore discussing whether to fund a new school using bonds or pulling from its $70 million in reserves.
"We don't have that luxury by any means," he said, adding that Dorchester County has a small, strategic reserve in case of a catastrophic event.
Pfeffer said that when it comes to the fiscal year 2026 budget, the council has concerns about what Blueprint costs will be for the county.
"We love our teachers," he said. "We love the children. We want to provide them the best education possible. It's just, we're out of money."
Pfeffer said that nobody on the council wants to raise taxes, they want to see the tax base increase.
"We have to figure ways that we can increase that tax base within the budget that we have right now," he said.

title: FY2025 Budget Introduced at Dorchester County Council Meeting

FY2025 budget introduced at Dorchester County Council meeting

 CAMBRIDGE — Dorchester County's proposed $86,523,125 fiscal year 2025 draft budget is a balanced budget, County Finance Director Karen Tolley said at a council meeting May 7."We're excited about that," said Tolley, who is also the mayor of Church Creek.
The proposed budget — an $81,938,414 operating and $4,584,711 capital budget — includes the council's efforts to implement "across the board" raises for county employees.
Tolley said that compared to the fiscal year 2024 budget, the fiscal year 2025 operating draft budget increased by about $2.5 million, or roughly 3%. She said the capital budget decreased by about $6.3 million, which is roughly 58%.
Within the operating budget, Tolley said the operating government funds budget increased about $2.9 million, or 4%. She said most of that increase is attributable to a 5% "across the board" raise to county employees.
"That was one of the council's missions," she said. "So therefore, that was one of the top priorities in this budget."
Tolley said that to balance this, other cuts needed to be made. She said those cuts were made in collaboration with department directors, and departments will still be maintaining full operations.
The county's proposed tax rates are the same as the fiscal year 2024 budget. The proposed real property tax is $1 per assessed $100 of value. The proposed personal property tax is $2.44 per assessed $100 of value.
According to the draft budget document, within Cambridge, the real property tax rate is $0.9267 per assessed $100 of value. Within Hurlock, the real property tax rate is $0.9179 per assessed $100 of value. This is due to tax differentials for these two towns.
Tolley also talked about the grants budget during her presentation. According to the draft budget document, the county is leveraging $903,919 for $3.9 million in grant funds.
At the council meeting, the Dorchester County Council introduced the budget. Public hearings for the proposed budget will be held May 14 and May 21. A final hearing and adoption of the budget is set for May 28 during the regular council meeting.
Along with introducing the draft budget, the council passed a resolution that gives the county the authority to invest in the Maryland Local Government Investment Pool.
"I think it will give us some great returns," Tolley said.

title: Budget and County Leadership Worries Shared with Eastern Shore Delegation
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Budget and county leadership worries shared with Eastern Shore delegation

 March 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 379
 Words 

 Read News Document

 With the state facing a budget shortfall in coming years, Maryland counties may see an increase in unfunded mandates.That was the message Maryland Association of Counties Executive Director Michael Sanderson delivered to the Eastern Shore Delegation Friday morning.
He began the presentation by saying that as the counties face many different issues, a state agency is "just never going to have the on-the-ground view" that local governments have connecting with the community and getting input from the people who live there.
Among the causes of concern for straining county budgets, Sanderson said, is the Blueprint education plan, an education bill passed in 2021 that increases annual education funding by over $3.8 billion over the next ten years.
Del. Christopher Adams (R-Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), delegation chair, later commented that the budgets could be similar to what happened in the 2007-2008 financial crisis when teacher pension costs were shifted to counties.
Sanderson warned that the projected state budget shortfalls over the next few years could squeeze county budgets, especially as the costs of fully implementing the Blueprint education plan begin taking effect a couple of years from now.
He said that local governments "don't have a bunch of money" like the state does to push this problem out and call it a "future problem." He said it is urgent for county budgets, mainly because of an existing transportation funding crisis.
Adams expressed his own concerns, saying that the budget that's coming up over the next two to three years will not only be stressful for local officials but may also put them in a position to handle an unfunded mandate.
"The state may or may not have any other choice but to take these education shortfalls, and that's what this budget shortfall is going to be in two to three years. It's all about education," Adams said.
Sanderson warned that the coming economic difficulties will be the first exposure for many local leaders to a situation where their county budget is in trouble.
"About 40-something percent of our local elected leaders only have experienced in the last three or four years with this kind of paper over the economy, healthy state budgets and surpluses and so forth," Sanderson said. "And this will be the first exposure for a lot of them, for suddenly their county budget is in crisis."

title: Local State Legislators Discuss Predicted State Revenue Shortfall
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Local state legislators discuss predicted state revenue shortfall

 December 7, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 759
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - Local state legislators gathered at the Chesapeake Grove Intergenerational Center Tuesday afternoon to share their expectations for the 2024 Legislative Session with constituents.At the event, hosted by the Dorchester Chamber of Commerce, attendees were served lunch before getting the opportunity to ask questions to District 37 legislators Sen. Johnny Mautz (R, Talbot County), Del. Chris Adams (R, Wicomico) Del. Tom Hutchinson (R, Dorchester) and Speaker Pro Tem Sheree Sample-Hughes (D, Wicomico) regarding the 446th session of the Maryland General Assembly that will commence in Annapolis on Jan. 10.The legislators answered questions on topics ranging from the Blueprint for Maryland's Future to economic development to juvenile crime.Matthew Teffeau, manager of government affairs and economic development at Choptank Electric Cooperative, asked the first question of the event. He asked for ways in which the estimated state revenue shortfall of more than $460 million could be addressed.Sample-Hughes, who spoke first, said that this situation with the budget is challenging."There have been many task forces that have taken place this interim to address issues," she said about the shortfall.When it comes to the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, for example, Sample-Hughes said the state won't have enough money in the budget to cover what has been proposed until 2027.Sample-Hughes also brought up fuel tax funds, which have decreased in the state due to the increase in electronic vehicles."That requires a whole other level of structure and planning to see what that looks like for the state," she said. "Do we put in fees for these electric vehicles and hybrid vehicles so we can come out into somewhat of a balanced budget?" New legislation regarding this could come out of the upcoming General Assembly session, she said.Adams followed Sample-Hughes in answering the question. He said the budget will be the "number one topic" of discussion going into Legislative Session this year.He said that COVID-19 emergency funding has helped the state's budget in the past couple years, but said he has noticed many municipalities and county governments using these funds for programs that move into the future, not just one-time appropriations."Many of the budget problems that we're going to have are going to come down to this: Ongoing spending of dollars for social programs for which there are no tax revenue sources to derive those from," he said.Adams said this could lead to fee and tax increases as well as cuts to spending "in places where we should not be cutting."Adams concluded his answer by saying that the state's budget deficit could reach $1.8 billion by 2027."So we're talking $400 million next year," he said, "In a couple years, if we don't right this ship, we're talking about multiple billions of dollars of revenue shortfall.That's going to hit hard."Mautz spoke next, saying that there is no simple answer to fixing the predicted budget shortfall."I think everything is going to be on the table this session," he said. "There's going to be all kinds of maneuvering."Mautz said that it's important to make sure that the burden of the budget shortage isn't left on local governments. He said that the best solution to the problem is to drive investment."The budget depends on revenues, and the way you do that is you try to get capital investment and you try to fuel small business," he said. "And that's the backbone of the Eastern Shore."Mautz said that lessening the economic burden on independent businesses and constituents at a statewide level is important to drive economic activity."Anything we can do statewide to loosen that burden, to drive economic activity, I think will be a fundamental policy that will help change that budget imbalance," he said.Hutchinson answered the question last, saying that government can only make money by raising taxes, raising fees or cutting spending."I'm sure - based on what I've heard from the chairman of appropriations - we'll see a number of bills about taxes and fee increases," he said.Hutchinson brought up the recent announcement from the Maryland Department of Transportation that it will be reducing funding for its six year capital budget for transportation projects."We'll probably start seeing that across the other departments as well," he said. "But there's a lot of projects that, if they're not announced by the end of January, won't be seeing the light of day next year."

title: Dorchester County Loses Credit Rating
author: Jim Brady; Whcp Radio
content:
Dorchester County loses credit rating

 September 22, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Jim Brady; Whcp Radio | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 507
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - Dorchester's County government has lost a key credit rating in the latest fallout from years of overdue financial audits that are only now becoming available.Moody's Investors Service late last week formally withdrew Dorchester's credit rating when county officials failed to produce financials under a 30-day deadline. Moody's cited the lack of information from the county in wiping out its credit rating.County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said Dorchester officials are engaged with Moody's to try to fix the information.The county posted the oldest of the overdue audits, fiscal year 2021, on its website Monday."We've instructed (Moody's) that as soon as we receive the audits that are complete, we will make sure that they have that information," Pfeffer said. "But in the meantime, we've sent them everything else that we could up to this point." With no credit rating, the county would be forced to pay much higher interest rates on any bonds or capital leases. The difference could be 12% to 15% higher than the desirable municipal bond rating it had enjoyed until now. That would mean more taxpayer dollars going to pay for higher interest.The lack of a credit rating means a likely discount in the resale value of at least $30 million worth of bonds the county previously issued.S & P Global, another rating service, withdrew its rating for Dorchester County in April.The county government has failed to file legally required financial audits to the state since 2020. With the 2021 audit complete, the county is still overdue on the 2022 audit. The fiscal year 2023 audit is due by the end of October.Officials previously cited high turnover in the finance department and a 2020 computer hack as reasons for the delay. But multiple extensions granted by the state last year had expired with no completed audit submitted.Pfeffer said the current delay is the matter of time auditors need to work."We're at the mercy of the third party independent auditor, so we can only go as fast as they go," Pfeffer said. "We've tried to supply as much information as personnel that they've asked for, but we're still at their mercy." At a council meeting Sept. 5, Pfeffer said the audits were 99% complete and predicted the oldest missing report, for fiscal year 2021, would be ready in two weeks. The posting on Monday of the 2021 audit comes one day inside his prediction.Pfeffer said he expects progress will accelerate."FY21, since they had to translate a lot of data for the system that was lost and stuff that was put in incorrect or whatever, the new information going into '22 should go much faster," he said.The county can submit a fee to Moody's to reevaluate a credit rating once it has the required financial reports finished.Moody's did not indicate how long it could take to reestablish a credit rating after financial audits are delivered.

title: 'Please Bear With Us' - County Council President Asks for Patience as Missing Audits Completed
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
'Please bear with us' - County Council president asks for patience as missing audits completed

 September 7, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: A1 | Section: News 
 
 632
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer read a statement about the county's failure to submit financial reports and audits in recent past years at a council meeting Sept. 5."The citizens of Dorchester County should rest assured knowing that our independent auditors have found no money missing and no criminal activity," Pfeffer said.The statement comes one week after a WHCP story broke which discussed the county's failure to submit these documents since 2020 and the possible ramifications of that failure.According to the WHCP story, Moody's Investors Service had published a notice that it was placing Dorchester County on review citing a lack of financial information. Moody's said that if it did not see up-to-date financial information within 30 days, it may de-list Dorchester County from any credit rating.No credit rating could mean that the county would be unable to issue bonds.Along with that, the Maryland Office of Legislative Audits, which oversees and collects these audits, states that failure to submit current audit reports on time could result in money grants and aid to the county being discontinued.In his statement, Pfeffer said county staff has been working "tirelessly" with the nationally-recognized, independent auditing firm UHY to complete the missing audits.He said the county has hired independent consultants and contractors and "devoted extra county staff " to complete the audits. He said the county is still in good relationships with its local banks and has been in communication with the offices of the governor and comptroller, as well as the Department of Budget and Management."To keep them abreast of our current status," he said.Pfeffer said that about two more weeks are needed for the final submission of the fiscal year 2021 audit. He said it is 99% complete."These actions to complete the 2021 audit should expedite the completion of fiscal year 2022 and ultimately fiscal year 2023," he said.The county has hired a second auditing firm to help expedite the completion of the 2022 and 2023 audits, he said.In his statement, Pfeffer said the county council takes responsibility for what has happened."That failure to submit ultimately falls upon the shoulders of the county council, both past and present," he said. "The current Dorchester County Council understands this and has made it the No. 1 priority of our staff." Pfeffer listed reasons for why the failure occurred, including software issues, limited staffing and a hack.New financial software, to replace an "antiquated system," made it difficult for staff to properly input and export data. Along with this, he said there was a failure to train staff on how to use the new financial software.Pfeffer talked about losing key personnel in the finance office and having trouble finding good candidates to fill the county manager and director of finance positions.He added that the COVID-19 pandemic caused a "backlog of daily, weekly and monthly duties." Last, he mentioned the county being hacked in January 2020, which forced staff to destroy 24 data servers to prevent personal data of residents being released."All necessary data had to be hand entered into the system's new servers from paper documents and storage, but all of our emails and some data was lost forever," he said.Pfeffer said that the county has contracted with the Government Finance Officers Association to do a detailed study of the finance office "to assure we have all possible best practices in place as we move forward in time." "We ask that our citizens, stakeholders and public please bear with us as we put forward all energy necessary to bring our status to current and learn from events of the past," he said.

title: A Day of Reckoning Here for Council in Dorchester County - Legally Required Audit Reports Not Filed Since 2020
author: Jim Brady; Whcp Radio
content:
A day of reckoning here for council in Dorchester County - Legally required audit reports not filed since 2020

 September 1, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Jim Brady; Whcp Radio | Page: A1 | Section: News 
 
 1690
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Dorchester County's government has failed to submit legally required annual financial reports and audits since 2020, and now the county is facing consequences.On Aug. 4, the ratings firm Moody's Investor Service published a notice that it was placing Dorchester County on review citing a lack of financial information.Moody's said, if it does not see up-to-date financial information within 30 days, it may de-list Dorchester County from any credit rating.Without a credit rating, the county might be unable to issue bonds that are used for capital projects and financing.And the Maryland Office of Legislative Audits, which oversees and collects these audits states and guidelines that failure to submit current audit reports on time can result in money grants and aid to the county being discontinued.County officials now say they're frantically scrambling to assemble years of financial statements and audits, and they say the problem was something they didn't much discuss until recently."This is priority one. Since the start of this council, basically Jan. 1st," says Lenny Pfeffer, president of the new County Council. "We have thrown a fair amount of extra money into this trying to get every person and firm that we can to help us with this situation. This is not something that we're taking lightly. This is not something that we're just saying, 'Hey, this is a rebellious action of Dorchester County not to do this.' It was just a whole cascading number of issues." County leaders have cited multiple problems that hit them in 2020. The county struggled with a new accounting software system, then COVID-19 hit along with a sudden exodus of senior staff in the finance office. Then computer hackers locked the county out of its own records.Dorchester recently has gone through four or five finance directors depending on who you ask, and ever since 2020, Dorchester has not had a full-time dedicated county manager.Even so, Mike Spears who retired last year as the county's longtime finance director, said the situation is incredible."At one point I was told by the auditor, well, we're two weeks away from a financial statement," Spears said."So I can't imagine that we are here in August of '23 and I left in November of '22 and we're still not with a '21 audit." If you're wondering how years of failure could take place without any notice to the public, consider the path one local resident took to discover some answers.Last year, Eugene Lauer, a Cambridge resident, was working with a group called Dorchester Citizens for a Better Government on a charter petition. He heard mention there could be things to discover regarding the county's finance department.Lauer, with 40 years experience himself as a county administrator in Prince George's County and as county manager of Charles County, was intrigued. He contacted Dochester County and filed a public information request.Among the documents he received was something that was not posted in the 2020 financial statements on the county's website. It was a report to the commissioners from the auditors citing serious deficiencies in the county's accounting and other departments leading to inaccuracies delays and faulty records."They also had 17 pages of correcting journal entries made worth about $27 million," Lauer said. "I've never seen anything like that in my 40 years in government quite that bad. Checks not deposited for up to three years. I mean, this is mind boggling stuff." "So my review revealed was rather shocking when I looked at what the auditor's comments were on FY 20, which plays into why they probably haven't been able to have an audited financial report for 21 and ultimately, I guess beyond," he said."They cited in the auditor's report material weaknesses," Lauer said. "Now, auditors classify weaknesses by three categories. Material is the worst. They also identified basically it's lack of internal checks and balances and controls that you got to have to make these financial statements accurate." Lauer said this is "fundamental stuff." "Every government does this, and it was very shocking to see these kinds of comments.So this is all perplexing about what really who was advised of what actions were taken." He said the former finance director advocacy was frustrated.He had staff turnover.He mentioned software."I said, well, has the council been directly advised about this?" Lauer asked."And I think the answer was no." There were records of the previous County Council, President Jay Newcomb, explaining to state officials why the 2021 finance report would be even later. In his Sept. 30, 2022, letter to the office of legislative audits, Newcomb stated that the county anticipated completing the fiscal year 2021 audit by December of 2022.He wrote: "Dorchester County is committed to ensuring that all future audits are completed and submitted to your office by the due dates." However, that didn't happen.The promised 2021 report remains outstanding to this day. Not only that, but Dorchester County has failed to submit any report for any year since 2020.Lauer sees this having an effect on the county's bond rating."I can tell you that first of all, if they downgrade whatever the bond rating is or just delist it, you've got bond holders holding these bonds.Now they're going to be paid out their interest when the bonds become due and presumably the face value. But what it can do is devalue the bonds if they want to sell those bonds before they come due," Lauer said. "So the implications of that, you would think there could be some very unhappy bond holders." "The lower the credit rating, the more interest the issuer, in this case the county, would have to pay on its bonds or capital leases," Lauer said. "And that is not a good thing." The current county council and management say they have been inherited a disaster, and they're working to fix it. Interim County Manager Jeff Powell listed an array of efforts."We brought in a second CPA firm to help catch up," he said. "We've had consultants, additional consultants in besides the audit firm. We're doing a GFO, a Governor Finance Officers Association study, on the finance office and procedures and best practices that haven't been being done. We've staffed up, we've got some new staff in there. We're throwing every resource we can at it." The situation with the county's finance department - high staff turnover, lack of accountability, missing leadership, scant oversight - raises questions about a continuing culture of half measures and temporary personnel substituting for thorough policies and experienced professionals in key positions in Dorchester County government.Spears, who served as finance director for 27 years, said attracting solid candidates for the finance department and making sure they stay is exceptionally tough for Dorchester, whose constrained tax base means salaries are among the lowest of any county in Maryland."A lot of it is tone at the top," he said. "You've got a really top-notch county manager and really topnotch HR person that can help with recruiting. I think you can overcome sometimes some of these lower pays." A charter amendment was proposed to cure the problem with the county manager."First of all, it's clear that very short-lived county managers, interim county managers, potentially unqualified county managers for that kind of position," said Lauer, who was a leader of the move for a charter amendment."I'm not talking about anybody currently on the scene." He added: "Council interference and the operations of government firing people without reason, we believe has created a severe morale problem in the government that prompts this kind of turnover." Lauer pointed to the city of Cambridge, the largest city in Dorchester County."We've had three city managers now; it's moved the city along wonderfully," he said. "The city manager we have now who I have a lot of respect for, he came from Ohio. He's amazing with the options alternatives. He provides very reasoned decisions.A county manager, let's say, with those kinds of qualifications and credentials would be on top of this thing - the minute something occurred." He called the county's "laxness, the inability to follow through to have and follow rigorous accounting and financial management procedures" very concerning.Lauer said, "(It's) something I've never seen anything like that in my time." He said the 2020 report "should have set off immediate alarm bells and somebody asking, 'What are we doing for fiscal year 2021?'" "This is a big thing, not being able to produce an annual financial report so that citizens are assured everything is on the up and up, that they're getting accurate information, and that the council's basing its decisions on accurate information," he said. "That's a big deal." Pfeffer, the current council president, said the county commissioners who were in the previous administration were unaware of the 2020 auditor's critique. But nobody could explain why they didn't notice for years that the county's annual audits were either late or never showed up.None of that makes a difference now, according to Pfeffer."Do I take responsibility?Absolutely, 100 percent," Pfeffer said. "I was on the council then; I'm the president of council now." "I'm not trying to shirk any of my responsibilities or fault with this," he continued, "but we're just hoping and asking for understanding from the state and the other stakeholders to work with us." He said the county is not trying to hide from anybody."What's current is available on the county website.Anything that's not current, that's not there, it's not available yet, but we're not trying to hide this at all, but it's just a fact," he said."That did happen, and we apologize for it." Jim Brady is a reporter for WHCP radio in Cambridge, the National Public Radio station for the Eastern Shore.

MA GGIE TROVATO/DORCHESTER STAR

title: Dorchester County Ballot Questions Will Not Take Effect Due to 'Administrative Error'
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Dorchester County ballot questions will not take effect due to 'administrative error'

 March 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 454
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Although Dorchester County voters who took to the polls in November voted on whether changes should be made to the county charter, those changes will not be made this year.During a Dorchester County Council meeting on March 4, Council President Lenny Pfeffer announced the county had made an "administrative error" by not advertising the referendum questions for five consecutive weeks after the council approved them.
"With it not being advertised correctly per state law, it would not make those referendum questions valid to change the charter," Pfeffer said.
The error in advertising was an accident, Pfeffer said, and he apologized to county residents.
"As far as blame for this, this entire (council) and Dorchester County takes general responsibility for this mistake," he said.
Pfeffer said the error was discovered in the process of reclaiming the county's sanitary district. He said that during the bond review process, legal counsel for the bond review discovered the oversight.
Pfeffer said the county waited for additional legal review before telling the public.
In an interview with the Star Democrat March 5, Pfeffer said the council was notified of the error a little over a month ago. He said the county had previously been trying to have the amendments made to the charter by spring.
In November, county residents voted to amend four parts of the county charter. The changes amended the charter to:
Have the review of administrative structure be conducted within the first fiscal year of each Dorchester County Council term. Currently, the charter says a review of administrative structure should take place at least every four years, but it does not state when in that four years it should take place.Push back budget-related due dates 15 days.Clarify responsibilities of the county manager, including day-to-day operations, and establish procedures for certain vacancies. Currently, the charter has procedures in place for council member and treasurer vacancies, as well as certain board and commission vacancies.Include language to ensure transparency of governmental functions as well as access to open meetings and public records.
Pfeffer said although these amendments cannot be made to the charter now, they could be voted on again in future elections.
"So it will be up to the wishes of the Charter Review Commission and the council before the next election on if any one, all of, or whatever list of referendum questions could get placed on the ballot next time," he said.
Dorchester County Attorney Chip MacLeod said the county is looking into whether the ballot questions that were approved by voters could be addressed through county code or policy changes.
MacLeod called the situation "unfortunate," but made it clear other opportunities might exist.
"One way or another, the county's going to be impacted by those charter amendments, even though they're not technically valid," he said.

title: Campaigning Practices Questioned at Cambridge City Council Meeting
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Campaigning practices questioned at Cambridge City Council meeting

 November 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 644
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — In the final week before Cambridge's heated run-off election for its next mayor, residents are bringing up concerns with candidate campaigning practices.During a Cambridge City Council meeting on Nov. 25, two residents detailed their concerns with candidates door knocking at apartment complexes where elderly people and people with disabilities live.
Cambridge Commission President Lajan Cephas and former Cambridge Mayor Andrew Bradshaw are both running to fill the open mayoral seat. Their campaigns have been gearing up as the city draws nearer to the Dec. 3 run-off election.
At the council meeting, resident Mya Woods read a letter from another resident, GeriLeigh Farrow, that called out Cephas and her campaign.
In the letter, Farrow said she was working at Conifer Village at Cambridge, an apartment complex for seniors, when she noticed a man standing outside.
"I noticed the man outside, which now I know as Lajan's boyfriend or husband, while she was inside," the letter read.
Before Woods could finish reading the letter, Mayor Stephen Rideout told her public comments must be made to or about the entire council, not a single commissioner.
Woods went on to ask that the city's elected officials make sure they make decisions with the residents best interests, not just their own.
"... Just remember, the town is broken and they need people who can lead them and not take advantage of them," she said.
Michael Jones, a resident of New Horizons Apartments, told the City Council he has seen people come in and out of his apartment for campaign reasons. He recounted an experience where he received a knock at his door and later found a campaign flier at his door.
Commissioner Laurel Atkiss said Conifer Village residents have been reaching out to her about "problems with their building being infiltrated."
"The measures that people go to these days to take advantage of our vulnerable and elderly and differently-abled is really heart wrenching," she said. "They do everything from selling fake extended car warranties or service contracts to stealing home equity lines of credit."
Atkiss — who has endorsed Bradshaw in the upcoming election — said she has also heard that a campaign gained access to New Horizons and the Bradford House Apartments. Atkiss later told the Star Democrat she was talking about Cephas' campaign.
Atkiss said that when she wanted to go door knocking inside Conifer during her campaign, she was told she couldn't as a security measure for residents.
"It's not up to me to decide that my cause is greater than their privacy and their right to not be disturbed," she said.
Atkiss continued on to say that no one voted for the commissioners "so they could see what we could get away with."
"But I know, if this is how elected officials act, I don't blame people for not coming out and voting," she said.
Cephas responded to the comments, acknowledging the issue has nothing to do with city business.
"But since people want to spin a narrative, I'm going to be transparent," she said.
Cephas said she was invited by a resident to do a meet and greet at Conifer on Nov. 26 and said she was invited by management to do a meet and greet at Bradford House on Dec. 2.
"I think we need to understand that canvassing is not illegal," she said. "Canvassing is an intentional way of interacting with the residents. Everyone doesn't have social media. Everyone doesn't have email. So we all knock on everyone's door that we're allowed to knock on."
She said her concern is not with "sensationalized behaviors," but with making sure everyone is able to vote.
"And I just really find it a shame that we have other people who are trying to say that (canvassing is) being used to take advantage when we're trying to engage," she said.
The Cambridge run-off election will be held on Dec. 3 at 447 Race St. The polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.

title: Criminal Records on Cambridge City Council: Mayoral Candidates Give Their Takes
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Criminal records on Cambridge City Council: mayoral candidates give their takes

 October 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 469
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — During a Cambridge candidate forum conducted by the League of Women Voters on Oct. 5, the city's three mayoral candidates gave their takes on whether a criminal record should disqualify someone from being a mayor or commissioner in Cambridge.The question is one of relevance to the city's mayoral election, specifically.
Mayoral candidate Andrew Bradshaw, who served as Cambridge's mayor in 2021, resigned from the position in January 2022 after being charged with 50 counts of distributing revenge porn on Reddit. He later pleaded guilty to five of those counts.
Now that the mayoral term — which he started but did not finish — is ending, Bradshaw is running for mayor again in the city's Oct. 19 election.
Mayoral candidate and Cambridge Commission President Lajan Cephas has also faced legal issues. In 2022, she was charged with second-degree assault in connection with a domestic violence incident in her Cambridge home. The charges were dismissed in January 2023.
During the forum, mayoral candidate La-Shon Banks-Foster, who is running against Bradshaw and Cephas, said the answer to whether a criminal record should disqualify someone from being on the City Council is not a yes or no question. She said it depends on the crime, whether that person has been rehabilitated and what steps they've taken since.
Cephas said the question should be up to the voters. She added that one of a mayor's responsibilities is to meet with different people.
"Are they going to feel comfortable being in a photograph with someone that's known for a nation-wide headline that was, not only embarrassing to that person, but the victim and also that community that person represented?" she said.
Bradshaw said he felt the question was directed toward him. He said that in a city where many people have made mistakes, a large portion of the population shouldn't be disqualified from serving on the City Council because of the "errors of their past."
"And likewise, when people have overcome the failures that they've made, when they can move forward in their lives, we shouldn't turn away from the people that have talent and ability to contribute to a community," he said.
In response to Cephas' comments, Bradshaw said his convictions were withdrawn and removed by the state and his probation has been abated.
According to court documents, in November 2023, Judge Thomas G. Ross ordered that the judgements of guilt for Bradshaw's five counts of distributing revenge porn be stricken and Bradshaw be granted probation before judgement.
In an interview with the Star Democrat on Oct. 8, Bradshaw said he didn't want to go into detail on how this came about, but it was a decision made by his attorneys, the Office of the state Prosecutor and Ross.
A court document filed in June said Bradshaw's probation abatement date — the end to active supervision of the defendant — was May 13.

title: Cambridge Candidates Dispute Peace Order Request, Residency Requirements
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Cambridge candidates dispute peace order request, residency requirements

 October 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 615
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — With questions swirling about the residency of candidates in Cambridge's Oct. 19 election, three candidates headed to Dorchester County District Court Wednesday morning for a peace order hearing between one candidate and another's wife.Ward 4 Cambridge Commissioner Sputty Cephas, who is running for reelection, was denied a final peace order Wednesday against Natalee Bradshaw, the wife of former Cambridge Mayor and current mayoral candidate Andrew Bradshaw.
Andrew Bradshaw called the peace order request "a malicious use" of the court system "performed specifically for political purposes."
Cephas told the Star Democrat he had no intent behind filing the peace order other than not wanting to be bothered.
On Oct. 2, Cephas was granted a temporary peace order against Natalee Bradshaw. The peace order entailed that Natalee Bradshaw neither abuse Cephas, nor contact Cephas, nor enter his residence.
During the hearing Wednesday, Cephas asked Judge Abigail Marsh to grant a final peace order, which would extend the length of the temporary peace order.
Cephas testified that on Oct. 1, after leaving a Cambridge Planning and Zoning Commission meeting, he noticed a white Lincoln follow him to his home. Cephas said when he backed into his driveway, he saw the white Lincoln slow down and the driver of the vehicle snap photos before driving away quickly.
Cephas said he got back into his vehicle and drove behind the white Lincoln to get identification. He was able to identify the driver as Natalee Bradshaw. Cephas said he then spoke with Andrew Bradshaw for a minute or so.
Cephas then brought the issue to his sister, Commission President Lajan Cephas — who is running against Andrew Bradshaw and La-Shon Banks-Foster in the mayoral election — before going to the police department.
During the hearing, he told the judge that he felt harassed and stalked.
"I just want to be left alone," he said.
Natalee Bradshaw's attorney Philip Cronan argued Sputty Cephas' petition should be dismissed because none of his allegations was sufficient. Cronan said Natalee Bradshaw never made contact with or approached Sputty Cephas the night of Oct. 1.
Before denying the final peace order, Judge Abigail Marsh said Natalee Bradshaw is on notice that Sputty Cephas does not want any contact.
Marsh said harassment and stalking allegations require a pattern of behavior for a final peace order to be granted, and this was a single incident.
RESIDENCY REQUIREMENTSDuring the hearing, Cronan brought up statements that have been made questioning whether Sputty Cephas and/or Lajan Cephas are following the city's residency requirements for candidates.
Questions regarding the residency of candidates have circulated through Cambridge in the last month.
At a City Council meeting Sept. 9, one resident brought up the importance of verifying candidate applications. In response, Assistant City Manager Brandon Hesson said city staff has heard rumors regarding applicants and their residency, but no formal complaints had been filed. He encouraged residents to submit formal complaints so that they can be looked into.
In an interview Wednesday, Andrew Bradshaw alleged that Lajan Cephas has not been residing at the Cambridge address on her application. He said that his wife "may well have been" seeing about residency the night of Oct. 1. He said if that is the case, her actions were based on "real and genuine" concerns.
Lajan Cephas said in an interview Wednesday that she is not sure of Natalee Bradshaw's intent. Cephas said she has met every requirement to be a candidate in the city's election.
Sputty Cephas said during the hearing that the city has a process to do its due diligence for candidate applications.
Andrew Bradshaw said his wife has never expressed to him why she was outside Sputty Cephas's home Oct. 1. He said that in the privacy of their home, she has sworn she did not take any photos.

title: Open Meetings Compliance Board Finds Cambridge City Council in Violation
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Open Meetings Compliance Board finds Cambridge City Council in violation

 July 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 694
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Maryland Open Meetings Compliance Board has found the Cambridge City Council to be in violation of the Open Meetings Act for actions made during and following a City Council meeting on Jan. 8At a City Council meeting on July 8, Cambridge Mayor Stephen Rideout read a portion of the board's July 3 opinion, which found that the council violated documentation requirements for a closed meeting preceding the open session council meeting in January.
"The city does not fully agree with this decision, but has read it as required by the Open Meetings Act board," he said before directing city staff to publish the opinion on the city's website.
According to the opinion, which was published on the Maryland attorney general website, the board found the city failed to prepare a written closing statement to enter into a closed session meeting, failed to put together "sufficiently detailed" minutes of the closed session and failed to put together a "sufficiently detailed" public summary of the closed session.
The board did not find that the council violated the Open Meetings Act by holding the meeting itself.
The opinion states the complainant filed an application in September requesting the city rezone several parcels of land. It says the council was scheduled to vote on the matter on Jan. 8, and at the beginning of that meeting, the council voted to postpone the vote on the application.
According to the Jan. 8 council agenda and meeting minutes, the council voted to postpone one item that dealt with rezoning: an ordinance that would have amended zoning to make four contiguous parcels at the corner of Washington and High streets the same zoning district.
At a council meeting on April 22, the council voted to deny the proposed ordinance, which had previously been tabled, in a three-to-two vote, with commissioners Jameson Harrington and Brian Roche voting against denying the rezoning.
Jim Chaney, complainant and managing member of Quality Housing Cambridge LLC — which submitted the application to rezone parcels on Washington and High streets — said he thought the Compliance Board did the best it could with the information it was able to obtain.
Chaney said it was concerning that the city did not keep "proper minutes" for the closed session meeting. He said that he didn't believe in the city's leadership.
"How do you attract businesses and people to come to the city when you're doing things like this?" he asked.
According to the opinion from the Compliance Board, the complaint alleged that the council:
Entered into closed session without convening the meeting in open session.Had discussions in closed session outside the parameters of what it said it would discuss.Failed to make required disclosures to the public after exiting closed session.Conducted business outside of a meeting that should have been conducted in an open meeting.
The complaint also alleged that the council violated the act by tabling the ordinance during the Jan. 8 open session meeting.
The Compliance Board said it could not conclude whether the council "improperly convened" in closed session Jan. 8 after the town said it made a public announcement before doing so.
The board said that although the council invoked two exceptions that allow it to enter into closed session, the council did not prepare a written closing statement, which is a violation of the act.
The board also said it could not determine whether the council talked about things outside the bounds of what it claimed to enter closed session for because the council failed to disclose anything regarding the substance of the closed meeting in its sealed minutes. The board found the council in violation of the Open Meetings Act because of that failure.
Regarding the allegation that the council conducted business it should not have outside of the meeting, the board said the question is really a matter of whether the council met in secret because the act only applies to meetings. The board said the council denies discussing the application before the regular meeting, and the board could not conclude whether the council met in secret.
The board said tabling an item is not a violation of the act and declined to find a violation based on that specific allegation brought forward by the complainant.

title: CWDI and Dorchester County Council not in violation of Open Meetings Act
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
CWDI and Dorchester County Council not in violation of Open Meetings Act

 February 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 785
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Maryland's Open Meetings Compliance Board has found Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. and the Dorchester County Council not in violation of the state's Open Meetings Act for a Nov. 13 closed meeting held by CWDI.In its opinions delivered Feb. 1, the OMCB stated that CWDI was not in violation of the act because it is not a public body. It did not find the County Council in violation of the act because the council did not go into a "meeting" at the Packing House Nov. 13.
At the meeting, which brought together city and county officials and development consultants, CWDI justified going into closed session using two exceptions listed in the Maryland Open Meetings Act: "to consider a matter that concerns the proposal for a business to locate, expand, or remain" and "to discuss a matter where public discussion would adversely impact the public body's proposal process."
CWDI, a nonprofit that was formed by the City of Cambridge, Dorchester County and the State of Maryland, has been tasked with planning and developing space along the Cambridge waterfront, known as Cambridge Harbor.
Plans include public spaces like a promenade and parks, a boutique hotel and residential and mixed-use spaces along the Choptank River.
CWDI Executive Director Matt Leonard said that during the meeting, CWDI talked about business deals it is working on.
Before CWDI entered into closed session on Nov. 13, WHCP reporter Jim Brady and Star Democrat Executive Editor Jim Johnson objected to the meeting being closed to the public.
Following the meeting, the Star Democrat and WHCP sent a complaint to the OMCB, alleging nine potential violations of the Open Meetings Act, including that the agenda topics were not consistent with the exceptions CWDI used to justify the closed meeting. The complaints were directed toward CWDI and the Dorchester County Council.
Although City of Cambridge staff and elected officials were also present at the November meeting, the Star Democrat and WHCP did not allege violations regarding the city's involvement in the meeting.
City Council voted against going into closed session at the Nov. 13 meeting, and one commissioner left so the city would avoid an Open Meetings Act violation.
OMCB OPINIONSAccording to the Feb. 1 opinions document, the OMCB found that CWDI didn't violate the Open Meetings Act because the non-profit is not a public body, and the act only applies to public bodies.
To determine whether CWDI could be considered a public body, the OMCB looked at how the entity was created and how its members were appointed to the board.
"As we have said before, '(p)erhaps the Maryland General Assembly might decide at some point to broaden the definition, so as to encompass all entities that carry out public functions,'" the opinions document says.
Leonard said he was not surprised by the decision made by the Compliance Board. He said it affirmed what CWDI "has said since it's beginning" — that it is a private corporation set to a public mission.
The reason CWDI listed the Open Meetings Act exceptions before going into closed session, he said, was to make CWDI's public partners feel comfortable.
"We list those exceptions, although we're not required to," Leonard said. "It's something we've done as a courtesy out of respect for our public partners since the beginning."
Brady, who objected to the Nov. 13 closed meeting, said it would be good for the state legislature to review what is considered a public body.
"I just find it unfortunate and unfathomable that an organization that's spending that kind of public money and ruling over that kind of land is not open to the public," he said.
The OMCB found that the Dorchester County Council didn't violate the Open Meetings Act because the Nov. 13 "gathering" wasn't a County Council meeting.
According to the opinions document, although all members of the council attended the gathering, the question was whether the Council "convened to consider or transact public business."
The OMCB said it could not conclude the gathering was a meeting based on the record presented.
"As we understand it, then, the Councilmembers attended the gathering to receive information, but the discussion was not a step in the Council's decision-making process regarding an item that was certain to come before the Council," the document says.
Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said he was glad to see the decision that was made.
"There was never an intention for the Dorchester County Council to be violating any confidence of trust," he said.
In its opinions, the OMCB noted that "the appearance" of business being secretly conducted doesn't "serve the purpose" of the Open Meetings Act to "increase the faith of the public in government."
"Our conclusion in no way condones the action of a quorum of the (Councilmembers) in creating what was, at the least, an appearance of impropriety," the board said.

title: Officials Talk Local, Federal Challenges with Cambridge Seniors
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Officials talk local, federal challenges with Cambridge seniors

 August 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 589
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Local, state and federal officials, including Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.), joined senior citizens at the Chesapeake Grove Intergenerational Center on Monday afternoon to discuss issues affecting Cambridge's older residents.Cambridge Mayor Lejan Cephas introduced Alsobrooks by describing local policies that help seniors, like the homeownership helper program, and affirming the city's commitment to providing protections for its aging population.
"I can tell you Cambridge is absolutely intentional about our seniors, about our older residents in the city of Cambridge," Cephas said. "We actually put policies in place to provide protections and also the opportunity that you can age and place."
Alsobrooks identified with the audience by describing herself as part of the "sandwich generation," with a 20-year-old child and parents who have been married for 50 years. Her father now cares for her mother, who has dementia. Because of this, Alsobrooks said she is familiar with the struggles senior citizens are facing after recent federal cuts.
The senator went on to slam President Donald Trump's Big Beautiful Bill, saying the brunt of what she called the "Big Ugly Bill" will fall on senior citizens and pointing to significant cuts to Medicaid, Medicare and nutrition programs.
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act was passed on July 4, extending Trump's 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act. The bill made a majority of tax cuts permanent and increased federal spending on border security, defense and energy production while significantly cutting health care and nutrition programs.
Maryland Department of Aging Secretary Carmel Roques said in early iterations of the Big Beautiful Bill, funding for older people in Maryland, primarily through the Older Americans Act, was zeroed out. But the funding was restored in the latest state budget through concerted federal and state efforts, she said.
While officials largely discussed state- and federal-level issues, Cambridge residents like Sandra Snowden sought answers to problems they face at the local level.
"I am politically astute," Snowden said. "And I do understand all that's going on on the national level. I need to kind of bring us down here, to Chesapeake Grove. Right now, we don't have enough money to keep this center going."
Snowden said it currently costs $64 a month for seniors to attend the center two days a week. It costs $5 more for lunch, and there are additional costs for extra activities. The cost of these services vary depending on use and means of transportation, but for Snowden, the cost is too much regardless.
Snowden, who is legally blind, is lives in one of three senior residence facilities in Cambridge. She said her complex has experienced bug infestations, sees high rates of crime and currently has no lighting in the parking lot.
Alsobrooks responded saying she does not have direct oversight of these issues in the city. Cephas and City Manager Glenn Steckman addressed Snowden's concerns directly, saying city officials worked hard with this year's budget to allocate funds towards issues concerning older residents.
The budget currently has $15,000 set aside for senior citizen activities and objectives.
Del. Sheree Sample-Hughes (D-Dorchester, Wicomico) encouraged Alsobrooks to maintain open communication so they can have a strong partnership moving forward.
"Whatever comes out at your level, it comes down to this state and just keeping us abreast so we can know what we need to fight for. The seniors, if they want to write a letter or make a phone call and know how it's going to affect the Department of Aging or the Department of Health, that kind of communication level. We need to be able to work with you as a strong partner," Sample-Hughes said.

title: 'Only Going to Get Worse': Talbot Officials Discuss Rise in Senior Homelessness
author: Konner Metz
content:
'Only going to get worse': Talbot officials discuss rise in senior homelessness

 July 31, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: News 
 
 648
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County officials and senior care leaders met Tuesday to discuss creating a task force to address senior homelessness, a rapidly accelerating problem, experts say.The request for the task force comes from Talbot County Council member Lynn Mielke. Based on council feedback, a resolution to create the task force seems poised for approval at the council's Aug. 12 meeting.
Members of the county's Commission on Aging and other health and housing experts spoke on mounting challenges faced by area seniors, from housing costs and food insecurity to mental health struggles.
Rachel Smith, chair of the aging commission, said a task force would help align local nonprofits, county boards and the health department. There's currently a "disconnect," she said.
"There isn't anybody who is behind all of these organizations pushing to keep everybody connected," Smith said. "And that's what we found is one of the biggest problems. We have all these organizations out here that are doing so much great work, but then we've got to figure out a way to connect so we can help all these people."
Mielke said there's no single solution to help the homeless senior population.
"Each agency would bring solutions or suggestions, but not one agency can deal with all of the issues," Mielke said.
As drafted, the senior citizens task force would consist of representatives from the following entities: Commission on Aging, Delmarva Community Services, Talbot Interfaith Shelter, Neighborhood Service Center, Talbot County Health Department, Easton Town Council and County Council. Members from Mid-Shore Behavioral Health and law enforcement agencies may also be added based on Tuesday's discussions.
The task force would make recommendations to the County Council on housing, transportation and meal services for homeless seniors.
Homelessness is growing
Julie Lowe, executive director of Talbot Interfaith Shelter, cited jumps in calls from seniors as evidence that homelessness is on the rise.
In 2023, the shelter received 15 calls from men 55 and older and 14 calls from women 55 and older. One year later, those marks increased to 30 and 23, respectively.
This year, the Easton-based shelter has already received 19 calls from men and 13 calls from women in that age range.
Talbot Interfaith has limited capacity, Lowe said. It runs a multi-year program to transition people into paying for partial rent before moving out on their own. But even when shelter residents move out, Lowe said finding a financially viable apartment in the area isn't an easy task, especially for seniors who can't work.
"Most of the people who we work with will never get to that point with the market-rate housing and where it is now," Lowe said.
Lee Newcomb, a Talbot County social worker for 26 years and the aging commission's secretary, said she's never seen senior need at such a high level.
Newcomb said the Days Inn in Easton is home to many unhoused individuals. Smith said seniors especially suffer in the winter months since Talbot County doesn't have a low-barrier homeless shelter.
Smith noted an incident at the Days Inn last December as a wake-up call. According to police, an unhoused man who was living in the woods behind the hotel was found dead on Dec. 14, 2024.
"I feel like we missed something there," Smith said. "We shouldn't have our senior residents — some of them have worked in our community — die."
Cambridge-based Delmarva Community Services has served many homeless people from Talbot County down in Dorchester, according to president and CEO Andy Hollis.
Hollis said a low-barrier, overnight shelter is a gap in Talbot County, and something that a task force could work on. Many others at the meeting on Tuesday emphasized the need for a physical location to consolidate services for the senior homeless population.
'We don't have this issue in Talbot,' we thought for so long," Hollis said. "And we truly do. It's something that is long overdue in terms of being addressed."
"The challenge is not leveling out and it's only going to get worse," he added.
