title: Eastern Shore Renters Face Challenges With Affordable Housing
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Eastern Shore renters face challenges with affordable housing

 March 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 1987
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Bradford House Apartments resident Linda Johnson doesn't carry mace on her keychain anymore.She doesn't feel the need to use a key or a cell phone instead of her finger to tap the buttons of the apartment's elevator.
After years of asking apartment management to address resident safety concerns, from mold and bug infestations to a lack of security, Johnson and other Bradford House residents finally feel safe.
"I feel better every day," said Johnson, who has lived at Bradford House on Race Street in Cambridge for nearly 25 years. "I'm not angry no more."
The complex — which offers multifamily, subsidized housing for low-income individuals who are elderly or have special needs — came under new management with a new principal owner in the fall, and residents started to see changes they had requested for years be made.
But as housing problems across the Eastern Shore persist, others have not been as lucky.
A SHORE PROBLEM
With a lack of affordable housing options on the Eastern Shore and a need for better enforcement over housing standards, renters living in poor conditions often feel stuck.
In the eyes of Larry Rooths, the head of the Public Safety and Intelligence Committee for the Eastern Shore branch of the Caucus of African American Leaders, the lack of affordable housing is a national issue.
"But it seems a lot worse down here because there's so little housing," he said, "and there's no infrastructure in place for emergency services, emergency shelters."
Rooths said he's noticed landlords don't feel like they have to do much for tenants because there aren't many other places those tenants can go.
"And then the residents feel like that also," he said. "They don't want to stir up too much trouble because they know if somebody comes in and shuts the building down, where are they going?"
Rooths sees a need for housing legislation with more enforcement power so landlords address the issues residents face. He said the Shore also needs more housing infrastructure.
"If you create a situation where there's enough housing, then the landlords lose control," he said. "...If you don't like the place you're living in, you get up and move. But if there's no place to move or you can't move to another apartment building close to where you work, then it gets difficult."
The caucus is working to get tenants to form groups, which Rooths said would help them know their rights and push elected officials to make change.
"Unless there's some change in legislation or there's some increased funding to create a bigger pool of housing, this problem is going to be the same," he said.
In October, the Tenant Safety Act of 2024 went into effect in Maryland. The act, which places responsibility on landlords to provide safe dwelling for tenants, guarantees tenants can form groups.
Shore Legal Access Executive Director Meredith Girard considers Bradford House's tenant association a critical piece of its success in getting new management.
"I think the tenant association was critical to really letting the management and the court know what the issues were and how widespread it was," Girard said. "And that prompted some really important changes so that now the building is managed by a new company."
Girard said rural counties don't always have enough resources to support a rental inspection and licensing system. She said it would be great if counties on the Eastern Shore could pool their resources to form a regional housing commission.
"Where you could set some basic standards for habitability to make sure that if you're renting a unit, that the oven works, that the heat works, that the plumbing works, that the roof isn't leaking," she said.
Girard acknowledged rural landlords may also be strapped for resources. She said in some cases, landlords might not have the resources to make needed repairs.
"Which then becomes this really problematic cycle," she said.
At Bradford House, previous management said the property had been neglected before they took over in 2022.
In an April 2024 statement to The Star Democrat, Millennia Housing Management, the previous management at the complex, said it had invested more than $300,000 into the maintenance and enhancement of the "severely distressed property."
Girard said that when problems in complexes are fixed, tenants are often scared to complain about the conditions because they don't have anywhere else to go.
"And they don't want to upset their landlords," she said. "But at the same time, they need landlords to fix the things that need to be fixed."
Maryland Legal Aid Advocacy Director for the Human Right to Housing Zafar Shah said further protections against evictions are needed so tenants aren't reluctant to use the Tenant Safety Act of 2024. He said the Maryland legislature is considering a good cause eviction bill "that would protect tenants from lease non-renewal without a good reason."
"This is the big priority for renters in Maryland," he said.
NO WHERE TO GO
De'Auntte Clark came to Cambridge for peace.
In 2016, her 14-year-old son was killed after being hit by a car in Anne Arundel County. Four years later, her husband died from COVID-19.
In September 2022, Clark brought her family to the Eastern Shore for a fresh start. But since moving here, Clark has found anything but the peace she was seeking.
"I'm so numb, I can't cry," she said.
With concerns about the safety of her apartment at Calvin Mowbray Park and Stephen Camper Park in Cambridge and nowhere else to go, Clark spent more than a month living out of a van with her family.
A few days after her family moved into the complex, Clark noticed what seemed like mold in the cabinets along one of the walls in the kitchen.
Maintenance came to clean the cabinets out, but as the weather outside got colder and she turned the heat on, Clark said she started to see black spots pop up on the walls.
In December 2023, Clark's son, Keith Dezurn — who has a medical history of severe, persistent asthma — was airlifted to the University of Maryland Children's Hospital because he was struggling to breathe. He stayed in intensive care for five days, Clark said, displaying symptoms consistent with mold exposure.
Clark said on the way to the hospital in Baltimore, she could barely see anything and was crying.
"I don't want to lose another child," she said.
Ed Cafasso, a spokesperson for the property that is managed by WinnResidential, said on Jan. 15 that the health and safety of residents is WinnResidential's number one priority.
"Any time a household reports a moisture-related issue, it is treated as an emergency and remediated immediately by a professional, licensed specialist," he said.
Cafasso said over the past year, there have been seven instances at the complex that required professional mold remediation. He said there were zero reported cases of mold at the 190-apartment community as of January.
Before Clark and her family could move into a new unit at the complex this past fall, the unit was condemned. Cambridge Assistant City Manager Brandon Hesson said that in condemning the unit, the city ordered mold and moisture testing be done.
An inspection report obtained by The Star Democrat from the city showed an early November analysis found aspergillus and penicillium spore counts in the unit that were "significantly higher than the baseline count and probably indicates a source of contamination."
The unit was later removed from the city's list of condemned properties after a report by Simple Mold Solutions, which was based on the analysis, found the numbers "indicated a normal fungal environment with no elevated concentrations of airborne mold spores." The report recommended the HVAC system be cleaned to prevent mold spores from circulating.
But Clark's son's health scare was enough to make her seek housing elsewhere. The search proved to be no easy feat.
Limited affordable housing options on the Eastern Shore and across the state have made it difficult for Clark to find somewhere new to settle.
Clark said she went to multiple shelters in Howard County, where her children are currently enrolled in school, but all of them were full. She said the places she did find that had space required she live in the county for six months, which she had not.
Moving from place to place hasn't been easy on Clark's kids. She said they are scared to go back to the complex.
"They don't want to go back there, and I don't know what to do," Clark told The Star Democrat while they were living out of a van. "But at the same time, I know we can't keep living like this."
In mid-December, Clark and her family were able to secure a hotel room after living out of a van for more than a month. On Valentine's Day, they moved into a townhouse on the western shore.
"It's much better," she said. "No mold."
ZOOMING IN ON THE PROBLEM
Clark's story isn't an uncommon one when it comes to tenants of affordable housing on the Eastern Shore.
Residential issues at affordable housing complexes in Cambridge have come to a head more than once in the last two years.
In an attempt to attack the bigger issue at the local level, Cambridge has beefed up its Code Enforcement Department and is working on projects intended to increase and improve the city's housing stock.
Hesson said although the issues at housing facilities are all unique, there are common themes among them.
"There have been failures by agencies at the local, state and federal level to hold up the standards we've set for housing providers here," he said. "It's not my place to point fingers, because it isn't going to fix anything. The city is part of that structure, and we're committed to being better."
Hesson said building "strong relationships" with the governing authorities for the different housing facilities has helped achieve "significant progress."
"We've been able to draw attention to where these systems and processes have fallen short, and residents are seeing some of the early results of those efforts," he said.
PROGRESS
For Linda Johnson, those results are clear.
On Feb. 13, Johnson moved into a new unit within Bradford House Apartments. The move is not just a win for Johnson, who has been a loud and consistent voice of the Bradford House community, but proof of a new era for the apartment complex and its residents.
For years Bradford House residents expressed concerns about the safety of the building. In September 2023, the property — which was then managed by Millennia — received a U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development inspection score that indicated health and safety deficiencies.
Three months later, Millennia received a debarment order from HUD, preventing the company from participating in any new business with the department.
In October, it was announced that Nuveen, an asset manager and subsidiary of financial planning firm TIAA, had been made principal owner of the apartment complex. Paths Management Services, a subsidiary of Nuveen, would manage the property.
Johnson's new digs, complete with a brand new, updated kitchen and laminate wood flooring, are a stark contrast from her previous unit.
When The Star Democrat visited some residents' homes last year, residents pointed out things like holes in ceilings, possible mold and problems with stoves. At that time, multiple residents had active rent escrow cases, where tenants pay their rent to a court, rather than to their landlord, until property issues are addressed.
The change at Bradford House isn't just visible in individual apartment units. The hallways have new flooring, the stairways are consistently clean, there is better lighting and new cameras and the community room has been renovated. Johnson said management is fixing the elevator that's been broken for more than a year.
"It's been wonderful," Johnson said. "I mean Paths came in here, they didn't talk, they worked."
Johnson is the president of the complex's tenant association, which was formed with guidance from Shore Legal Access.
"Just because we're low income people doesn't mean we have to live like that," she said.
Johnson said other renters going through housing issues should fight for what they believe in, adding that tenants have the right to withhold rent and form tenant associations.
"Your voice matters," she said.

title: Cambridge Aims to Improve Its Housing Stock with Programs, Projects
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge aims to improve its housing stock with programs, projects

 December 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 733
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Visiting the corner of Douglas and Bethel streets in Cambridge is an exciting trip for Cambridge Housing Program Manager Ed Crosby.The four homes being built there, in Cambridge's historic Pine Street neighborhood, are part of a plan slowly unfolding.
"We went out to the site yesterday," Crosby said in an interview with the Star Democrat on Dec. 11. "(The developer) said to me, 'You're looking at (the houses) like they're your babies.' I said, 'Yes, they are my babies.'"
The project is one of multiple the city is working on in order to achieve its goal of improving its housing stock, uplifting the community and fostering a culture where residents want to stay in Cambridge.
"Everything from renovations to restorations to demos even, if that's the case, depending on the situation," Crosby said. "But in those areas, making sure that the community is fully engaged and informed that the city is committed to having a healthier home environment."
As housing program manager, Crosby sits at the helm of this mission. His position, which he took on in March, was created out of a need identified by former City Manager Tom Carroll.
Crosby was brought on board to oversee the execution of an "umbrella program" called Healthy Homes, which provides support services to residents to help them navigate home-related challenges.
Under that umbrella program, the city offers a variety of housing-related help for residents.
The Homeowner Helper Program, for example, is a financial program that gives qualifying seniors financial assistance to make needed repairs to their homes. Crosby said that so far, a resident has had their roof replaced through the program.
"We're looking at our residents having piece of mind," he said. "We want them to know that they come first and that we care."
Another program, which the city started through a grant from the U.S Department of Housing and Urban Development, will allow the city to do lead remediation. The three-year grant has a training component so local contractors can be trained in lead remediation and even become trainers themselves.
In March, the Cambridge City Council voted to establish the Land Bank Authority of Cambridge, which will have the power to take on, manage and sell vacant land in order to stabilize neighborhoods and encourage redevelopment. Crosby said the city has identified potential board members for the land bank, but the City Council has yet to appoint anyone to the board.
After the city finishes building the Douglas Street houses, it plans to build at least 10 more homes on Chesapeake Court and School House Lane.
Crosby said it's important that Cambridge is seen as a "livable community."
"We want you to feel not only that is this a destination, but this is going to be a permanent place of residence for you," he said.
The new Douglas Street houses will be sold at 80% of area median income. Crosby said people interested in purchasing the homes will have to qualify for them based on income and HUD standards. He said they will also have to complete homebuyer education training.
As the Housing Department builds up their programming, it is focusing on community engagement. The department now has a community engagement specialist who is responsible for engaging with and mobilizing the community in different housing discussions.
Crosby said community engagement is such an important piece of the city's housing goals because there needs to be "buy in" from residents.
Commission President and Mayor-elect Lajan Cephas said the Cambridge Housing Department is the city's first housing department.
"We have areas in our community, such as the historic Pine Street community that have been, in a sense, either ignored or maybe was not a priority," she said.
With the Housing Department, the city can make those areas a priority. Cephas said she thinks the city is doing a "great job" of this.
"Of course, we can't fix this overnight because this is something that's been neglected (for), I would say, more than 50 years," she said. "But absolutely within the next three to five years, as far as that gateway street known as Washington Street — and all the other streets that feed into that — there's going to be a huge difference."
Five years from now, Crosby hopes to see Cambridge's housing that's currently in a "dilapidated state" either repaired or replaced with newly built homes. He acknowledged it's an ambitious goal, but said he thinks it's doable.
"I think the community is looking for that kind of transformation," he said.

title: Harriet Tubman Posthumously Commissioned to Rank of Brigadier General
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Harriet Tubman posthumously commissioned to rank of brigadier general

 November 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 533
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHURCH CREEK — More than a century since Harriet Tubman served as a spy, scout, nurse and cook in the American Civil War, she has been officially recognized as a general officer in the Maryland Army National Guard.On Veterans Day, Tubman's descendants, local and state officials, veterans, military personnel and others packed a tent outside the Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad Visitor Center in Church Creek for a ceremony to commission and recognize Tubman as brigadier general.
The event brought an array of elected officials to the podium to speak, including Gov. Wes Moore (D), Maryland House of Delegates Speaker Adrienne Jones (D-Baltimore County) and Del. Edith Patterson (D-Charles).
Patterson, who sponsored a House bill that led to this posthumous commission, talked about Tubman's legacy.
"As we honor her legacy today, may Harriet Tubman inspire us all to strive for a more just and equitable world," she said. "Her life and legacy remind us of the courage that it takes to stand for and the profound impact one person's dedication can have on future generations."
Moore talked about Tubman's service to the country, connecting it to what Veterans Day celebrates.
"This is a holiday that is a celebration of those who chose to raise their hand," he said, later adding that Tubman was one of those individuals who raised their hand. "... Because she believed that you cannot just rail about a system being flawed. You actually have to be the one to go in and work to change it."
Maj. Gen. Janeen Birckhead, adjutant general for Maryland, explained why Tubman was given the rank of brigadier general and not captain or major. Birckhead said Tubman "lived the unique traits and responsibilities" of brigadier general.
"Like them, Harriet Tubman was a lightning rod, a role model," she said. "Her willingness to risk everything compelled others to action. Her actions communicated the audacity of hope and the potential of a vision."
Birckhead said generations of Maryland communities have known this about Tubman, and this commission honors that in a formal way.
Following the presentations of a resolution from the Maryland General Assembly and a proclamation from Moore, Tubman's great great great grandniece, Tina Wyatt, spoke. Wyatt said she loves her Aunt Harriet for her inspiration, faith, tenacity and ability to discern.
"And that is what helped her during the Civil War," she said.
Wyatt said her aunt was selfless.
"She gave up any rights that she had obtained for herself to be able to fight for others," Wyatt said about Tubman. "... She never thought about herself, she thought about what others needed."
In an interview with the Star Democrat, Michele Jones Galvin, another great great great grandniece of Tubman, called the ceremony astounding, heartfelt and emotional.
"Her work (in the Civil War) was just amazing," Galvin said. "And to be able to see her today to be commemorated and also recognized for that work so many years later is truly amazing."
Galvin came from Syracuse, New York to attend the event along with around 20 other Tubman descendants. She said they all came to the ceremony to do the same thing: come together to recognize their ancestor.
"To be able to all be here today is just a wonderful way to have a tribute to her," Galvin said.

title: Dorchester County to Put Pickleball Courts on Glasgow Street
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Dorchester County to put pickleball courts on Glasgow Street

 November 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 274
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — After a decision to resurface the Glasgow Tennis Courts left pickleball players high and dry, pickleball courts are coming to Glasgow Street.At a Dorchester County Council meeting Nov. 4, the council voted unanimously to move forward with the acquisition of property behind the Judy Center on Glasgow Street, which will allow for the creation of six new pickleball courts.
In August, the Dorchester County Board of Education approved a project by the James G. Busick Tennis Foundation to resurface the Glasgow Tennis Courts. A United States Tennis Association grant for the project — which required that only tennis lines be drawn on the courts in the first five years after resurfacing — meant that pickleball players would no longer be able to play on the courts.
The decision left many local pickleball players disappointed and frustrated.
The Nov. 4 County Council vote to acquire land for new pickleball courts comes after the Board of Education agreed to transfer a parcel of land to the county.
At a Board of Education meeting in September, Dorchester County Recreation and Parks Director Duc Trieu proposed the property transfer on behalf of the County Council. Trieu said the county would be able to create pickleball courts behind the Judy Center next to the Glasgow Tennis Courts and offer youth and adult pickleball programming.
At the Nov. 4 County Council meeting, Council President Lenny Pfeffer thanked Trieu for his efforts to make this happen and told those watching the meeting to spread the word about the plan for new courts.
"It's been very important to this community," he said about the pickleball courts. "So I'm glad we can go forward with this."

title: Hurlock Opens Walking Trail, First of Three-Phases
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Hurlock opens walking trail, first of three-phases

 August 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 570
 Words 

 Read News Document

 HURLOCK — Hurlock residents have a new place where they can soak up the final weeks of summer: a paved walking trail.Using funds from the Maryland Department of Natural Resources, the town has completed the first phase of a three-phase, 1.5-mile trail project. This first part of the project, a 2,080-foot trail, stretches from Jackson Street to Delaware Avenue.
Hurlock Town Manager John Avery said the trail is a "relatively flat," six-foot-wide, paved asphalt trail with eight solar streetlights, three steel benches and trashcans placed along it.
Since its opening, the path gotten a lot of use. Avery said residents have reacted positively to the new public space.
"Everybody said that it's great they can have a place they can walk that's safe, that's lit at night," he said.
Hurlock Town Council Member Russell Murphy said in an email that the trail has been used "much more than expected."
"Every time I have been on it or ridden by it, there are people using it," he said. "We are so looking forward to completing phase two and phase three."
Murphy said he first introduced the idea for the trail as a way to light up Railroad Avenue and make it safer.
"Once seeing some of the rails-to-trails projects going on, it was brought up again as a way to provide a path from one end of town to another with safety and health also being in the forefront," he said.
Once all three phases of the project are complete, the trail will stretch 1.5 miles from one end of the town to the other, ending at North Main Street Park. To complete the last two phases of the project, Murphy said the county will need to take ownership of the railroad and then the town can ask for the county's permission to proceed with applying for grant funding.
Murphy said the Town Council hopes the trail will draw in visitors.
"We are hoping that anyone passing through will want to walk the trail and see what Hurlock has to offer," he said.
On Aug. 3, the town held a grand opening for the trail. Avery said the event went well, with Hurlock Mayor Rev. Charles T. Cephas and four of the Town Council's five council members in attendance.
Murphy called the grand opening "a monumental event." He said although the turnout was light, he hopes that word will get out and the trail will bring in prospective residents and businesses.
It took about two years for the trail to get built. Avery said the majority of that time was spent securing grant funding from the Maryland Department of Natural Resources, which funded $82,000 of the approximately $105,000 project through the Community Parks and Playgrounds Program.
"The property is owned by Delmarva Power, so there was a joint-use agreement that had to go in place between Delmarva Power, the Department of Natural Resources and the town," Avery said. "And it took quite a while to get that worked out."
Avery said that after the agreement was worked out, the town was able to secure the grant funding for the project.
Murphy said the project could not have come to fruition if not for Avery and Cephas. He said the trail can bring residents closer together.
"When an activity, such as a park or trail, gets people outside, it will bring the community closer together," he said. "Its great to see neighbors and friends out and about so we can communicate and stay in touch with each other."

title: Cambridge Hears Presentations About Youth Services, Day Shelter
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge hears presentations about youth services, day shelter

 November 16, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 602
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - Commissioners heard two presentations at a Cambridge City Council meeting on Monday evening.The first was from a Baltimore-based nonprofit, Lead4Life, about a possible partnership with the city. The second was about the need for a day shelter in Cambridge.Jennifer Gauthier, founder and executive director of Lead4Life, spoke about the services which the nonprofit offers and inquired about partnering with the city."Allow us to hire people who can go into the community," Gauthier said. "Allow us to have that peer-to-peer model to be able to spend some of the resources that we have on these two initiatives in your community." Founded in 2008, Lead-4Life aims to lower the number of youth entering the juvenile justice system.According to its website, the nonprofit offers 10 different programs, including alternative placement programming, mentoring and individual and family therapy.At the Council meeting, Gauthier talked about two pilot programs, a gun diversion program and a returning citizens program, which it wants to offer in Cambridge.Gauthier said Lead4Life has the funding to provide these services in Cambridge and "all the way down to the Lower Shore." "We just want to hear any concerns that you have or any opportunity for us that you want to be able to partner (with us)," she said."We're not asking you for money." After Gauthier spoke, Commissioner Sputty Cephas said that he thinks it would be great to partner with Lead4Life and try to expand the program in Cambridge."From everything that I've heard so far, we need you here," he said. "Any way that we can continue to funnel this information and get the word out there about all that you guys are doing, I would love to." Valerie Nwakudo Davis, with Delmarva Community Services, spoke to the Council next about the need for a day shelter in Cambridge."This presentation is not for any agency," she said."It really is on behalf of our homeless population in this city, in this county." Davis said that there is a growing population of homeless people and talked about the importance of having a shelter for people to go to, particularly the aging homeless population."We cannot afford, as a community, to have people sitting on benches when it's 22 degrees outside, or when it's 92 degrees outside," she said.Davis said that although The Salvation Army provides shelter at night, those people in need of service don't have somewhere to go in the day. She said this problem is most apparent on the weekends."Sunday is the most miserable time of the week when you're homeless," she said, adding that places like the library and One Mission Cambridge are closed then.Delmarva Community Services hosted a meeting last week, Davis said. The Overflow Cafe, One Mission Cambridge and The Salvation Army were at the meeting."We talked about what was here already and what we need," she said.To get a day shelter in Cambridge, Davis said support from the local government is needed. She also said support from churches is needed."Because that could be an awesome volunteer segment of this," she said.After Davis spoke, Mayor Stephen Rideout said he had spoken with Davis about this a few weeks ago."I thought it was very important," he said. "It was something that we have not really paid attention to enough. So we're having an ongoing series of meetings with the churches and citizens and agencies to see what we might be able to do here to address this particular issue."

title: 'It felt like we were abandoned' - Management working to address problems at Altair Apartments as residents seek housing elsewhere
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
'It felt like we were abandoned' - Management working to address problems at Altair Apartments as residents seek housing elsewhere

 November 9, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 1489
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - In August, everything came to a head at Altair Apartments.Trash piled high outside the apartments on Greenwood Avenue for an entire week. Broken water heaters and air conditioners couldn't be fixed. Even the internet stopped working.Resident Rodaisia Brummell said she felt disgusted."It felt like we were abandoned," Brummell said. "Like they didn't really care about us." The reason for these conditions: its new California-based management company, FPI Management, hadn't been paying all of the bills since taking over the property in April.Property Manager Judkya Murray said that overtime, vendors stopped showing up, causing trash to build up and plumbing to remain broken.She said the problem was all caused by one person at FPI Management, who has since been let go. That one person wasn't paying the bills to keep everything at Altair running. FPI Management could not be reached for comment."I was literally sitting here pulling my hair out because we had no internet," Murray said. "We had no phones. I couldn't call anybody.I couldn't email anybody." At the time, Murray was the assistant property manager acting as the property manager. The previous property manager had left for another opportunity, Murray said.The week the garbage trucks didn't show, Murray remembers the garbage being so plentiful that the building's maintenance worker had to take garbage cans from inside the building to fill with the overflowing trash outside."We were trying to do everything we could possibly do to keep the trash contained somewhere," she said. "It was just too much trash." The building's staff was quitting left and right."Nobody really wanted to leave but it's like, the conditions - you have no choice but to leave," Murray said.Even Murray quit.However, in about three weeks, she was back."The senior director of FPI (Management), she actually reached out to me one day," Murray said. "She was like, 'Can you please come have lunch with me.'" At the lunch, Murray explained why she quit and said the senior director told her they were already working to let go of and replace the the person within the company that hadn't been paying the bills for months.With that conversation, Murray agreed to come back in early October, this time as the official property manager.Having a boss who pays the bills has made Murray's job easier since coming back, she said. But she still has a significant list of to-dos and goals, especially because so many people quit a few months ago.In mid-October, Murray said she has hired a new assistant and interviewed a potential new maintenance worker."And if we hire him, we'll just need one other maintenance guy and we'll be fully staffed," she said. "Once we're fully staffed, everything flows perfectly." Murray also has some big picture goals in the works to increase occupancy and create new community programming.She is working to increase the property's occupancy rate by filling the vacant apartments. Of Altair's 144 total units, Murray said 20 are vacant. She hopes to bring the occupancy rate from 86% to 94% by the end of the year.While the waitlist of applicants is "a mile long," Murray said maintenance has to get the apartments fixed up and ready before new residents can move in.PROBLEMS PROMPT RESIDENTS TO LOOK ELSEWHEREWhile Murray is taking applications to fill apartment vacancies, Millie Lewis and her husband Willie are filling out applications for other apartments in Cambridge. After more than 40 years of living in the Altair Apartments, the Lewises are tired of dealing with the problems.Recently, they dealt with the outcome of a recent water leak, which affected their kitchen, living room and bathroom. In all three rooms, water spilled out from the ceiling. In the kitchen and bathroom, water filled in the ceiling lights.The edges of the carpeting against one wall in the living room has turned from beige to rusted brown.For years, even before the leak, the carpeting in Lewis' bedroom has been coming undone from the floor.Lewis covers these spaces - where pockets of air separate the carpeting and the floor - with small area rugs. She said Altair won't fix this issue, even though she has complained about it.Although the ceilings were patched up by maintenance following the leak, it took weeks and a citation from the city for the mold, which grew from one of those patched up spots in the bathroom, to be removed.Lewis has COPD and asthma, which made her even more concerned about being in a home where there is mold in the bathroom that she and her husband use everyday."I pay my rent every month," she said. "Before I'm supposed to pay it.Why can't the head people do their job? Why can't they pay? Why can't they take care of what's got to be taken care of at these apartments hereft" Lewis isn't the only resident looking to live elsewhere.Tieonna Wisher, who has lived at Altair for three years, said she has already filled out an application for another apartment.She has concerns about how long it takes for management to respond to problems.Wisher has a hole in her wall that she said management hasn't done anything about for months."They keep saying they're going to come in here," she said.Wisher remembers one day when she unplugged a cord from a socket in her home and it sparked and caused half of the lights to go out in her apartment."They told me to call the emergency number," she said. "Call it and nobody answers. Go to the office.Like, nobody wants to do nothing." Brummell, who has lived at Altair for over a year, said she has also started submitting housing applications.In the time that she's lived here, Brummell has experienced a months-long leak in her bathroom and a leaking dishwasher. She said that when her dishwasher was leaking, all maintenance did was drop off a shop vac. She has yet to receive a working dishwasher.It took about three months before Brummell could get someone to fix the leak in her bathroom. She said that gnats are still flying around the apartment because of it.A mother of two young kids, Brummell has noticed her children keep getting sick. She fears it is from the building. The one time she saw mold in her home, a previous property manager told her to spray it with bleach."That's all she told me to do," Brummell said.THE CITY's INVOLVEMENTTo get problems solved, Brummell said she has started reaching out to the City of Cambridge. She said this has been effective because code enforcement can fine Altair for property violations."A couple weeks ago (workers hired by management) came in and painted and fixed my stuff that was supposed to be fixed," she said. "Only because I called the City of Cambridge.Because, if I didn't call them, it wouldn't have been that." Cambridge Assistant City Manager Brandon Hesson said a goal of the city is to solve quality of life issues."That's not always going to be possible from the outside of homes," he said."We need to get people to the point where (residents) trust us and they are contacting us and they're aware of their tenants rights and they're ability to call us about issues they're having with their rental homes and their apartments." Hesson said they have been able to do this at Altair and are "still very present." Since August, Hesson said communication with upper management has been satisfactory. He said they shared an action plan with multiple items they plan to address. As of Nov. 3, Hesson said he was still waiting to see if they are following that plan.Hesson clarified that communication with Altair's on-site management "has always been pretty good." Murray said she is making sure that she stays in communication with the city."I know their biggest thing is nobody was communicating anything back to them," she said about the city. "They just need to know if somebody's on top of (a problem)." With all of the issues at Altair, Brummell said residents are paying rent and not getting the services they should be getting as tenants."Everything's being prolonged," she said. "But ya'll want things from us. You want rent money from us.You want us to go in the house at a certain time. But we're not getting the things that we properly need." 
 
 Caption: TOM MCCALL/STAR DEMOCRAT
 
Judkya Murray, Altair Apartments property manager, was so frustrated with surmounting issues that she quit. Now she is back and trying to get the tenants resources.
 
TOM MCCALL/STAR DEMOCRAT

title: Ophelia a Bust but Still Causes Flooding
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Ophelia a bust but still causes flooding

 September 28, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 480
 Words 

 Read News Document

 HOOPERS ISLAND - Tropical Storm Ophelia caused flooding in parts of Dorchester County this past weekend."Luckily we didn't make out too badly with the storm," Dorchester County Emergency Management Planner Jimmy Windsor said.According to the National Hurricane Center, the storm made landfall near Emerald Isle in North Carolina Saturday.On Sunday, the center warned of continued coastal flooding "along portions of the Chesapeake Bay and its tidal rivers" for the rest of the day.Cambridge received 2.61 inches of rain between Friday, Sept. 22, and Sunday, Sept.24, according to the National Weather Service.The storm resulted in "moderate to borderline-major tidal flooding" in the county, particularly in its southern and far western areas, Windsor said. He added the areas most affected were the Hoopers Island area, Taylor's Island and the Wingate, Toddville and Bishops Head areas.Dorchester County Council member Rob Kramer monitored how the storm affected the county over the weekend.He said the road past the Hoopers Island Causeway "took a little bit of a beating." While the causeway had been closed Saturday, it has since been reopened.Windsor said Water Street in Cambridge also shut down temporarily due to the storm.Over the weekend, the Sheriff's Office was trying to limit traffic through Worlds End Turn as well, he said.The county's Department of Emergency Services had few, if any, flood-related calls over the weekend, Windsor said."I know the [Hoopers Island Volunteer Fire Company] assisted some people with getting back to their residences from places they were at on the island after it had started to flood," he said.As part of the county's contingency plan, the National Guard was brought into the county. Kramer said the county received the guards once Gov.Wes Moore declared a state of emergency in response to Tropical Storm Ophelia on Friday."They had brought a couple Humvees with them," Kramer said. "They were just a contingent plan in case we needed them." Windsor said while the county didn't end up needing assistance from the National Guard, it did some pre-deployment area reconnaissance "just to make sure they knew where they were going if they had to go anywhere." As of Wednesday, Windsor said most of the flood water has receded."There is still some high water areas in the lower part of the county, which is not being helped by the fact that we currently have a higher than usual tide cycle," he said. "But everything is back open." Windsor asked that the public use caution when traveling in those lower parts of the county in case the water has made it difficult to navigate the roads."In the grand scheme of things, this was minor compared to some of the storms we've had in the past," Kramer said.

title: Cambridge Commissioners Remove Solar Cap
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Cambridge commissioners remove solar cap

 July 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 483
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Cambridge City Commissioners adopted an ordinance at last week evening's meeting to amend the city's unified development code to exempt medium, large and community solar energy projects from the town's current 350-acre cap.The move essentially removes the cap, which was implemented in 2014, paving the way for a community solar project from Pivot Energy, a Denver-based renewable energy provider and independent power producer. Commissioners unanimously voted in favor of the ordinance to remove the cap.
The plan for community solar was first introduced to commissioners in December, 2024, when Pivot Energy's lawyer Anthony Kupersmith said getting rid of the cap would be critical to the project's success.
Cambridge City Planner Brian Hermann presented Pivot Energy's community solar proposal to commissioners again last week. "The community solar projects are designed to provide opportunities for residents of the community who don't own their house, or are living in the woods and have shade, or don't want to look at solar panels," Hermann said.
Community solar is a way for multiple individuals to share in the benefits of a single solar installation, according to the U.S. Department of Energy. "The term refers to the pooling of resources to develop a community-scale solar energy project that provides the benefits of solar energy to a group or neighborhood," the USDE website states.
After around an hour of questions from commissioners, Mayor Lajan Cephas thanked the gentlemen from Pivot Energy and attempted to move on to the next agenda item, but Commissioner Roche had one more question he 'demanded' be answered before voting on the ordinance.
"So at the end of the day, how do we know, and how does the state know that this power is actually for its intended purpose, which is to lower the utility rates of, in many cases, income constrained individuals, or the community, where it's located?" Roche asked.
Kupersmith told Roche this word isn't neutral and lends authority to regulatory oversight from the Public Service Commission through an application, bonding, subscriber certification and annual reporting to ensure benefits, especially for low- and moderate-income customers.
Hermann and Pivot Energy representatives were uncertain of how many acres they will need for the new community solar project, but it will exceed the current cap. Kupersmith and Pivot Energy Development Project Manager John Shields made it clear that if the city does not remove the cap, Pivot Energy is willing to go to the state, which can supersede the city's code.
Commissioners asked if there were decommissioning protocols for the end of the project's life or in case of damage. The decommissioning plan and bond would follow the city's existing zoning rules and Public Service Commission standards.
When it comes to what exactly the community solar project will look like, Pivot Energy is keeping its options open.
Shields said at the current moment, there is not a drawn-up project plan. "We'd rather kind of look at it more holistically if we can," Shields said.

title: Eastern Shore Legislators Push for Gov. Moore to Veto Solar Bill
author: Konner Metz
content:
Eastern Shore legislators push for Gov. Moore to veto solar bill

 May 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 626
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Eastern Shore legislators, House Republicans and agricultural advocacy groups in Maryland are making one last effort to nix controversial solar energy legislation by asking for a veto from Gov. Wes Moore.Senate Bill 931, the Renewable Energy Certainty Act, was passed by the General Assembly in April. It aims to increase the state's solar generation by streamlining the regulatory process for solar projects. Fencing, setback and vegetation requirements would be standardized.
House Republicans and the Eastern Shore Delegation both wrote letters to the governor urging him to veto the bill. While Moore (D) hasn't publicly signaled whether or not he's considering a veto, some believe it could be in play given he hasn't yet signed the legislation.
"I've heard it is possible," said Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) in an interview Wednesday. "I'm hopeful that he would see the opportunity and the wisdom and just say, 'No, not yet.'"
Qualms with the solar legislation largely relate to a reduction in the control local governments would have over solar project approvals, and the increase in Public Service Commission authority.
The legislation outlines a cap on how much land the Maryland Public Service Commission can grant to solar projects in each county — 5% of land designated for agriculture and forests.
Republicans attempted but failed during session to lower that cap.
Del. Chris Adams (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) said Thursday that Eastern Shore counties could have thousands of acres up for solar development even with the 5% cap.
At a legislative wrap-up discussion in Easton Wednesday, Mautz said solar interests came into Annapolis and "cleared the decks."
"They wanted to set up their own regulatory system, they wanted to set up their own siting system," he said. "And they wanted to run this through the Public Service Commission."
"It puts an X on the Eastern Shore," Mautz added. "We are the prime target for solar investment."
The Chesapeake Climate Action Network, an environmental nonprofit that's one of the bill's many advocate groups, encouraged supporters to contact Moore's office and lobby for no veto. Brittany Baker, the organization's Maryland director, said rumors of a veto were floating.
"The rumor mill was churning, and no one had a concrete answer here or there," Baker said.
Baker said in addition to streamlining processes that otherwise vary greatly across the state, the bill is set to codify best practices. And it could help local farmers who are looking to remain economically viable, she said.
"It provides another way for people to be able to stay on their farms and make revenue," Baker said.
PUSH TO VETO
The governor's office didn't comment specifically on whether Moore is considering a veto, but did provide a statement.
"As Governor Moore reviews the hundreds of bills put forward this session, he will continue to work with the State Legislature, local leaders, and all partners involved to ensure that we are signing legislation that will make Maryland safer, more affordable, more competitive, and the state that serves," the statement read.
Baker said despite rumors, the Chesapeake Climate Action Network believes Senate Bill 931 will become law.
"We're pretty sure at this point that the governor will not be vetoing this bill," she said.
Mautz acknowledged a veto is a tricky, party-line situation. He said it would be messy, but "less messy" than what happens down the line if the bill becomes law.
"For the governor to veto it, he's going to cross his own party," Mautz said. "He's going to cross some of his own advocates. It's going to be extremely controversial."
Adams acknowledged that vetoes are rare. But he said the bill not yet being signed may signal "at the minimum, that the governor's paying attention."
If Moore doesn't sign the Renewable Energy Certainty Act by May 27, it automatically becomes law. The governor's next slate of bill signings is scheduled for May 20.

title: ESLC Talks Land Values at Dorchester County Council Meeting
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
ESLC talks land values at Dorchester County Council meeting

 February 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 608
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — When it comes to acreage and land value, Dorchester County is expected to be one of the most affected counties by sea level rise and storm surge in the year 2100, according to the Eastern Shore Land Conservancy.During a Dorchester County Council meeting Feb. 18, Eastern Shore Land Conservancy Land Use and Policy Director Owen Bailey presented data on land value throughout the Eastern Shore. Bailey said the data was acquired with the help of Urban3.
The land trust estimates that an average of three feet of sea level rise in 2100 would mean the loss of 270,000 acres of the Eastern Shore and $2 billion in property tax values.
"And then when you add in storm surge, then that really puts into perspective the financial distress that our communities are going to face in the future with the loss of properties and property tax revenues," Bailey said.
After Bailey showed a map that accounted for storm surge in 2100, County Council President Lenny Pfeffer pointed out that more than half of Dorchester County's land is projected to be gone.
Bailey said Cambridge alone is projected to lose 280 acres and $63 million in value by 2100.
Throughout his presentation, Bailey advocated for concentrated development on the Shore to increase property value. At the same time, he spoke about the importance of maintaining the value that could be loss to sea level rise.
Bailey said the efficiency of land use can be measured by looking at value per acre.
"You take the appraised value of each parcel and you divide it by how many acres it sits on," he said.
When the Eastern Shore Land Conservancy applied this to the Eastern Shore, it noticed historic downtowns are "much more productive than the more suburban, car-focused development" that has been popular since the 1950s. This means that those downtowns, which often are more vulnerable to sea level rise, bring in more property tax revenue per acre than more sprawling areas of the Eastern Shore.
Bailey said that before the Bay Bridge was built in 1952, only 10,000 acres of land — valued at approximately $560,000 per acre — had been developed on the Shore. An additional 163,000 has been developed at less than half of that value since.
With the additional developed land, there has been a need for more sprawling infrastructure, he said.
"So we've built all this infrastructure," Bailey said. "But we haven't really built the value to help us with the maintenance of that infrastructure, which is why a lot of our jurisdictions, pretty much all of our jurisdictions, are struggling with how to keep up with that kind of maintenance."
Bailey said many historic communities on the Shore, which bring more value per acre, are built on waterfronts, meaning sea level rise will most likely affect them.
"So we're encouraging every town to think about how are you going to account for that," he said. "How can you either move that property, protect it or replace that value somewhere else in our community?"
Along with concentrating development, Bailey recommended the county look at zoning restricting the county from allowing value to grow.
"This is something we're encouraging every jurisdiction to take a look at," he said. "It's not our job to tell you what to do. We just want to provide the data and perspective. ... Use your land wisely."
At the end of the presentation Dorchester County Council Vice President Mike Detmer asked if the land trust had any recommendations specific to Dorchester County zoning ordinances.
Bailey said they have been focusing on municipalities, looking at zoning in historic districts.
"And how can we ease up on that zoning just to allow that historic pattern to continue," he said.

title: Southern Dorchester County Residents Push for a Seat at the Table
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Southern Dorchester County residents push for a seat at the table

 January 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 1121
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TODDVILLE — Around a big wooden table in the back corner of Elijah's General Store in Toddville Wednesday, three generations of south Dorchester County residents outlined a plan to save their home.Dick Dawson, a lifelong resident of Bishops Head, has watched over the years as areas in the southern part of Dorchester County turn from woods to swamp. He's seen land where cattle used to graze become water holes and mud holes that would take a boat to get through.
"The ground is sinking, there's no doubt about that," he said.
Sea level rise has become a significant issue in Dorchester County over the years, particularly in the southern part of the county. Dorchester County Council Vice President Mike Detmer said the area has faced environmental challenges "as the relationship between the land and the water changes."
"There's massive erosion, there is saltwater intrusion and just a variety of other really relentless environmental challenges," he said.
In an effort to protect these communities in southern Dorchester from disappearing, three men are working to incorporate Blackwater, a new town, giving the communities that call this area home a seat at the table and a chance for survival.
The communities included in the plan for Blackwater are Andrews, Robbins, Wesley, Lakesville, Crapo, Wingate, Toddville, Bishops Head and Crocheron.
Each community would still exist within the new town, the planners said. But incorporating would give the communities a voice, said Drew Dawson, Dick Dawson's 17-year-old grandson.
"Because on our own, the communities aren't large enough to incorporate," he said.
David Beverley, who owns Elijah's General Store, said that by incorporating, the communities would have a better chance of receiving funding from government agencies.
"As you can tell when you're driving down here, it's beautiful landscape," he said. "But unfortunately, regulations and all kinds of things have made it really hard to fix properties here."
Beverley, who owns Elijah's General Store, sees a direct correlation between critical area regulations and deteriorating roads and houses in the area. According to the Maryland Department of Natural Resources, the state's critical areas include land within 1,000 feet of tidal waters, wetlands, and the Bay and its tributaries.
"If you buy a property down here, if you put so much money into it based on the tax assessed value, you have to raise it," Beverley said. "And the people don't have the money to raise it. ... Why are we even going to raise it if you aren't going to put the money into the roads because of the population decrease? And would you consider a priority road fix? So it's a whole circle of problems."
Beverley and the Dawsons — who make up the organizing committee to create the town — see incorporation as the path to being able to apply for state and federal grants so residents can do things like raise their homes.
Dick Dawson said the area is in need of a good road that doesn't flood "just because the tide comes up" and drainage so that when the tide does come up, it can go back down.
The effort to incorporate isn't "a move against the county," Drew Dawson said.
"We understand that the population is very low and a lot of times it doesn't make sense for them to do everything that really needs to get done," he said. "The idea is just to do what the county can't, not necessarily drill the county for what they're not doing."
PULLING UP A CHAIR A drafted charter for the proposed Town of Blackwater sat in the center of the table where the trio sat Wednesday.
Under the charter, the town would be able to elect five members to a council for a term of four years. The commissioner with the most votes would be named mayor, and the commissioner with the second-most votes would be named deputy mayor. The town would not impose new taxes.
"The idea is to give more power to the people of the area, not add an unnecessary level of government," Drew Dawson said.
It took a couple weeks for Drew Dawson — who is a dual enrollment high school student at Chesapeake College — to write the charter. His initiative in creating it is something his grandfather is proud of him for.
"Drew has written the majority of this," Dick Dawson said.
Drew said he used other charters, mainly Eldorado's, to create Blackwater's charter. "But a lot of it was also written myself," he said. "It's nearly double the size of the charter of Eldorado."
Once they can get enough signatures on their petition, the three plan to go to the county to submit the charter for review. If the county accepts the charter, the decision will go to the registered voters within the area that Blackwater would encompass.
If those residents vote in favor of creating the town, Blackwater will become Dorchester County's newest incorporated town.
As the group moves forward with the process to become a town, other residents are getting involved. Drew Dawson said "public sentiment is positive" among residents they've spoken to so far. Dick Dawson said they plan to host a public meeting to explain the idea and what incorporating a town could do for residents.
"We're interested in their comments as well," Beverley said.
Drew Dawson said the length of time it could take for Blackwater to become a town is "hard to tell" because of all of the smaller steps necessary in the process.
"The hope is to get it done by the end of this year," he said.
Detmer said that although he doesn't know how his fellow councilmen feel about the idea to create Blackwater, the chance for residents to make a decision at the ballot box has his "full personal support."
"The best thing about their initiative, to me, is not just that it's looking to the future and the picture of how business is done with local, state and federal government, but the real advantage of their initiative is they are actually going to give the residents of the area a chance for their voice to be heard about whether or not they want to do it," he said.
If Blackwater becomes a town, both Dick and Drew Dawson are interested in serving as commissioners.
"I am one of the older people that is down here," Dick Dawson said. "And I have seen a lot of changes. And not many of them have been for the good. I'd like to be here to help get this thing started."
Drew Dawson said he encourages everyone to read the drafted charter to understand what incorporating would mean for the area.
"If we continue to do nothing, the land and the roads will continue to sink, and the land will erode away," he said. "We'll lose more and more residents and they'll just keep creating regulations until it becomes nearly impossible to live here."

title: New Cambridge Solar Ordinance Will Have 'Immediate Effect'
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
New Cambridge solar ordinance will have 'immediate effect'

 December 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 561
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Along with passing an ordinance regarding solar energy systems on wooded lots, the Cambridge City Council has directed city staff to look into removing community solar from a 350-acre maximum on solar permitted in the city.During a City Council meeting on Dec. 9, the council unanimously approved an ordinance amending the city's Unified Development Code for solar energy systems on wooded lots. Specifically, the amendment allows small-scale solar and community solar on wooded lots as long as the solar project complies with the city's Forest Conservation Ordinance or the state's Model Forest Conservation Ordinance.
Before the ordinance was passed, Cambridge Planning and Zoning Director Brian Herrmann said it was consistent with the city's comprehensive plan and the Planning and Zoning Commission had approved it in early November.
Herrmann said the ordinance would apply to sites that are at least 40,000 square feet. He said requirements of the ordinance include that the area cleared on the wooded lot cannot exceed 10 acres and impacted trees must be replanted at a 2-to-1 ratio or a fee be paid in lieu.
Small-scale solar energy systems are typically located on a homeowner's property, Herrmann said.
"It's essentially generating electricity where it is used," he said.
Community solar energy systems provide power to the residents of a community. Herrmann said that in Maryland, 40% of the output of a community solar system must serve low- to moderate-income residents.
During the meeting, Tony Kupersmith, a lawyer representing a renewable energy company, said the company he represents has a community solar project on Leonards Lane and this ordinance is "critical" for that project.
"So I get to let you know that what you do tonight would have an immediate effect for an actual project that is ready to go forward, that wants to go forward, and the only issue right now holding us up is the wooded lot issue," Kupersmith said before requesting the council adopt the ordinance.
Herrmann told the council that the city's 350-acre solar maximum — which it is close to reaching — limits the impact of this ordinance.
"We have two projects in the final stages of the development review process," he said. "If those two are to go through, we're going to be at 325 acres. So there's only about 25 acres left before we actually hit this amount. So I guess you can see we're not talking about a lot of solar systems that are going to be built even if this does pass."
Commissioner Brian Roche asked why community solar is included in that 350-acre maximum that also includes medium- and large-scale solar energy systems. He said it should be excluded.
"We don't want to see our entire land base covered with solar panel projects, but the way I understand community solar is really it is to the benefit of people that cannot either put it on their roof (and) they want to collaborate ... or they otherwise may not be able to have it," he said. "To me, I would strike that out from that maximum."
Roche asked that only medium- and large-scale solar energy systems be included in the 350-acre maximum and not community solar energy systems.
City Attorney Patrick Thomas said that because Roche's request goes "beyond the scope" of the ordinance on the table, it would need to go through a separate text amendment process. He said a separate ordinance to address the maximum could be prepared.

title: Dorchester County Council passes solar legislation, says more may be coming
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Dorchester County Council passes solar legislation, says more may be coming

 November 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 680
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — In a 3-2 vote, the Dorchester County Council passed a bill that addresses setbacks and buffers, ownership, and decommissioning plans for accessory, small scale and utility scale solar energy systems.After the bill was passed at a meeting on Nov. 4, Council President Lenny Pfeffer said this is a start for solar legislation in the county.
"Laws can be amended and modified," he said. "But if we don't do something now, before the start of the General Assembly, we could be facing much worse without any safeguards in place."
Council members Rob Kramer and William Nichols voted against the bill. Council member Ricky Travers, Council Vice President Mike Detmer and Pfeffer voted in favor of it.
Under the new bill, solar developments located off scenic byways will need to be set back 100 feet from all property lines, and developments that are not located off of scenic byways will need to be set back 75 feet. Requirements regarding vegetative buffers, perimeter fencing, topsoil and site plans are also in the legislation.
The bill defines who the owners of a solar site are. Pfeffer said in an interview with the Star Democrat in September that the owners of the property and the operator of the solar development would both be considered the owner.
The bill was reintroduced in September after getting tabled in March. In the reintroduced bill, a section was added regarding decommissioning solar projects. Per the legislation, a decommissioning plan will need to be submitted and approved by the county prior to the building permit application.
In the September interview, Pfeffer said the bill was tabled so the council could wait for state solar legislation to go into affect and make sure the county was in line with it.
At the meeting Nov. 4, residents thanked the council for their efforts and shared concerns that the county bill doesn't do enough to restrict solar development.
The reintroduced bill left out a section in the original proposed bill that put a cap on how many aggregate acres of the county can house utility-scale solar energy systems.
Beth Hill said although she feels the bill is a step in the right direction, she thinks there needs to be a cap on the number of acres in the county that can be used for solar development.
"Other counties around us do have caps," she said, mentioning Caroline County, which has a 2,000-acre cap on total rural land available for solar development.
Tracy Whitby-Fairall, who attended a town hall on the subject that Detmer hosted the previous week, said she recognized the county's efforts. She called the bill a "good foundation for a strong framework" for the county.
"I think there are some things that could be improved," she said, later adding, "I hope this isn't the end of the legislation. I hope this is the beginning."
Erick Windsor, who asked the council to vote against the bill, talked about the county's history of thriving tomato, dairy and lumber industries, which are now gone. He said that large solar operations take land away from grain farming.
"And this is going to affect all the other industries in this county that work around grain farming, like chicken farming," he said. "So you hurt the chicken farmers and you're going to hurt the industry in Hurlock that processes all this stuff."
Windsor said more restrictions need to be put on solar so it doesn't "decimate" the north part of the county.
Detmer said the bill — especially the decommissioning component — is "crucial" to have at the county level before the Maryland General Assembly session begins in January. He talked about the possibility of additional legislation coming down from the state.
"The Wild West of solar that we are in right now, I'm very bothered by it," he said. "I think we have to plant our flag here in this place that we're ready to go right now. If we don't act tonight, the law's not going to be in place when the session starts."
Detmer said this isn't the end of creating legislation around solar, but action needs to be taken now.
"We've got to put the seatbelt on," he said.

title: Solar Energy Discussed at MACo Summer Conference
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Solar energy discussed at MACo Summer Conference

 August 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 543
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OCEAN CITY — Solar energy was one topic of discussion that captured the attention of multiple Mid-Shore counties at the Maryland Association of Counties Summer Conference.Caroline County Commission President Travis Breeding said solar energy came up a lot at the four-day conference, which went from Aug. 14 to Aug. 17 in Ocean City. Breeding said there are elected officials from different Maryland counties who feel that solar lobbyists are pushing the state to take away local authority when it comes to where solar energy system sites can go and how close those sites can be from roads and neighboring structures.
Caroline County currently has a 2,000-acre cap on solar projects. Once that limit is reached, the county will stop permitting new solar energy system projects on county land, Breeding said.
Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said his fellow council member Ricky Travers asked about solar site acreage caps in a MACo session with the Maryland Public Service Commission. Specifically, Travers asked about how the commission feels about these caps.
Pfeffer said that after the session, the Dorchester County Council members had a conversation with Public Service Commissioner Kumar Barve, and the council was able to explain its concerns about increasing solar sites in the county. Pfeffer said the only part of the county that can host these sites is the north part of the county, and that is where the council hopes to grow the county's tax base.
"They were very interested and didn't realize some of the demographics and logistics of Dorchester County," Pfeffer said about the Public Service Commission. "So I'm hoping that is successful for us, they'll take a look at it and they won't establish any legislation that's one-size-fits-all."
Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher called the conference one of the best he's been to. He said it ran smoothly and was well put together.
Breeding said that MACo's summer and winter conferences give Maryland counties an opportunity to get together, discuss and "try to come up with a unified message."
"It was a good conference," Breeding said. "We got to talk to all of our partners in other counties, bounce ideas off of them, discuss problems and issues that we're all facing and kind of brainstorm on how to resolve those issues."
Pfeffer, who is the secretary of MACo this year, said that all counties have problems.
Pfeffer said the opportunity to discuss these common problems, no matter how many zeros come after them, can benefit each county.
Breeding said he is taking some ideas on solar power back home to Caroline County this year. He talked about the systems that Talbot and Queen Anne's counties have in place, including Talbot County's point system that is used to help preserve prime farmland for farming and determine where solar sites can go.
Lesher said he didn't attend the solar session at MACo, but said the Talbot County Council tackled legislation dealing with solar energy sites last year when it put the point system in place.
"Which I think is model legislation for other rural jurisdictions," he said. "Right now we're in the testing period for this. Will this hold up? title: Solar Energy Discussed at Dorchester County Council Meeting
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Solar energy discussed at Dorchester County Council meeting

 February 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 721
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Solar energy systems were discussed more than once at a Dorchester County Council meeting on Feb. 6.During the meeting, the Council introduced legislation that would amend a part of the Dorchester County Code that deals with utility-scale solar energy systems.
Specifically, the legislation would put a cap on how many aggregate acres in the agricultural conservation zoning districts of the county can house utility-scale solar energy systems. The legislation would also make it so that a 75-foot-wide alive and maintained vegetated buffer must surround the solar energy systems.
Council Vice President Mike Detmer said he thinks this legislation is not a move for or against solar, but a move against "bad solar."
"You know, when you go driving in your car, you hope you don't need a seatbelt, but you always put it on," he said. "We need that seatbelt there for (this)."
If this legislation is passed, up to 1,800 acres of land in the agricultural conservation zoning districts of the county could be used for utility-scale solar energy systems. County Planning and Zoning Director Susan Webb said that currently, 1,574 acres are developed or being developed for these systems.
Webb said making sure the vegetated buffer is maintained and alive will be key.
"A 75-foot buffer that's alive, it's going to do its job as compared to a 100 or 200-foot (buffer) that's dead," she said. "So we just have to make sure that we're staying on it. And we will."
Webb said the requirement of a fence around these types of properties and adequate fire suppression devices on site are also in the proposed legislation. She said that any solar energy system that has not operated for a continuous period of 12 months would be considered unused and abandoned.
Council President Lenny Pfeffer asked Webb if this kind of legislation is something surrounding jurisdictions have tried to do.
Webb said it is very typical for jurisdictions to have a cap on aggregate acreage of solar energy systems. She said she understands the state has been looking into banning these caps.
"Right now, there's nothing in place," she said. "We're doing exactly like our neighbors."
PROPERTY TAX EXEMPTION
Also at the Feb. 6 meeting, Pfeffer brought up a bill that has been introduced in the Maryland Senate and Maryland House of Delegates.
The legislation, Senate Bill 783 and House Bill 1435, would make it so that nonresidential solar energy systems constructed on rooftops or parking facility canopies don't have to pay property taxes.
Personal property taxes would also be exempt for community solar energy systems that provide at least half of its energy to low or moderate-income customers at a lower cost than electric companies in the area, and are installed on a rooftop, brownfield, parking facility canopy, landfill or clean fill.
The legislation would also make it so that counties would receive $2,500 per megawatt when entering into an agreement with a solar facility owner to exempt real or personal property taxes for ground-mounted solar energy systems. This means that counties would no longer be able to negotiate individual payment in lieu of taxes, or pilot, agreements with solar developers.
Detmer said he disagrees with this legislation because he thinks the county should be able to negotiate pilot agreements.
"This is them taking away some of the scant leverage that we have," he said.
Pfeffer brought up that the negotiations the county has had with solar developers have, in some ways, set a standard.
"The pilots that we've done so far, we've set a standard, basically, on the amount of money on the megawatt-age," he said. "That's what everyone coming to us generally expects that we'll negotiate. ... So haven't we almost already set a price by doing that?"
County Attorney Chip MacLeod said he thinks every pilot agreement the county negotiates can be different.
MacLeod said he thinks this proposed legislation would result in less local control.
"I've personally been involved in many pilot agreements in various counties," he said. "And it is really one of the few (opportunities) that you get to sit face to face with these solar developers and say, 'This is what's important in my county.'"
Detmer said this isn't about banning solar.
"It's just we're trying to have some modicum of control over bad solar," he said.
Detmer said this makes the county's proposed solar legislation even more relevant.
"It just raises the stakes of us doing it now and doing it right," he said.

title: CWDI Gives Project Updates and Addresses Concerns
author: Lily Tierney
content:
CWDI gives project updates and addresses concerns

 August 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester
