 CAMBRIDGE — Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. gave an update on the Cambridge Harbor project at a July 31 community update meeting, outlining a vision built around four zones: Town Center, Walkable Neighborhoods, Maritime Trade, and Community Recreation.CWDI Board President Angie Hengst also addressed community concerns that have caught traction on social media regarding a potential YMCA, a board position and planning committee meetings.
Hengst said CWDI's operations are all "100% above board."
CWDI's Cambridge Harbor project aims to develop Cambridge's waterfront, similar to the Inner Harbor in Baltimore.
The first major step in the waterfront project will be a boutique hotel, which CWDI hopes will open by early 2029, Hengst said. Plans also call for new commercial and residential spaces, townhomes on Byrn Street, and a 1,000-foot fishing pier to replace the condemned Bill Burton pier.
"The biggest thing is that we showed some of the renderings and really zoomed in on those four zones so people could get a better idea of what our actual concept design is, kind of our vision for the site," Hengst said of the July 31 meeting.
These renderings are a guide to understand CWDI's vision, but they are subject to change depending on the developers{span}, she said{/span}.
At the meeting, {span}CWDI members{/span} also addressed community concerns regarding a potential YMCA on the waterfront. CWDI emphasized that no YMCA is planned, though the organization could submit a proposal in 2026.
Hengst said she believes the YMCA rumor got started because an old concept design that had a space for a potential YMCA was shown by mistake at a recent Cambridge Association of Neighborhoods meeting.
During an interview, Hengst addressed other concerns regarding CWDI Treasurer Frank Narr's appointment to the CWDI board. Hengst said Narr's seat on the board was formerly a CWDI-appointed position.
Last year, the policy was changed to have three positions appointed by the Cambridge City Council and three by the Dorchester County Council. CWDI appointed Narr before the policy change, so some people think he should have to be reappointed by the county council.
"I do want to note that when CWDI as an organization made Frank's appointment, it did have to be approved by both the city and the county, so they did approve of that appointment at the time, as with CWDI," Hengst said. "They didn't directly appoint him, but they did approve of the appointment at the time."
Hengst said CWDI has a signed letter from the county council acknowledging Narr as one of their three appointees.
The final concern Hengst addressed were CWDI's Planning Committee meetings, which she said are not open to the public.
Previously, CWDI was in hot water for not allowing the public meetings where they held discussions with elected officials. But Hengst said these specific meetings are for the Planning Committee to work with city officials to compile information that will then be publicly presented at a community update meeting.
"It's our planning committee working directly with the city as they work through the regulating planning and zoning guidelines," Hengst said.
To see the updated renderings of the Cambridge Harbor Project, visit CWDI's website.

title: The Big Pour: Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. Promenade Makes Progress
author: Lily Tierney
content:
The big pour: Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. promenade makes progress

 May 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: News 
 
 429
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Last week, Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. did its first "big pour," according to Treasurer Frank Narr.The concrete base for CWDI's promenade was poured May 10, a visible sign for the community that progress is underway. The project aims to develop the waterfront similarly to Baltimore's Inner Harbor.
Progress has been slower than many hoped as CWDI has faced significant headwinds.
Tensions between the developer and the City of Cambridge came to a head when the city filed a lawsuit in May of 2024 over a transfer agreement. The lawsuit was dismissed without prejudice a few months later, and the city and CWDI entered a memorandum of understanding to address issues that were not included in the lawsuit settlement.
"And, you know, honestly, that has actually kind of been a blessing in disguise," said CWDI Board President Angie Hengst about the lawsuit. "It has allowed us to open up those doors of communication with the county and city even more," Hengst said.
The city and county managers now sit on the board of CWDI, which has helped bridge divides between the development project with the community. "It is really great to have their constant input," Hengst said.
Narr has been with the project for over 30 years and cares deeply about making sure it is done right. For Narr, it isn't about finding partners who can simply fund the project, but finding partners who care about the mission.
That mission aims to foster community engagement, economic growth and further development projects in Cambridge. "It really needs to be a place where everyone in our community feels there's a place for them," Narr said. "And so continuous access to the waterfront, public open space, no gates, no walls, nothing that would say you're not welcome."
Narr acknowledges that the negative backlash CWDI has received from the public has been tough, but he chooses to focus on what is in his control. "There's times when people question, 'Why are you still doing this? You must be getting a benefit from this,' and I'm thinking, 'No it's my commitment to my community to make sure we get what we deserve and we get what will make us all proud,'" Narr said.
Now that they've overcome the litigation hurdle, the main challenge CWDI faces, like many nonprofit organizations at the moment, is funding. "I think that's really our biggest challenge right now," Hengst said.
The promenade is slated to be finished by the end of summer and CWDI is holding a meeting on May 20 to deliver updates to the County and City Council and is open to the public.

title: Cambridge to Receive More Than $1 Million from State for Revitalization
author: Staff Report
content:
Cambridge to receive more than $1 million from state for revitalization

 January 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Local News 
 
 531
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The City of Cambridge has been awarded $1.15 million from the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development for four of the city's revitalization projects.Projects receiving grant monies include the Mace's Lane Community Center, the 444-448 Race Street development project, the old City Hall renovation and Cambridge's façade improvement program, according to a news release from the city.
Cambridge City Manager Glenn Steckman said in an interview with The Star Democrat on Friday that the grants were awarded about a month ago.
"I think this shows that city staff is working very hard to create a good first impression for people visiting our community," he said. "And that they see Cambridge as a happening place and not a sleepy backwater."
The Mace's Lane Community Center has been awarded $500,000 to complete construction and renovation at the former Cambridge high school. Founded by The Good Shepherd Association and the Mace's Lane High School Alumni Association, the community center will offer a variety of programs — including sports, arts and education programs — to support Cambridge's youth.
In November, about $8 million had been raised for the community center and $4.5 million was still needed. The $500,000 in grant money is from the Strategic Demolition Fund, which is a state program that aims to activate local economic development and create jobs.
In order to complete the third phase of the 444-448 Race Street development project, the state has awarded the city $500,000 from the Community Legacy program. The third phase of the Race Street project includes creating three retail spaces and nine apartments.
Community Legacy grants are awarded to projects in Maryland's "sustainable communities," a designation that Cambridge received in December 2023.
A total of $100,000 from the Community Legacy program was awarded to the "Old City Hall" renovation project on Gay Street. The grant money is for the creation of a community room in the building. Renovating and preserving the old city hall is a priority for the city.
The city was also awarded $50,000 to go toward improving the city's commercial building façades. The grant is through the Maryland Façade Improvement Program. Steckman said he expects this grant to benefit the city's downtown area.
"The City is grateful for these generous awards from the State of Maryland, which demonstrate its ongoing support of Cambridge's work to improve its buildings and economy for the betterment of the lives of all our residents," Steckman said in a news release. "We look forward to the continued improvements these projects will bring to the City of Cambridge over the next year."
Along with the city's awards, the Packing House received two awards totaling $550,000 from Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development programs, according to the city. The grants, from the Community Legacy program and the Strategic Demolition Fund, will be used to furnish the building's shared commercial kitchen and to complete the building's interior and exterior event space.
Margaret Norfleet-Neff, the development manager overseeing the Packing House renovation, said the Packing House appreciates the support from the state.
"The Packing House is most appreciative of the ongoing support from DHCD and looks forward to unveiling the completed interior and exterior spaces for the benefit of the community and public use," she said.

title: Cambridge City Council Hears Plans for Harriet Tubman Mural Area
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Cambridge City Council hears plans for Harriet Tubman mural area

 January 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 677
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Cambridge mayor and commissioners spent a significant portion of their three-hour meeting Monday learning about Alpha Genesis Community Development Corporation's plans to revitalize the area surrounding the Harriet Tubman mural behind 424 Race St.Adrian Holmes, president and program director of Alpha Genesis, said the second phase project will help extend the stay of tourists in Cambridge.
"Right now, most people who go back there stay no longer than five or ten minutes because there's nowhere to sit, it's hot, it's just not really appealing," she said. "So this is what we want to do to help the people who come to the mural extend their stay. And when they extend their stay, they'll spend more money ... and they'll just have a better experience."
The plan, which extends into Cannery Way off Race Street, is to add two retail spaces adjacent the mural. One of the spaces will be a souvenir shop, Holmes said. The building itself will also include Alpha Genesis' headquarters, three other retail spaces that face Race Street and an exhibition deck.
In front of the mural will be the Harriet Tubman Pavilion, which will shield viewers from inclement weather. Near the pavilion, there will be a community garden.
"We affectionately call this project the North Star Village, a tribute in honor of Harriet Tubman," Holmes said.
Alpha Genesis has been working with the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development, the Maryland Historical Trust, the Rural Maryland Council, state legislators and the City of Cambridge to make enhancements to the space. Alpha Genesis is still raising funds for the second phase of the project, which will cost around $1.5 million. The project has received funding from the Maryland General Assembly and the city.
"And then we have a couple grant opportunities that can cover the rest of it," Holmes said.
According to council meeting documents, the proximity of Alpha Genesis' property to city property has made the project a "joint venture" between the two. One document from Alpha Genesis states the city will improve Cannery Way and the adjacent parking lot, and Alpha Genesis will focus on 428 through 432 Race St.
Alpha Genesis is asking the city for the installation of public restrooms, the repositioning of the brick wall on Cannery Way and the addition of a replica of the Ben Ross Cabin on the Cannery Way property.
Holmes said restrooms would benefit tourists who come from far distances to see the mural. Alpha Genesis' proposal is to construct a "North Star Station" that includes two all-gender bathrooms, a 135-square-foot public meeting room and a small lobby space with digital kiosks that have information about the city.
RESTROOM DISCUSSIONCommissioners asked a variety of questions about Alpha Genesis' plans. Multiple questions focused on the restroom proposal.
Commissioner Brian Roche shared his concern with the North Star Station blocking the view of the water from Cannery Way. Holmes said a possible change to the proposal could be to remove the meeting room from the station to make it smaller.
Commission President Sputty Cephas asked who would be responsible for maintaining the public restrooms. Alpha Genesis Executive Director Jermaine Anderson said he thinks it would be a good idea to form a youth or recidivism program where those in the program would be tasked with maintaining areas around the mural.
"Now's the time," he said. "Let's get real creative. Let's continue planning, continue talking, developing relationships. ... I think we can find the solutions we need."
During public comment, Chuck McFadden said he supports revitalizing the area, but the city should be careful about how much it commits. McFadden also cautioned that bringing youth in to clean the public restrooms might not be an easy feat.
After council discussion, the City Council unanimously voted to have city staff work closely with Alpha Genesis on its proposal and make sure it gets through the Historic Preservation Commission and the Planning and Zoning Commission. The vote, which Cephas motioned, also called for a presentation on the fiscal impact of the proposal and made sure Roche and any other interested commissioners can work with city staff on the matter.

 CAMBRIDGE — The Cambridge City Council unanimously voted to approve a property tax abatement for a property tucked between Peking House Restaurant and Advance Auto Parts on Ocean Gateway at a meeting on Oct. 7.During the council meeting, Assistant City Manager Brandon Hesson said this property, located at 2721 Ocean Gateway, is the site of an old gas station that hasn't been operational for more than a decade. "We do want to incentivize it, but we also want to incentivize it now," Hesson said.
After Hesson spoke, multiple commissioners said they were happy to see the abatement program used.
"That is prime real estate because it is right there on 50," Commission President Lajan Cephas said. "So thank you for using this resource."

title: Cambridge City Council Moves Toward Creating TIF Policy
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge City Council moves toward creating TIF policy

 August 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 512
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Cambridge City Council voted at a meeting on Aug. 26 to direct its attorney to prepare a resolution creating a tax increment financing, or TIF, policy.During the meeting, Acting City Manager David Deutsch recommended the council make this move. He brought up the Cambridge Harbor project, a project to develop Cambridge's waterfront. Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc., the group spearheading the project, has been looking into using tax incremented financing to help fund the project.
TIFs increase taxes in a certain area due to development. The increased tax revenues are used to pay for bonds, which have been issued for public improvement projects in that area.
CWDI's proposed TIF would cover the Cambridge Harbor development project area. The TIF would increase taxes on the property as it gets developed to pay for two $30 million bonds taken out by the city and county. According to a CWDI presentation at a Dorchester County Council meeting in December, the net tax increment from the TIF is expected to be around $10 million each for the city and county.
In March, CWDI Board President Angie Hengst said they had completed a seventh run of a TIF model and it looked "very stable."
At the council meeting on Aug. 26, Deutsch said that a TIF project is different from a general obligation bond issued from a municipality.
"This is a method of financing that is unique to a specific project," he said. "And in order to position the city to be able to seriously consider that, we need to have a policy document in place."
RECOMMENDATIONS FOR THE POLICYIn an Aug. 22 memo to the City Council, Deutsch pointed out parts of TIF policies used in other Maryland jurisdictions that he said were "worth noting." These include creating an application process, using an outside financial advisor, requiring analysis of a test that demonstrates whether there is a need for the TIF and requiring developers to pay for fees and expenses of the city's consultants.
In creating a report with recommendations, city staff looked at TIF policies in six jurisdictions in the state. According to the report, staff recommend that the city use Bowie's policy and application, adding select practices and language from Frederick and Howard counties.
Deutsch said that if a policy is approved by the Cambridge City Council, the city would be ready with an application process in the event that a developer requests a TIF.
"And then we can sit with them and make sure that all the various elements are proper and in place so that the folks on city staff and our advisors can advise mayor and council properly," he said.
Before the council voted unanimously to direct the city attorney to prepare a resolution creating a TIF policy, Mayor Stephen Rideout said he thought the policy was an excellent idea.
"I'm delighted that we're moving in that direction," he said. "Not only will it help the city and the commissioners, but it will help a developer understand what they're going to have to go through in terms of making the application and what they're going to have to produce."

title: Pinnacle Hospitality Group Hopes to Build Hotel on Cambridge Harbor
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Pinnacle Hospitality Group hopes to build hotel on Cambridge Harbor

 August 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 600

 CAMBRIDGE — Less than a week after the city and Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. settled a lawsuit regarding the ability to transfer certain land, members of the CWDI Board of Directors sat in the front row of an Aug. 26 Cambridge City Council meeting.With them: a hotel developer interested in building a hotel on Cambridge Harbor, the project led by CWDI to develop Cambridge's waterfront.
The first half of the meeting, the developer, Tauhid Islam, spoke about why he would like to build a hotel on Cambridge Harbor and what he would like that hotel to look like.
No deal has yet been made with Islam to develop on Cambridge Harbor. On Aug. 23, CWDI Board President Angie Hengst told the Star Democrat that CWDI will be working with the city and county to identify the appropriate time to sign a deal after "various details" have been worked through.
Islam, the founder of Eastern-Shore-based Pinnacle Hospitality Group who started his own venture in 2016 after spending two decades with Choice Hotels, has been in talks with CWDI for the past year. Islam said that in the past eight years, his group has built seven hotels, including a Cambria Hotel and a Hampton Inn & Suites, both in Ocean City.
Islam said in an oceanfront hotel room, when you turn off the lights, all you can see from the balcony at night is darkness. By contrast, in a hotel room "on the tip of the bridge," it's not just darkness, he said.
"The rumbling of the bridge, the beauty of the dolphins swimming by and the moon actually glistening on the water," he said. "That's what attracted me to Cambridge."
Islam sees this venture as an opportunity to embrace a working waterfront. He said it's an opportunity for the younger generations to learn about a "forgotten art."
"Things that our children and their children may not have the opportunity to see first hand," he said, mentioning boat repair. "I think Cambridge does bring that and it will resonate with people who are just trying to get away from the city. ... I want to create something that will make them stop."
Islam said his plans include a rooftop restaurant and a conference center. He said he wants to bring in a franchise that doesn't exist in Cambridge.
During the meeting, Islam and his team unveiled an initial rendering that shows the project concept. The rendering included balconies that overlook the Choptank River and a pool steps away from the river.
Maryland Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), who sat in the front row of the meeting along with two CWDI board members, acknowledged that this hotel would take a few years to build and open if a deal is made.
"But boy, we have a great vision, and I think this is a great restart of Cambridge Harbor," he said.
Over the past year, tensions between the city and CWDI over the Cambridge Harbor project have received significant attention. With the lawsuit settlement — which includes both parties entering into a memorandum of understanding to address certain issues — representatives from both the city and CWDI Board have expressed hope about their relationship moving forward.
At the meeting, multiple City Council members thanked Islam for the presentation and shared their excitement for his approach to the project.
"There's an old adage that says a home without a heart is nothing but walls, roof and floor," Commissioner Laurel Atkiss said. "And its nice to hear you speak of the buildings, that they have heart in them as well. I think that's something we definitely want to have moving forward in our projects in Cambridge."

title: Housing Secretary Jake Day Tours Dorchester County, Talks with Local Officials
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Housing Secretary Jake Day tours Dorchester County, talks with local officials

 April 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 751
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Cambridge — Kicking the day off riverside at the Dorchester County Visitor Center, Maryland Secretary of Housing and Community Development Jake Day, along with members of his staff, spent Wednesday touring Dorchester County.Day and his team visited the Cambridge Harbor site, Pine Street Community Market and Wells Street in Cambridge before traveling to East New Market to visit the Trading Post Museum. The tour ended in Hurlock at Suicide Bridge Restaurant for lunch and a stakeholder discussion led by Day and Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer.
The tour and discussion gave Day and his department a chance to hear from county and municipal leaders about what is needed, get updates on state-sponsored housing and development projects underway and visit completed projects in the county.
Dorchester County hosted the tour, with Pfeffer, County Council Vice President Mike Detmer, interim County Manager Jeff Powell and other county employees attending.
A variety of local elected officials attended, including Cambridge Mayor Stephen Rideout, Cambridge Commission President Lajan Cephas, East New Market Mayor Stephen Tolley, Hurlock Mayor the Rev. Charles Cephas Sr., Hurlock Town Council President Earl Murphy Jr. and Church Creek Mayor Karen Tolley.
At the state level, Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) were present for parts of the tour.
In an interview after the tour, Day said the participation from different parts of the county indicate there are good relationships and good communication.
"And not just with DHCD or our administration, but among the local officials here," he said
During the stakeholder discussion, Powell and county Planning and Zoning Director Susan Webb gave a presentation on the projected loss of land in the county to sea level rise by the year 2100 and the need for developing infrastructure in the area that connects Cambridge to Hurlock.
Municipal representatives spoke about redlining, the need for investment in North Dorchester and housing needs.
Day talked about three bills — the Housing Expansion and Affordability Act, the Housing and Community Development Financing Act and the Renters' Rights and Stabilization Act — passed in the General Assembly this session. These measures, he said, aim to increase and incentivize development, invest in low-income communities, bring down the state eviction rate and offer more protections to renters.
In an interview after the tour, Day said he was most surprised by the level of local interest in growth. He mentioned Hurlock's mayor, the Rev. Charles Cephas Sr., starting a round of applause in response to Day explaining the Housing Expansion and Affordability Act, which will, in part, reduce "regulatory obstacles" at the local level that can slow down development.
"I think that's really telling that this community wants to grow," Day said.
THE TOUR
On the first leg of the tour, Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. Executive Director Matt Leonard talked about Cambridge Harbor. After the presentation, he led the group around the project site. The goal of the project is to develop space along the Cambridge waterfront.
In response to Leonard's presentation, Day said it would be nice to see a complete assessment of the sources and uses for project costs for both the first and second phase of the project. He said it would be good to see the full picture.
Next, the group visited Pine Street Community Market, which owner Eddie Beasley opened a little over a month ago. The Department of Housing and Community Development helped fund the creation of the market.
The tour group walked around the corner from the market to see the homes being constructed by Habitat for Humanity Choptank on Wells Street. Community Development Block Grant funding, through Day's department, is going toward sidewalks and utilities on the block, Day said.
At the end of the block, city of Cambridge employees talked about the city's efforts to revitalize the area. City Planner Holly Baldwin said they expect the 12 homes on Wells Street to be completed by the end of the year. Talking with Day, Baldwin said investing in the historic Pine Street neighborhood isn't just about dollars and cents, it's about making sure residents know public spaces like Cornish Park are for them.
"The community owns this," she said.
At the Trading Post Museum, East New Market Mayor Stephen Tolley talked about the importance of the museum and shared some history about the town.
After lunch and the stakeholder discussion, Pfeffer thanked Day and his staff for coming to visit to see what the county is dealing with and hearing about the county's challenges.
"We're not coming here trying to whine and complain about it," he said. "We just need you to understand."

title: City Council Discusses Cambridge Harbor TIF, CWDI Articles in Closed Session Meeting
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
City Council discusses Cambridge Harbor TIF, CWDI articles in closed session meeting

 April 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 1067
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Following a Cambridge City Council closed session meeting Monday, April 22, Mayor Stephen Rideout publicly shared three decisions made behind closed Council Chambers doors that evening relating to Cambridge Harbor and Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc.TAX INCREMENT FINANCING
For one, the council has determined that it is a "worthwhile undertaking" to look at establishing a policy or an ordinance on how the city should deal with tax increment financing, commonly called TIFs.
TIFs increase taxes in a certain area. The tax revenues from that increase are used to pay for bonds, which have been issued for public improvement projects in that area.
CWDI has proposed a TIF for its Cambridge Harbor project — a project to develop the space along the Cambridge waterfront — that would increase taxes on the property as it gets developed to pay for two $30-million bonds taken out by the city and county.
In October, the city expressed its concerns with the proposed TIF in a letter to CWDI Executive Director Matt Leonard. It said the council had concerns that the TIF would take too much tax revenue from too large of an area for too long, and the city and county would not receive a "meaningful" tax revenue benefit for decades.
After the council returned to open session April 22, Rideout said that pending getting information about sample policy and getting advice from counsel, "the city will not be moving forward with any consideration of TIFs or a TIF program."
ARTICLES OF INCORPORATION
The second decision Rideout shared is that he will hold off on amending the CWDI Articles of Incorporation until after the CWDI Board of Directors has had it's next meeting on May 22.
Rideout said that council had a discussion on this in closed session and that he requested direction from the commissioners. He said the commissioners voted in favor of holding off on amending the articles, with Commissioner Brian Roche abstaining.
Last week, the Star Democrat reported that Roche's brother-in-law, Mike LeMire, is an attorney with Miles and Stockbridge, a law firm that represents CWDI. In an interview April 19, Roche said he has followed protocol with this potential conflict of interest, including asking for an opinion from the Cambridge Ethics Commission.
April 16, Rideout held a meeting where he proposed amendments to the Articles of Incorporation. At that meeting, Rideout said he thought the amendments would make it more likely that the project is successful. He said he would make a decision in the 10 days following.
Rideout said CWDI has indicated its Board of Directors will discuss the proposed amendments at its May 22 meeting. He said he will hold off on amending the articles to give the board time for comment.
As mayor, Rideout is the sole member of CWDI. Similar to the a shareholder of a company, under Maryland law, a non-profit can have a member or members that represent the group which founded the nonprofit, Rideout said in an interview. As sole member of CWDI, Rideout said he has the authority to make amendments to the articles.
Before the City Council went into closed session Monday, both Commission President Lajan Cephas and Commissioner Sputty Cephas commended Rideout for holding the meeting April 16.
Sputty Cephas offered his support to Rideout.
"We're in support of development," he said about the CWDI project. "It's just how we get it done."
MEETING WITH HUTCHINSON
The third piece of information Rideout shared after the closed session was that he and Commissioner Laurel Atkiss would be meeting with Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), CWDI board President Angie Hengst and CWDI Board Secretary-Treasurer Frank Narr on Tuesday, April 23.
Rideout said he told the council during closed session that he and Atkiss had been invited to meet with the others to discuss the challenges with collaboration on the Cambridge Harbor project. Rideout said he and Atkiss will report back to council with any information worth sharing.
TRANSFER AGREEMENT
Before the City Council went into closed session Monday, Roche said he wanted to make it clear that he supports the sale by CWDI of the Yacht Maintenance Company parcel and the prospect of a hotel being built on the Cambridge Harbor site.
Both of these properties were discussed in an April 12 memo to City Council from City Manager Tom Carroll.
According to council meeting documents, in his memo, Carroll said he recently learned that CWDI is in breach of the covenants of a March 2022 property transfer agreement between the city and CWDI.
In the memo, Carroll said the city conveyed approximately 10 acres of property to CWDI in the agreement. He said CWDI was supposed to issue a request for proposal, select a developer or developers and make a public summary of the request for proposal, per the covenants of the agreement. He said CWDI didn't do any of those things.
Carroll said that under the transfer agreement, CWDI can't transfer property the city has conveyed to it until all the covenants are fulfilled.
This means CWDI would not have the legal grounds to transfer the Yacht Maintenance property to Yacht Maintenance, a Cambridge company that offers boat and yacht services, or the land for the construction of a boutique hotel.
At a CWDI Board of Directors meeting March 20, Narr said CWDI plans to sell the Yacht Maintenance property to Yacht Maintenance this year. At the same meeting, Hengst said CWDI is making progress on its agreement with a boutique hotel developer to build on the Cambridge Harbor site, and she hopes the signing of the agreement is imminent.
At the City Council meeting Monday, Roche said the transfer of the Yacht Maintenance property is important so that Yacht Maintenance can invest in and install an 850-pound boat lift.
"This is a comparative economic advantage unique to Yacht Maintenance and the city of Cambridge," he said. "It is also a fundamental step in expanding the education and employment opportunities alongside the Richardson boat works facility for our citizens."
Roche said he supports CWDI's efforts to bring a hotel to Cambridge's waterfront.
"And although some members of this council and our outgoing city manager have made it known that there are other aspects of CWDI that they want to continue to discuss, that is fine," he said. "But I do think it's the obligation of every commissioner here tonight to make it abundantly clear that we will support and take whatever steps are necessary for the expansion of Yacht Maintenance and the prospect of a hotel being built at the site on the waterfront."

title: CWDI Holds Community Update Meeting, Answers Some Questions
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
CWDI holds community update meeting, answers some questions

 April 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 1272
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Cambridge residents packed the Chesapeake Grove Intergenerational Center Thursday night to hear from the Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. Board of Directors, its executive director and project partners.At the community update meeting, CWDI representatives talked about various aspects of the Cambridge Harbor — a project to develop the space along the Cambridge waterfront — before launching into a question-and-answer segment.
Resident Lauren Mross called CWDI's presentation "polished."
"I felt like they had many of the right answers," she said. "But I don't feel that they paid attention to the actual questions."
CWDI has been a major topic of conversation in the city recently.
On March 18, Cambridge City Manager Tom Carroll submitted his resignation and said he was resigning over concerns with the Cambridge Harbor project. Two days later, residents lined the conference room of the Dorchester Chamber of Commerce for a CWDI Board of Directors meeting, where multiple residents asked questions and voiced concerns during public comment.
Two days before the community update meeting Thursday, Cambridge Mayor Stephen Rideout held a meeting where he proposed amendments to CWDI's Articles of Incorporation. As mayor, Rideout has the authority to make amendments to the articles, according to provisions in the articles themselves.
After the community update Thursday, Mross said she is excited and optimistic about the idea of the project but has concerns with the transparency of it. She called Carroll's resignation disappointing.
"I also thoroughly respect Steve Rideout," she said. "I trust his opinion on what's going on, and I want his transparent involvement in the project."
Before answering questions submitted for the event, CWDI addressed various parts of the project, including the plans for the project's first and second phases, funding and proposed tax increment financing, or TIF.
The TIF would increase taxes on the property as it gets developed to pay for two $30-million bonds taken out by the city and county.
Much of the presentation included information that has already been made available to the public through CWDI reports and previous presentations.
Dorchester Chamber of Commerce President Bill Christopher, who led the question-and-answer portion of the event, said 65 questions —including repeats — were submitted by 20 different people. He said most of the questions fell into two categories: the YMCA and the Board of Directors. Christopher read nearly 20 questions Thursday.
YMCAThe first question Christopher read was about the current status of the YMCA and why CWDI would consider putting a nonprofit on the waterfront.
Many residents have expressed concerns about the possibility of Cambridge's YMCA, currently located at 201 Talbot Ave., moving to Cambridge Harbor. In late August, CWDI included a design for a new YMCA facility in its 2023 mid-year report.
At the meeting Thursday, CWDI Executive Director Matt Leonard said CWDI is not negotiating with the YMCA at the moment. He said the YMCA came to CWDI with an expression of interest that CWDI put out two years ago.
"They submitted to us what they would like to do and why they would like to do it," Leonard said. "We reviewed them like we did every other potential government partner or investor."
YMCA of the Chesapeake CEO Robbie Gill, who was at the community update Thursday, said in an interview after the meeting that he was at the event to learn, and there were no new developments with the Cambridge YMCA.
When asked what would happen if the YMCA did move locations, Leonard said he thought it should become residential to match the rest of the neighborhood. He said that is something CWDI could help with if it "needs to be done."
Part-time Cambridge resident Steven Van Dorpe said the clarification that CWDI was not negotiating with the YMCA was "interesting."
"But it seemed like it was still a little bit vague as to whether or not they could come back into the equation," he said.
BOARD APPOINTMENTSAnother question asked at the meeting was whether the CWDI Board of Directors is responsive to the bodies that appoint them.
The seven-member board is made up of one governor-appointed member, two county-appointed members, three city-appointed members and one CWDI-appointed member. Currently, one of the county-appointed seats is vacant.
Board President Angie Hengst said part of a board member's job is to relay information to their appointing body, but their main responsibility is to CWDI and its mission. She said she hopes the appointing bodies have chosen representatives that they have full confidence in.
"At the end of the day, we are the board members of CWDI, and that's (who) we're really beholden to for any decisions that we're making," she said.
Board Vice President Shay Lewis-Sisco said she is responsive to her appointing body, the city. She said she has been in constant communication with the city manager and Cambridge City Council and called it "unfortunate" that press has gone out that does not make that clear.
Carroll, Cambridge's city manager, said in an interview that he has had a couple meetings with Lewis-Sisco, but she hasn't listened to his suggestions, which include making sure the project benefits Cambridge's workforce and its disadvantaged community.
CONFLICTS OF INTERESTAnother question brought up at the meeting had to do with Cambridge City Council Commissioner Brian Roche's connection to an attorney at a law firm that represents CWDI.
The question asked about a lack of disclosure regarding a council member and his brother-in-law, an attorney for one the law firms representing CWDI.
Leonard said CWDI uses three different law firms, including Miles and Stockbridge. He said he believes that "one of the hundred or so" Miles and Stockbridge attorneys "may be related to one of the City Council members."
Leonard said it was not a conflict of interest and quickly moved on to talk about what one of the other law firms CWDI uses has provided.
In an interview Friday, Roche confirmed that his brother-in-law, Mike LeMire, is an attorney with Miles and Stockbridge.
Roche said that when he learned of the potential conflict of interest, he reached out to City Attorney Patrick Thomas.
"There's been no votes or anything that would be, according to (Thomas), a conflict," Roche said. "But I was very careful. I take that allegation very, very seriously."
Roche said he has followed protocol with this, including getting an opinion from the Cambridge Ethics Commission to determine if it is a conflict of interest. He said the Ethics Commission has called and asked him questions, but he has not received a statement from them.
Roche said the City Council is aware of this potential conflict of interest.
LeMire did not immediately answer phone calls for comment.
ARTICLES OF INCORPORATIONRegarding Rideout's proposed amendments to CWDI's Articles of Incorporation, Leonard said CWDI appreciates when a concerned person comes forward with ideas to help the project.
Leonard said the CWDI Board of Directors will look at Rideout's suggestions at its meeting on May 22 to determine whether the amendments are necessary for improving CWDI and accelerating its mission.
At the meeting where Rideout proposed the amendments on April 16, Rideout said he would convene another meeting in the next 10 days to make his final decision on the amendments.
In an interview, Carroll said Leonard's comments at the community update indicate the board won't comment before Rideout convenes another meeting on the subject.
"So we will have no feedback on them," Carroll said about the amendments. "So it will be up to the mayor to decide what he does."
Overall, Carroll said the questions that needed to be answered by CWDI at the community update weren't. He said the city's fundamental questions still remain unanswered.
"I didn't learn anything that I didn't already know," he said.
Van Dorpe said he thought the questions were answered well. He said CWDI should have done more of these events in the past.
"Just kind of be open and direct," he said. "It's always about communication."

title: County Council Sends Letter of Support for H-2B Visa Cap Exemption
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
County Council sends letter of support for H-2B visa cap exemption

 April 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 250
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Dorchester County Council is sending a letter of support for a United States Senate bill that would exempt seafood processors from the numerical limit on H-2B nonimmigrant visas.At a regular meeting April 2, the County Council voted unanimously to send the letter of support.
According to the U.S. Department of Labor, the H-2B program allows employers in the United States to temporarily hire nonimmigrants for nonagricultural labor or services.
Currently, there is a cap on how many H-2B visas can be issued every year. According to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security Citizenship and Immigration Services, the cap is currently 66,000 H-2B visas per fiscal year.
If Senate Bill 3013 is passed, seafood processors would be exempt from this cap.
County Council Vice President Mike Detmer said at the meeting that it is important to emphasize in the letter the "huge impact" that the limit on H-2B visas issued has on crab picking houses in the county every year.
"Especially in the southern part of our county where everybody is working on the water or adjacent to them," he said.
Detmer said the letter should include the number of workers needed in the county to open all the local picking houses, "and maintain our heritage and our economic development." He said this number is a small one "compared to a larger pool."
Council President Lenny Pfeffer agreed and said that county staff could contact the Dorchester Seafood Heritage Association for those numbers.
"We can have good factual information put in our letter," he said.

title: CWDI Board Talks Finances, Hotel Deal at Board Meeting
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
CWDI Board talks finances, hotel deal at board meeting

 March 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 742
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Cambridge — Cambridge residents lined the conference room of at the Dorchester Chamber of Commerce for a Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. Board of Directors meeting Wednesday, March 20.The board addressed a variety of topics related to Cambridge Harbor — a project that will create public spaces like a promenade and parks, a boutique hotel that has a restaurant and bar, and residential and mixed-use spaces along the Choptank River — before entering into closed session.
HOTEL DEAL
Board President Angie Hengst said CWDI is making progress on its agreement with a boutique hotel developer and hopes the signing of the agreement is imminent.
"There's just a little bit of back and forth with some final legalese with our lawyers," she said.
CWDI Executive Director Matt Leonard said the board would meet with lawyers in the closed session portion of the meeting.
2023 AUDIT
Board Secretary-Treasurer Frank Narr said the 2023 audit is currently underway. He gave a preview of what that report will look like when it is presented at the May board meeting.
Narr said CWDI has two separate entities when it comes to finances: CWDI Holdings, which is for real estate, and an operating entity.
In 2023, CWDI Holdings received a grant income of more than $2 million, Narr said. This income went toward pre-development costs including professional, design and consulting fees, he said.
CWDI Holdings had a net income of around $817,000, which Narr said is the cost of the Richardson Maritime Museum property that CWDI purchased in early 2023.
Narr said a lot of the operating entity's revenue for 2023 came through public sources, including a commitment from former Gov. Larry Hogan's administration and City of Cambridge American Rescue Plan Act funds. He said revenue also came through property leases and docking fees.
The operating entity had a net income of $24,000 in 2023. Narr said this would have been higher if CWDI had sold the Yacht Maintenance property to Yacht Maintenance, which it expected to do in 2023. He said CWDI now expects that sale to occur this year.
Narr said that other than an increase in legal fees "due to a couple issues we had to deal with here locally," costs to the operating entity stayed in line with what CWDI expected.
TAX INCREMENT FINANCING
Hengst said the Cambridge Harbor tax increment financing model looks "very stable," as a seventh run of the model was recently completed.
TIFs increase taxes in a certain area due to development. The increased tax revenues are used to pay for bonds, which have been issued for public improvement projects in that area. CWDI's tax increment financing would cover the Cambridge Harbor development project area.
According to a CWDI presentation at a Dorchester County Council meeting in December, the net tax increment from the TIF is expected to be around $10 million each for the city and county.
"We continue to try to work with the city and the county to provide them all the information that we can on the TIF and to hold public meetings with them," Leonard said at the board meeting Wednesday. "We did have a couple with the county already. We're waiting for the city to agree to do that with us so we can move it forward."
OTHER NOTES
During public comment, some residents said they were unhappy with the look of the fence currently at Cambridge Harbor. Cathy Hanson called the fence "unsightly and industrial looking."
According to the meeting agenda, the board discussed government relations in closed session. This came just days after Cambridge City Manager Tom Carroll submitted his resignation. Carroll said he resigned over concerns with the Cambridge Harbor project.
Hengst said the board is still in need of one county-appointed member and is waiting for the county to put out a request for interest.
Hengst said CWDI is waiting for final approval on the plans for the promenade extension at Cambridge Harbor. CWDI expects to bid the project before May so it can break ground in July.
CWDI agreed to having the Girls on the Run 5K take place on its property on May 4. Leonard said 85 boards on the boardwalk were replaced to make it safe for the event.
The Rotary Club of Cambridge will place 40 to 50 flags on the Cambridge Harbor property for Memorial Day.
CWDI is planning a public update meeting where people can attend in person or virtually to get a detailed update with what is going on at Cambridge Harbor. Leonard said they plan to hold the meeting sometime in the second quarter of the year.

title: Cambridge Council Not in Support of Harbor Project Plan
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge Council not in support of harbor project plan

 October 26, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 690
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - In a letter addressed to Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. Executive Director Matt Leonard, the city of Cambridge expressed City Council's concerns with the Cambridge Harbor project.The letter, signed by City Manager Tom Carroll, states that City Council does not support CWDI's current plans for Cambridge Harbor.In late August, CWDI, a private nonprofit, released a 2023 mid-year report to the community that detailed what the group has done so far and what it plans to do moving forward. The Cambridge Harbor project will include creating public spaces like a promenade and parks, a boutique hotel that has a restaurant and bar, and residential and mixed-use spaces.In an interview in September, Leonard said the goal is for the entire project to be complete in somewhere between five and 10 years from now. By 2025, CWDI expects it will no longer need public funds to operate Cambridge Harbor.The letter from the city gives four reasons for the council's lack of support for the project. First, the council thinks CWDI seems like it wants to be the site developer instead of hiring a "capable master developer." "The redevelopment of a site of this size and complexity requires a private sector development partner with a proven track record of success in similar projects," the letter says.The second reason cited is that the proposal for the project "does not generate enough economic value" for developing the project without "an unacceptably large public subsidy."The third reason is that the proposed tax increment finance district will take too much tax revenue from too large of an area for too long, and the city and county would not receive a "meaningful" tax revenue benefit for decades."The city and county need to be involved in shaping these public financing plans from the start," the letter says.The fourth reason for the lack of Council support is that the council does not approve of the governance of CWDI. The letter states that CWDI is not being transparent, accountable or responsive to the Council.In a September interview, Carroll said that communication between CWDI and the city has not been enough. He said that, having spent 27 years in local governments and having been a part of two major economic development projects, he has concerns about the financial feasibility of CWDI's plan.In an interview Wednesday, Leonard said he was shocked by the letter. He said CWDI met with the city back in S eptember to discuss the project and got "relatively positive feedback."Leonard recognized that not all Council members agreed with every aspect of the project, but he said they seemed generally OK with it.While Leonard said he and the CWDI board take the concerns of all stakeholders very seriously, he said they do not share concerns with the city for the direction of the Cambridge Harbor project."Our direction has come from community input over the last three decades," he said. "We have accounted for the community development aspects ofwhat the community says they want and the economic development aspects ofwhat we believe will be valuable to the city and the county, and the state and the community, of course, at large."Leonard said CWDI is concerned about its relationship with the city, however."That means a lot to us," he said. "And we've tried, and continue to try to make that relationship positive and productive."Moving forward, Leonard hopes to address the city's concerns during a meeting scheduled for Nov. 13. Leonard said CWDI has issued invitations to all of its stakeholders and development team members to discuss some of the more confidential development matters of the project."We hope that members of the City Council and leadership of the city staff will attend the meeting so we can address, in essence, a number of the issues that they raised in the rest of their letter," he said.In the letter, it says that the City Council thinks the Nov. 13 meeting is premature and the City Council will be reaching out to Dorchester County Council to talk about how to get the project "back on track."

title: Body Cam Video Released of Cambridge Officer-Involved Shooting
author: Staff Report
content:
Body cam video released of Cambridge officer-involved shooting

 October 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Dorchester 
 
 455
 Words 

 Read News Document

 BALTIMORE — A man who was shot and killed by a Cambridge police officer asked the officer to shoot him as he charged the officer with a knife.On Thursday evening, the Maryland Office of the Attorney General released the body-worn camera footage from the fatal officer-involved shooting that occurred Sept. 4 in Cambridge.
The preliminary investigation released in the days following the incident revealed Jacob Weber, a corporal from the Cambridge Police Department, fatally shot 30-year-old Ryan Garcy of Cambridge after Garcy charged at Weber with a knife.
The nine-minute video released by the attorney general's office includes footage from the body-worn cameras of three police officers — Weber and two officers identified only as "witness officer from the Cambridge Police Department."
The footage shows an exchange between Weber and Garcy that lasted under a minute.
During the interaction, Weber repeatedly tells Garcy to drop the knife he is holding and to stay back. Garcy, who was naked, can be seen slowly approaching Weber's police vehicle before pausing and asking Weber, "Will you just f------ shoot me?"
Garcy can then be seen rapidly approaching Weber. Weber is seen deploying a Taser, which is ineffective, then running from Garcy before firing five shots in Garcy's direction.
"I can say that I'm very proud of the officer that, from what I see, with all his training and knowledge of the job, he did what he, unfortunately, had to do to survive, and that's about all I can say about that for now," Cambridge Police Chief Justin Todd said Friday.
Garcy was transported by Maryland State Police Aviation to Tidal Health Peninsula Regional Medical Center in Salisbury, where he later died.
Weber, who has been with the police department for six years, has been placed on paid administrative leave until the investigation by the attorney general's office is finished, Todd said.
According to Todd, this is Cambridge's first fatal police shooting in about 15 years.
"I can say my condolences for the family of Mr. Garcy having to go through that and have that video out there. I can't imagine the pain and heartache," Todd said. "Mental health is a real problem."
Todd said he has been in contact with Garcy's family via email since the incident and considers the experience traumatic for both the family and the officers involved.
"We all sign up to do this job, and yes, we know it can come to that, but I don't think anyone can speak for it until you actually have been through something like that," Todd said.
Todd does not know when the investigation from the independent investigations division will conclude, but he said the investigators have been in touch and have been great to work with.
This article was updated to add comments from Cambridge Police Chief Justin Todd.

title: Serving, Protecting for 250 Years - The Caroline County Sheriff's Office Celebrates Its Sesquicentennial
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
Serving, protecting for 250 years - The Caroline County Sheriff's Office celebrates its sesquicentennial

 November 15, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 1A | Section: News 
 
 979
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - To mark the 250th anniversary of the Caroline County Sheriff's Office, a new badge has been struck, containing symbols of its history dating to colonial Maryland.But the badge itself is a symbol of the long line of sheriffs who have held the office since 1773, when Thomas Hughlett of Greensboro was appointed by the British governor after the county was formed from parts of Dorchester and Queen Anne's counties.Bookending the long blue line is Sheriff Donnie Baker, who, like Hughlett, is also a Greensboro native. He's the county's 77th sheriff.Caroline County Deputy Lt. Jacob Andrew is the unofficial historian of the sheriff's office. And because he's the fifth generation of the Andrew family to serve the office during the past century, he's well-qualified for the job."Jake was just teaching me something," Baker said. "I didn't know that the first sheriff was buried up there (in Greensboro)." According to Andrew's research, Hughlett was a plantation owner appointed to a one-year term by the governor to be in charge of weights and scales because he was deemed trustworthy.Ironically, the next year he became captain of the Caroline County Militia Fifth Company, which encompassed Greensboro, Goldsboro and Bridgetown during the American Revolution.Hughlett later became a judge. He is buried in a crypt in a tiny, privately-owned graveyard in a Greensboro subdivision, the site of the Hughlett family farm.During the Civil War, John Wilson Saulsbury served a two-year term from 1861 to 1863 and was required to swear allegiance to the Union.Andrew said Sheriff James Temple, who served from 1923 to 1926 "was actually a pretty cool guy." A veteran of the Spanish-American War, Temple was known as the walking sheriff."He had the first Buick in Caroline County. He always told everybody that," Andrew said. However, "he hated driving it.So, if he had to go serve a warrant on somebody, he'd walk from Denton to Ridgely, lock them up and walk them back." "The original sheriff's office was pretty much a shed on the courthouse green, and it was very easy to break out of," Andrew said. The lynching on the green of Federalsburg blacksmith Marshall Price following accusations of murder in 1895 prompted the government to build a new jail across Gay Street on the Choptank River, where it stands today.In 1921, William Curtis Andrew, Jacob Andrew's great-great grandfather, became sheriff and served a two-year term. His son, William E. Andrew served from 1938 to 1946 and, following a four-year term by Saulsbury Sparks, served again from 1950 to 1961, dying of a heart attack in his office.William's son Louis C. Andrew served from 1961 to 1994, retiring when he was 70. His son, then-Deputy Charles Andrew, served as acting sheriff until Phil Brown was elected sheriff the following year.Back then, the sheriff and his family lived in the center section of what is now the Caroline County jail. Two wings were added to the large brick structure, but Charles Andrew remembers when the original section was home."I got to know a lot of inmates," he said.He recalls the night his "mother had a fit" when a naked woman was brought in by the state police."They had to come in the front door and walk down the hall which separated the living room and dining room directly back to that one-room office" at the back of the house, he said."I would have been seven or eight" years old, Charles Andrew said. "So, she made my father go to the commissioners, and that's when they put stairs on the side of the building to come in the outside door." "Back then, when my father started, he was only making $2,600 a year," he said. "They had to supply their own vehicle. The only thing the county gave them was a radio that went into their own private car." That center section of the current jail is called the Andrew Building today.Until 1994, both the sheriff's office and jail were under the jurisdiction of the sheriff, according to Charles Andrew. When Brown became sheriff, the county Department of Corrections was formed as a separate agency, and Charles Andrew served as the superintendent for 13 years, after serving in the sheriff's office for 20 years.Charles's son Jacob, now the fifth generation to serve in the sheriff's office, serves the county with almost 50 fellow deputies. After serving in the Air Force, Jacob Andrew joined the sheriff's office and has been on the job for 19 years. "I love it. I love my job," he said.The commemorative badge symbolizes not only his family's history of serving county citizens in the sheriff's office, but a long legacy of the office's commitment to public safety stretching back to the nation's founding.At the five points of the badge's star are a Revolutionary War soldier, the Caroline County Circuit Court building, the original courthouse before the renovations, the original sheriff's office on Gay Street, and the current office, completed in 2021 on Double Hills Road."One of the things that former Sheriff Randy Bounds wanted to do was have a wall of sheriff's (pictures)," Baker said."So I told him that Jake is going to fulfill that dream of his." The sheriff's office is seeking memorabilia from the public for a future museum or showcase. If you have any artifacts, photos or clippings you'd like to share, contact Lt. Jacob Andrew at 410-479-4124 or jandrew@carolinemd.org.

title: '25 Kids Should Not Take This Whole City Down' - Cambridge Council Grapples with Youth Crime in City
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
'25 kids should not take this whole city down' - Cambridge council grapples with youth crime in city

 September 14, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 610
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - Youth issues were the overwhelming theme for the third Cambridge City Council meeting in a row.At the Sept. 12 meeting, residents and commissioners alike made comments about juvenile crime.Lance Cephas, who is the father of Commission President Lajan Cephas and Commissioner Sputty Cephas, said crime is affecting everyone, including the children and families who aren't part of the problem.He further noted the children who aren't contributing to juvenile crime are being punished for the actions of about 25 children, "25 kids should not take this whole city down," he said.Lance Cephas stressed the importance of educating the kids that are caught doing things they shouldn't be."Because if you send them back home to that same environment, ain't nothing going to happen," he said. "A lot of police officers, they'll pick them up, they'll let them go, and soon as they're around the corner, they've done something else to somebody else. So you've got to get them and educate them." He said he understood both his children's, Lajan and Sputty, and Mayor Stephen Rideout's points of view regarding the juvenile curfew but said the council shouldn't be "at each other's throats" and "controlled by 25 kids." "We've all got to come together," he said.In late August, Rideout vetoed a juvenile curfew ordinance which commissioners had passed Aug. 14.Before that, in July, Rideout had proposed an alternative curfew ordinance which had additions and changes from the original curfew ordinance. These included adding definitions and altering language on enforcement procedures and penalties.Since Rideout vetoed the original curfew ordinance, Sputty Cephas has made amendments to Rideout's alternative ordinance in an effort to compromise and "find middle ground." According to council meeting documents, Cephas plans to recommend these amendments Sept. 25 when Rideout's proposed ordinance will be read for a second time.During the meeting, Sputty Cephas talked about finding that middle ground."Commissioner Atkiss made a point to say that $100 is a lot of money for a struggling parent," he said."My day job is in banking, so I understand that struggle as well." Sputty Cephas said he would like to keep fines as part of the penalty for not following the curfew, but said he cut them in half in his amendment. Instead of a $100 fine, it would be $50.At the end of the meeting, Rideout suggested to Sputty Cephas that the two of them get together to talk about the proposed amendments to the alternative ordinance. Sputty Cephas agreed to meet.Two presentations were given during Monday's meeting, as well. One presentation was given by Pam Gregory, president and CEO of United Way of the Lower Eastern Shore, and one by Lisa Molock, chief executive director at Let's Thrive Baltimore and an organizer for Moms Demand Action for Gun Sense in America.Molock talked about the work she has been doing in Baltimore, and Gregory talked about the economic issues that many Marylanders face. She shared data from a report that focused on asset limited, income constrained and employed (or ALICE) Marylanders and shared data on Dorchester County residents specifically. Gregory said that in Dorchester County, 45% of residents are below the ALICE threshold.During public comment, Theresa Stafford said poverty is a "lead driver" for many other issues in Cambridge."We need to get serious about fixing the problem of poverty," Stafford said."Bringing in industries or businesses that will pay good wages, and of course, supporting getting kids educated because that's the other key driver that keeps driving up the crime."

title: State's Attorney's Office Investigating Dorchester Employees After Viral Video
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
State's Attorney's Office investigating Dorchester employees after viral video

 March 27, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 517
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Dorchester County State's Attorney's Office is investigating a complaint made against multiple Dorchester County employees to the Dorchester County Council's office March 20.According to a news release from Dorchester County, the complaint was filed March 20 about an incident that occurred earlier that day at the Dorchester County Department of Corrections. The news release states the council's office immediately contacted the State's Attorney's Office so that it could determine whether a criminal investigation is "warranted."
The incident was filmed and posted on YouTube by the user Long Island Audit. In the video, entitled "Unhinged Jail Warden ATTACKS Journalist For Recording! Sheriff REFUSES To Take Criminal Complaint!" Dorchester County Warden Don Satterfield appears to push the person who is filming.
The person filming, who identified himself as independent journalist Sean Reyes, says in the video that he is at the Dorchester County Department of Corrections "to peacefully exercise our first amendment right to film public and publicly accessible areas to promote transparency and accountability within our government and to ensure that our public servants recognize our rights and treat us with respect."
According to his YouTube channel, Reyes conducts and films First Amendment audits.
First Amendment auditors are people, typically private citizens, who film encounters with public employees and officials, according to the Local Government Insurance Trust. Oftentimes, the auditors enter public property and ask questions while filming.
In the video, Satterfield, who is seen with other county employees, tells Reyes that under Maryland law, phones are prohibited in detention centers. In the video, Reyes is told multiple times by different correctional employees that he cannot have his phone inside the building.
When Satterfield tells Reyes to get out of the building, Reyes replies, "Do not touch me, sir."
Satterfield then says, "I said get out of the building," and appears to push Reyes.
In another scene of the video, Reyes says, "I got assaulted by the warden of the correctional facility."
Later in the video, Reyes is seen trying to file a complaint with the Dorchester County Sheriff's Office. The Sheriff's Office directs him to file the complaint with Dorchester County Manager Jerry Jones.
In an interview Wednesday, Jones told The Star Democrat the county has been receiving calls from all over the country regarding the matter.
The practice of First Amendment auditing is something that occurs across the United States.
Easton Deputy Police Chief Capt. Greg Wright said that in February 2022, Easton officers were given information and discussed best practices when it comes to speaking with First Amendment auditors. Wright said First Amendment auditors try to "push the envelope" and have a goal of catching someone that knows less than them. He said it is the job of police officers to understand the law.
"You don't want to take action when you shouldn't have or not take action when you should have," he said.
Regarding the complaint filed in Dorchester County, Jones said he could not comment further on the matter because an active investigation is underway.
Dorchester County State's Attorney Amanda Leonard, who confirmed the matter is under investigation, said she could not comment on the matter either.
Satterfield and Reyes did not respond for comment.
